title: The 5 Biggest Disappointments For The Ravens So Far
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens have played one of the easiest scheduled in the NFL, but that’s about to change.
They are going to need more consistent performances from all three phases of this football team if they are going to challenge for a Super Bowl. The first third of the season is complete, the time for growing pains and working out the kinks with a rookie coaching staff is over and they are about to be tested at a much higher level.
Oh, and it seems far certain that two-time MVP Lamar Jackson, who the highly-suspect general manager cant get signed to contract extension like everyone else with a top QB does, might not be back for Sunday's against the Bengals in another big divisional game. If that’s the case, then the individuals on this list of biggest disappointments so far are going to need to figure something out.
Last week we gave you the five biggest standouts from this roster thus far. This is the opposite end of the spectrum.
He’s been cooked for a long time and it’s been obvious to everyone except that cocky GM who wanted to prove some ridiculous point to former Ravens TE Isaiah Likely – who is a top three tight end in the NFL right now – and give Andrews a $13M/year contract extension last December despite Andrews being cooked.
Well, I don’t want to give too much away but you might be getting a hint for who is the leader in this list. Giving Andrews essentially $35M guaranteed from December of 2025 through the end of the 2027 season was ridiculous. He cost the Ravens 16 points in the Atlanta, game, he leads all NFL tight ends in drops, he averages less than eight yards per catch, he has all of one catch for four yards with the offense in desperate need of help Sunday.
When Matthew Hibner comes back from injury he needs to be seeing a whole lot more of the bench HYPER. Averaging two yards after the catch the past two years is ridiculous. He ranks 28th among TEs in Expected Points Added/Target (-.18) and is 67th in yards/target.
He was brought in for $30M a year because DeCosta got cold feet on a trade for Maxx Crosby -a dominate edge defender who does more than rush the passer. He bailed on that trade for injury concerns to sign an older pass rusher who has injury concerns; Crosby is playing 95% of the snaps and Hendrickson can’t stay healthy.
His hand/finger injury seem like a big deal and if anything Hendrickson is an opener – starting games quicky – who cant do anything in the fourth quarter (10.8% pressure rate). Baltimore remains a fourth-quarter failure, they already blew three more 10-point leads and inept against the pass in the fourth quarter despite facing most bad QBs and they have three total sacks in the fourth quarter despite facing the most dropbacks.
They rank 25th in fourth-quarter pressure rate. If this guy is limited with the hand issue for weeks to come, guys like Joe Burrow and Trevor Lawrence and Josh Allen and, yeah, Bryce Young, will cook them.
Lumping them together. Two of DeCosta’s favorites who he kept too long and paid too much. Remember when defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver vowed how both would be making people eat crow with comeback years in 2027? Um, notsomuch.
Smith carried a cap hit $14M higher than any middle linebacker in the NFL ($33M), but is fourth on the team in solo tackles and doesn’t make impact plays and isn’t a thumper around the line of scrimmage anymore and needs to be protected in coverage. He makes Fred Warner money and is often invisible for long stretches of games … for years now.
Humphrey is a liability in coverage who wants to take on top receivers but has a lot to do with why top receivers have shredded this secondary. Ravens corners and safeties do not have an INT. He is the 10th highest paid corner in the NFL at $19.3M and has the top cap hit. Not going so well. This is one of the worst second-half defenses in the NFL, and these two have plenty to do with that.
When do these guys make big plays? The defense goes as they go , and Week 1 looks like an outlier for them thus far.
We are going to give him some grace as a rookie head coach (we’re putting that on DeCosta, who wanted a novice head coach under his thumb), and he has a lot more on his plate than ever before.
But as a defensive coordinator – his forte and where he is a proven commodity, well, we’ve got issues. Continuing the fourth-quarter collapse thing is kind of unthinkable (we know its mostly the roster, but this had to be job No. 1 for him on that idea of the ball). Minter didn’t have star players with the Chargers by and large but he has a dominant pass defense and they eliminated big plays and won with scheme and were sound as heck.
So what happened? How do you explain this?

Opp Pass Rt 71.8 (4th)          102.3 (22nd)

The best coordinators win the second half and tighten the screws at the half. Minter’s defense is consistently put in great positions in the first half and wilt when it counts on money downs (third-and-fourth down) against mediocre passers in the clutch. He might be spread too thin on game day and he might need to be willing to blitz more and play more man coverage and mix things up.

His OL has been awful for years. He got the coaches pushed out and got the new ones he wanted, but his offensive line still stinks so bad he made a panic move for an injury risk who was probably getting benched despite being in the concussion protocol and missing two games. (In his defense, he comes from a personnel family tree that never blossoms) .
He has ceded all leverage to Jackson and repeatedly blew it with this contract situation. And put Jackson behind a bad line with only one proven downfield target – Zay Flowers – in a walk year despite running a $370M payroll (with a lot of the money blown on the other guys on this list).
Put the 16 blown double-digit leads for a loss since 2019 on him; put the franchise’s sick disease with the choke gene on the guy who keeps building the choking rosters. He’s the one constant – it’s cut across seven coordinator and two head coaches. No one, it seems, can overcome DeCosta.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: 10 Winners and 6 Losers From Ravens' Ugly Road Loss To Browns
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens had their win streak snapped in Week 6 of the 2026 regular season on Sunday by allowing the Cleveland Browns to rally in the second half and defeat them 13-10 on the road.
Despite franchise quarterback Lamar Jackson being out with an ankle injury yet again, they came into this game as favorites to come out on top but blew another double-digit lead instead . For the second time this season, they let an inferior opponent outplay them in multiple phases and are no longer in the top spot in the AFC North standings, with their second division game next week.
Here are several Ravens players and coaches who stepped up and showed out, and others who made some costly mistakes from coaching and execution standpoints.
In his first game back after missing the previous two while recovering from finger surgery, the four-time Pro Bowler and prized free agent addition of the Ravens looked every bit the elite disruptive force off the edge that they're paying him to be. Hendrickson gave Browns first-round left tackle Spencer Fano all he could handle and then some by recording his second sack of the season and eight pressures on 26 pass-rush snaps, according to NextGenStats .
With fellow rookie Matthew Hibner out with a hand injury, the fifth-rounder got a chance to use his more as a pass catcher. Cuevas set new career highs across the board by finishing second on the team with four catches on five targets for 44 receiving yards and his first career touchdown.
The two-time Pro Bowler continued to look like his old dominant self since returning from injury in this game, both as a run defender and interior pass rusher. Madubuike had several impressive run stuffs at the line of scrimmage for minimal to no gain, led all defensive linemen on the team with five total tackles, including four solos, recorded half a sack and two quarterback hits, one of which nearly resulted in a strip sack.
The third-round rookie also had an impressive return to the lineup for the Ravens after spending the last four games on injured reserve. Lane tied Cuevas for the second-most receptions and targets on the team and finished third with 40 receiving yards. He was a reliable chain-mover, especially in some high-leverage moments, with all four of his snags resulting in first downs.
The three-time All Pro had another stellar game, especially when it came to playing fast and physical downhill and making plays in the backfield. He finished with the second-most total tackles with seven, four of which were solos and three were for a loss. On his tackles behind the line of scrimmage, Hamilton snuffed out and blew up a wide receiver screen and well-timed his blitzes off the edge for the other two.
The six-time veteran had a strong game and joined elite all-time company for the second week in a row. With his first-quarter lunging sack of Watson, who was threatening to scramble, he became just the third player at 40 years old or older to record a sack since at least 1982. The other two were Hall of Famers Bruce Smith and Clay Matthews.
After playing one snap in the previous four games, the second-year pro was back in the regular rotation at the nickel spot for the first time since Week 1 and had an excellent game. Martin finished with three tackles, all of which were solo, including a clutch tackle for loss in the open field to chop down a running back behind the line of scrimmage on a checkdown. On the Browns' final drive of the first half, he recorded a pass breakup in tight coverage and his first sack of the season on back-to-back plays. Martin was unjustly and incorrectly called for defensive pass interference on a pivotal red zone play in the fourth quarter that wound up setting the Cleveland up for its only touchdown of the game.
The four-time Pro Bowler had an incredibly strong start to this game, ending the Browns' second drive with clutch back-to-back plays, with the first being his second sack of the season on a blitz and the second on a quarterback hit that was nearly his third. Smith finished with five total tackles, including three solos.
The third-year pro had a strong day, both playing in coverage and being physical in run support. He recorded a pair of solo tackles, a pass breakup and erased a couple of angles on outside runs that resulted in negative plays.
Even though he didn't record any splash plays like a sack, pass breakup or forcing a turnover, the fourth-year pro had another great all around performance. He tied for the team lead in total tackles with eight, including four solos and finished with the highest Pro Football Focus grade of any player on the team with a overall of 90.2.
A week after bulldozing the top-ranked defensive front against the run for a season-high 208 rushing yards, the same configuration struggled mightily to gain any consistent traction on the ground after the first quarter against what had been one of the worst run defenses in the league. The Ravens were held under 100 rushing yards as a team for the first time this season and just the second time in their last 16 games.
The second-year pro continued to struggle with second-half kicks in close games by going 1-of-2 on his attempts in this game, with his 49-yard miss in the third quarter looming large in a game where the Ravens lost on a walk-off chipshot attempt.
As bad and leaky as the blocking was in front of him over the final three quarters, the former Pro Bowler was inconsistent as a thrower, missing open targets and making bad decisions. He had a pair of passes late in the game that could've been intercepted, took three sacks and finished 19-of-31 for 161 passing yards and a touchdown and ran five times for 28 yards.
The first-year play-caller went from being in his bag and looking like an offensive mastermind to start the game to not having good enough answers for the adjustments the Browns made over the final three quarters. He kept calling the type of plays that Cleveland kept keying on and snuffing out, resulting in negative plays and little to no gains.
The five-time Pro Bowler and future Hall of Famer didn't have much running room after the first quarter, as he was met in the backfield by a host of Browns defenders far too often. He was held out of the end zone for the first time this season and finished with 17 carries for 58 rushing yards with a meager average of 3.4 yards per carry. While the poor blocking wasn't on him, he picked the worst possible time to have his first lost fumble of the season, as it set Cleveland up for its only red zone possession of the game that resulted in a game-tying touchdown eight plays later.
With the loss, the Ravens blew their 17th double-digit lead since 2018, which is the most in the league during that span. Just when it seems like they've kicked this recurring bad habit, it rears its ugly head again and reminds the players and fans alike that they continue to be their own worst enemy with the lead too often. If Jackson had been available for this game, they likely would've cruised to a lopsided victory, but no matter who they had under center, there's no reason they should've lost this game.
Josh is a writer for Baltimore Ravens On SI focusing primarily on original content and reporting. He provides analysis, breakdowns, profiles, and reports on important news and transactions from and about the Ravens. His professional resume as a sports reporter includes covering local events, teams, and athletes in his hometown of Anchorage, Alaska for Anchorage Daily News. His coverage on the Ravens and other NFL teams has been featured on Heavy.com/sports, Maryland Sports Blog and most recently Baltimore Beatdown from 2021 until 2025.

title: Ravens Are Addressing Their Kicking Situation After Another Miss From Tyler Loop Sunday
full_text:
The Ravens are once again tinkering with their kicking situation after youngster Tyler Loop missed a 49-yard kick Sunday.
Head coach Jesse Minter spoke cryptically of his Loop’s status at his Monday press conference and was critical of his consistency and, according to a league source, the Ravens are signing veteran kicker Jake Moody back to the practice squad. Baltimore originally signed Moody to the practice squad late in the summer when Loop was missing kicks in preseason games. Loop had a chance to put the Ravens up two scored Sunday and his miss loomed large in a 13-10 loss at Cleveland.
Minter was loathe to couch it as a kicking competition at the time, though general manager Eric DeCosta framed it more in that regard. Loop did not do anything to lose the job once Moody came on board, and he reached a career pinnacle in Week 3 making a game-winning kick in Brazil from 56 yards and he has also made a 60-yard kick after kicking from distance proved to be a problem in his rookie year.
Loop entered this offseason under scrutiny after missed a 48-yard kick in Pittsburgh in Week 18 which knocked the Ravens out of the postseason and gave the Steelers the AFC North title. Minter was staunchly behind the kicker even as he missed kicks at M&T Bank Stadium throughout the preseason, and Moody’s time here was brief as the practice-squad spot went to more needy positions after Loop’s fast start.
"I think like any position — you're always looking at ways of how to impact the roster, how to impact improvement,” Minter said Monday of the kicker position. “So, that one would be no different."
Moody has bounced around to three teams in his NFL career and was with Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle in Chicago last season. He finished last season strong and is a former second-round pick of the 49ers who has ties to Minter from their time together at the University of Michigan.
Loop’s issues this season are from 40-49 yards. He is just 2/5 on kicks of that distance and 10/13 overall on field goals, placing him outside the top 20 in the NFL. He has made all 16 extra points.
“Confronting issues and confronting problems is really what this whole thing's about,” Minter said, while also updating Lamar Jackson's injury status on Monday . “So, there have been a few times where it's not the end-of-a-game kick that everybody sees as a game winner, but there are kicks that take a lead from a two-score game to a three-score game a few games ago, or take that game from a one-score game to a two-score game, which, the way that game is going, is really, really critical.
“So, those are critical misses. There is a confidence level for how he prepares and how he practices and how he operates and how he strikes the ball, but at the same time, that position itself is completely results-driven.”
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Head Coach's Update On Lamar Jackson Seems Alarming
full_text:
Ravens head coach Jesse Minter spoke about Lamar Jackson’s availability for Week 7 in a nearly identical manner as he did the past two weeks, which might be very bad news for the team with the Bengals coming to Baltimore.
Minter continues to stick to his “day-to-day” mantra for the two-time MVP quarterback, which is quite odd considering Jackson has not even stepped foot on the practice field in any sort of meaningful manner since injuring his ankle at the end of the first half in Week 4. We never expected to see Jackson until Week 7, as we have reported, but also thought that Minter’s tone would have changed at his Monday press conference of Jackson was truly in a significantly better position to play this week.
"I’d still put it as a day-to-day thing,” Minter said. “We’ll know a lot more on Wednesday, I would say.” When pressed as to whether he believed Jackson would be cleared to practice when the team returns to the field on Wednesday, Minter said: “Potentially, but we’ll see how it goes.” Minter is not shy about throwing in “optimism” and “he’s close”’ when he thinks it’s warranted and we haven’t heard anything close to that about this injury.
Given how Minter has been calling this ankle injury “day-to-day,” for over two weeks now, he was also asked yet again if Jackson is truly making progress in his rehab (Minter has been maintaining for weeks that he is). To that he responded with a simple "yes."
Sounds to us like backup Snoop Huntley, a seriously limited passer who constricts the scope of any offense, will be getting practice reps again this week, perhaps the bulk of them. Best case scenario might be for Jackson to get on the field in a limited fashion on Wednesday and see how it goes, but as someone with over 20 years of studying these injuries and how coaches talk about them and knowing Jackson’s history with easily-aggravated injuries, color me far from convinced that Jackson gets the start for a huge divisional game against the Bengals.
It continues to sound like newly acquired center Cam Jurgens, who general manager Eric DeCosta made a desperate move for despite being in concussion protocol, will actually be activated fully this week where he will take over as starting center. “He came a long way over the weekend,” Minter said. The expectation is that moving rookie Vega Ioane back to guard will allow an offensive line that was overwhelmed in Cleveland and has struggled much of the year, to reestablish the ground game, at least.
Trey Hendrickson, the team’s signature offseason signing who is making $30M to close out games for a fourth-quarter defense that is arguably the NFL’s worst since 2019 , continues to get adjustments made to his hand following a finger surgery recently. He returned Sunday after missing two weeks and got off to a fast start but seemed to fidgeting with both hands as the game went on and was seen awaiting X-Rays after the game . Minter refereed to the situation as “ongoing” but did not seemed concerned about his stats for a rematch with his former team Sunday.
“For his first game back, I thought he rushed well,” Minter said.
Minter also expressed some optimism that receiver Rashod Bateman, who missed practice last week with a shoulder problem and left the game early on not to return, could be back soon.
Tyler Loop is just 2/5 on kicks between 40-49 yards and Minter’s frustration with his inconsistency seeped out some in his comments Monday. He is no longer as defensive of the second-year kicker after misses as he once was, and it would not be surprising if the Ravens leaned into bringing another veteran in this week.
Loop survived an early challenge from Jake Moody a few weeks back, and won a game in Brazil with a last-second kick and has been perfect from 50+, but is clearly a work in progress, and this team still clearly lacks the clutch gene in other aspects, compounding the problem. Loop, who missed a season-ending kick at Pittsburgh in Week 18, could have given Baltimore a two-score lead late Sunday but missed from 49 yards, pushing the ball wide again.
“You always look at ways of how to improve the roster … with that one being no different,” Minter said, bluntly.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: The 3 Biggest Mistakes Declan Doyle Made With Ravens Offense Sunday
full_text:
Ravens rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has faced no shortage of challenges this season. And he has risen to the occasion more than anyone could have reasonably expected .
Sunday, however, was not a masterclass for him , even considering the fact he was without two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson (ankle) and working with another suspect offensive line (there is a very real chance the team was simply constructed that way and a desperate trade for a veteran who may have been about to be benched by the Eagles wont fix it). And the Browns adjusted by run blitzing and attacking holes where they believed running back Derrick Henry would be going and blew up Doyle’s rushing attack, making the challenge even tougher.
Doyle flashed some positives in a 13-10 loss, getting rookie receiver Ja’Kobi Lane fed early and productive in the slot in his first full NFL game . And he adroitly shifted out of a Wild Cat look for Henry and into a pass play that resulted in the only touchdown of the day. But after scoring on the first two drives Doyle’s offense sputtered for no points on nine drives with seven punts, a missed field goal and Henry's fumble for a turnover. All against a Browns team missing two of hits best defensive tackles and dealing with injuries at multiple levels and that entered the game ranked 30th in run defense Expected Points Added and 30th in Success Rate vs the run.
It wasn’t nearly good enough.
“We just didn't execute well enough,” Henry said. “We couldn't get any momentum, and [the Browns] played better [on defense] than we did [offensively] for us not to be able to move the ball like we did on that first drive. We just couldn't get anything going. Hats off to them; they played a hell of a game.”
Henry had eight rushes for 41 yards in the first quarter, and then 9 for 17 the rest of the day. With Snoop Huntley an  incredibly limited passer (5.3 yards/attempt), that quickly became a toxic combination for Doyle’s offense and he didn’t have the answers and contributed to the downfall, even considering the hand he was dealt. These were the biggest mistakes:
The Browns figured out pretty quickly that Henry behind the tackles and Henry on pitch plays was what the Ravens had going with this game plan and this allotment of players (the loss of “Joker” blocking tight end Durham Smythe for the season will loom large) faltered after the hot start. The adjustments never came.
This game as screaming out for some shotgun runs for Justice Hill – more speed and sprint plays to the outside – be he never got the ball handed off to him. The pony package that produced a huge run against the Falcons (Henry and Hill in the backfield together) never showed up.
Some option football, and option football with someone other than Henry, trying to get the perimeter stuff going in that regard, just didn’t happen. The under center stuff wasn’t happening and the interior of the offensive line was struggling even without Mason Graham playing for the Browns, but Doyle rode it anyway:
Ravens Shotgun Runs: 8-37 (4.1), 5.0/carry on 1st Down, -.36 EPA
Ravens Under Center Runs: 14-50 (3.6), 3.1/carry on 1st Down, -50 EPA
If he wanted that ratio of under center runs, then he should have had a tackle eligible on the field for more than just three snaps. Get heavy a different way without Smythe. A lot of worked vs the Falcons had a chance to work Sunday but that's not where Doyle was.
Maybe Doyle was leaning into option stuff and the back-up QB was killing it all over the place, but something needed to be said and done to get Huntley’s legs into the game plan. The Browns play far and way the most man coverage in the NFL and though they cut back on that Sunday it was still nearly a third of Huntley’s dropbacks.; those are ripe for QB runs.
Mostly they sat in Cover-3 and Doyle didn’t utilize the RPO game at all to attack it, though I thought he would. At least make the Browns think that Huntley had to be defended some in the run game might have opened things up. Creative looks with Huntley and Zay Flowers in the backfield?
He didn’t do nearly enough to sell this proposition, let alone actually see if it could have helped unlock something for an offense that was miserable for three quarters – 123 yards in those 45 minutes for a disgusting 3.2 yards/play. Henry leads the NFL with 130 carries already, and is on a record pace for age 32 running backs, so when it's not there best to try something else.
"They were doing a good job of switching it up all throughout the game," Huntley offered about the Browns defense. "I don't know how many times I can say they changed it up, but they did a great job of switching it up every drive that we came out."
Doyle was in his bag with the screens against the Falcons and there was every reason to believe Hill catching five balls in this game could have sustained things. Cleveland played a base nickel defense the entire game and sat in Cover-3 60% of the time and I kept waiting for a delayed screen for Hill or even just more of Hill in the backfield.
Bubble screens for Flowers, getting the ball in Devontez Walker’s hands around the line of scrimmage, considering he is almost always a deep threat, might have been an interesting curveball. Doyle utilized his best tricks – the killed Wild Cat look and lining up Cuevas at guard – on the opening drive and then the offensive was suffocated from there on out. Not much creative after that.
Henry has been better in the screen game this season than ever before in Baltimore but he and Hill combined for 11 receiving yards and Hill saw a few checkdowns in two-minute situations but they needed to bring some of those looks into their base offense.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: 3 Biggest Problems With Ravens 4th Quarter Defense After Another Collapse
full_text:
The Ravens fourth-quarter defense remains as broken as it ever was.
Whatever you thought of it under Wink Martindale his final few years in charge, or in Mike Macdonald’s first year-and-a-half in charge and during both of Zach Orr’s years in charge, it’s just as bad under rookie head coach Jesse Minter.
And it’s only getting worse.
The parable that was pushed by Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta, who has been a vastly overhyped evaluator and pedestrian roster-builder going on a decade on the job, was that the former coaches were preventing this team from breaking through. And Minter, a former Ravens assistant, was supposed to arrive with the secret sauce, and DeCosta added a $30M pass rusher to a $20M defensive tackle and a $20M inside linebacker and a $19M corner and a $20M hybrid safety and all those first-round picks on the defense, and yet it’s same as it ever was.
Maybe, just maybe, the Ravens (4-2) defense simply includes some of the most bloated contracts and overpaid players in the NFL (linebacker Roquan Smith and corner Marlon Humphrey carrying the top cap charges at their positions), who continue to succumb to mostly bad quarterbacks when it matters most. And maybe, just maybe, DeCosta getting carte blanche to build a rookie coaching staff after John Harbaugh was fired after nearly 20 years on the job, came at a price too.
Because for all of the issues this defense has – lack of late-game pressure and lack of late-game interceptions and lack of late-game playmakers – the novice head coach trying to run a sideline and manage a game for the first time,  while also getting the best out of his defense in the clutch, is proving to be a massive issue, too. Sunday’s debacle to the Browns , allowing 130 yards and 8 first downs and getting outscored, 10-0, in the final quarter in a 13-10 loss, was all too familiar; Minter’s defense has already blown three double-digit leads and lost twice, and the disparity between his first half and second half defense is kind of sickening.
This team now has a record 16 losses with a double-digit lead since the start of 2019, Lamar Jackson's first full season at QB, his first MVP season and the start of a ridiculous run of dominant offensive football in which the Ravens were the second-most prolific teams in the NFL through three quarters but can't hold leads like everybody else.
“I'm not going to sound like a broken record,” said hybrid defender Kyle Hamilton, the voice of this team who played his tail off Sunday. “It's 'Groundhog Day' with this question. I don't know. I'm not going to give you an answer. I really don't know. So, sorry, that's the best I can give you, but we've had this conversation so many times. I don't even feel like addressing it again."
For the season, here are the Ravens defensive ranks in the first half and second half:
First Half          Second Half
Passing Yards: 462 (5th)          780 (28th)
Oppo Passer Rating: 71.8 (4th)         102.3 (22nd)
Points/Drive Allowed: 2.55 (24th)      1.44 (4th)
Points Differential: +52 (1st)          -35 (31st)
The nasty trends get most acute in the fourth quarter and Minter needs to get all of this turned around quickly:
You can’t manage to consistently suffocate teams in the first half like noted above, and then become a total sham in the fourth quarter and tell me coaching isn’t playing a role in this. Come on man. You can’t tell me that Minter has  far superior roster in his two years running the Chargers defense and those teams did get turnovers and key sacks to close out games and were above average in points per drive allowed in the fourth quarter and touchdowns/drive in the fourth quarter.
Is he spread too thin, too soon?
I’m not saying I think defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver would have all the answers, either, but this has become a deeply-entrenched, personality flaw of the Ravens. And while DeCosta is the common denominator, he ain’t fixing it and he won’t be taking any accountability for it and he hasn’t been able to fix it despite inheriting a two-time MVP quarterback. So Minter best consider any and all options to redistribute game-day responsibilities to try to keep his defense from falling apart late.
The Ravens fourth-quarter rankings:
Yards: 113/G (29th) Pass Yds: 94/G (31st) First Downs: 7/G (29th)
Pts/Drive: 3.5 (29th) TD/Drive: 37.5% (28th) Points Allowed : 56 (30th)
Watson picked them apart in the middle of the field – an issue for years – in mustering two scoring drives in the fourth quarter after virtually nothing in the first 45 minutes.
“The frustrating part is the fact that we lost,” defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike said. “That was a game that we believed that we should have won, and we didn't. We didn't make the plays that we were supposed to make. [We have to give] credit to the Browns, but that's on us, and we are going to get it fixed."
The Ravens corners and safeties still do not have an interception all season (Kyle Hamilton’s pick came when he was deployed as a linebacker). Free safety Malaki Starks at least broke a pass up. But when Browns head coach Todd Monken – one of the coaches the Ravens fired – opened up the pass game late when he had to, Baltimore suffered.
Deshaun Watson threw for 94 yards on them in the fourth quarter and rookie KC Concepcion, who works the slot where the Ravens really stink , finally got going. Minter benched struggling rookie nickelback Chandler Rivers on defense but the problems persisted. Hmm.
Minter doesn’t want to blitz or go with heavy fronts, but his nickel and dime defenses got exposed in the fourth quarter once more (again, I don’t see play makers). Seems he gets pretty predictable late in games and better change his spots some. Here are the season numbers in the fourth quarter:
Pass Yards: 583 (31st) Comp %: 70% (24th) Opp Pass Rating : 107.8 (23rd)
Third Down Conv : 37% (22nd)
Watson can still move some but he’s no Josh Allen or Trevor Lawrence (oh yeah, the Ravens will see them soon). Anyone a little slippery gives the Ravens fits with the game on the line. The Ravens got a push off the edge and were getting pressure at times even with a three-man rush … until the fourth quarter. They're lucky Michael Penix couldn't come back in the game in OT last week.
This Sunday the Ravens had five sacks in the first three quarters but none on 14 dropbacks in the fourth quarter and just a couple of pressures. On the season in the fourth quarter:
Pressure Rate : 30.1% (26th) Sack Rate: 3.9% (T-27th)
Hendrickson got his first sack, though the finger injury and bandage on his hand still seems to be impacting him. He’d better have a helluva second half. Again, Minter didn’t have this problem with the Chargers, but he also better figure out that trying to replicate what he did there, with this GM in charge who has repeatedly put coordinators in positions where they had to gamble more than they’d like, probably won’t work, either.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Choke Away Another 10-Point Lead To Browns In 13-10 Loss: Here's How They Did It
full_text:
The choke gene may have gone dormant for a couple of weeks, but it remains. The hiring of Jesse Minter as head coach certainly didn’t eliminate it, and all the hallmarks of all the collapses of the past played out again Sunday in Cleveland. Minter’s defense once again was far worse in the second half that it’s been in the first half, they got crushed on third down when it mattered most, young kicker Tyler Loop missed a critical field goal and running back Derrick Henry, who rarely fumbles but when he does it tends to come in these collapses, gave the ball away late, too.
And so, for the 16th time since 2019 the Baltimore Ravens lost a game in which they led by double digits, this time, 13-10, to the Browns and rookie head coach Todd Monken, Baltimore’s former offensive coordinator who was fired along with John Harbaugh, because of all those  blown leads and blown games. Minter now has blown three leads of 10 points or more himself, and he’s lost two of them, and his second-half adjustments remain quite questionable.
“In all three phases we had chances to gain separation,” Minter said after the game.  "It was our own self-inflicted things – we put ball on the ground and missing a kick, getting a penalty down in the low redzone allowing the game to get there.”
The Browns lead the AFC North, while the Ravens fell to 4-2. The Ravens hope to get two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson back from his ankle injury next week. Backup Snoop Huntley, who was great for two drives in Week 5 but is a very limited passer and a player the Ravens quit on after the 2024 season for myriad reasons, could generate almost nothing. The Ravens had 235 net yards (despite the Browns being down two top defensive tackles) and they will face more probing questions about their inability to manage leads and beat teams they should beat when getting up that big.
A week ago Minter opined how the overtime win at Atlanta could be the start of a new identity for the team. Welp. Baltimore scored on its first two drives, then not again and Minter's defense gets worse as games go on. They allowed 130 yards in the fourth quarter and eight first downs and it's the same as it's always been there. No more Harbaugh and Zach Orr to blame, but you could certainly wonder why the guy who puts together overprices choking defenses keeps his job (mediocre-at-best GM Eric DeCosta).
Here’s what you need to know about how it went down, in DeCosta's record 16th choke at the helm:
The Ravens had a great chance to make it a two-score game in the fourth quarter when young kicker Tyler Loop, who continues to struggle for consistency but did hit a game-winning kick in Brazil l ast month, pushed a 48-yard attempt that could have made it a 13-3 game, and the Ravens fell into a funk.
It’s a kick he has to make and looked like some key misses in the past. The next time the Ravens got the ball running back Derrick Henry, who was bottled up after a hot start, broke free for a strong first-down run but was stripped of the ball, setting up the Browns in Baltimore territory. And, after controversial pass interference call on third own, Cleveland capped the drive with a TD run to tie it at 10.
On the ensuing kickoff, Rasheen Ali muffed the ball, putting the Ravans back at their own 15 to start the drive, and the tenor of the game has shifted entirely from the point of the missed field goal on.
"I didn't hit the ball clean," Loop said after the game, while continuing his refrain about sticking to his process.
This was a rough day for Henry. The Ravens got the perimeter run game going, tearing off first-down runs off left tackle and right tackle. But the Browns started to run blitz more and crowd the line of scrimmage and dominated the final three quarters with their defensive line against the Ravens makeshift offensive line.
Henry had eight rushes for 41 yards in the first quarter .. and then nine for 17 the rest of the day. He repeatedly got bottled up and tackled in the in backfield in short yardage situations again and could not make an impact in the second half and his fumble was devastating and, while he does it rarely, when he it does happen it tends to be part of Baltimore’s overall collapse. It conjures too many images of past choke jobs.
"I need to be better," Henry said. "I have to take care of the ball."
The line could get no push, rookie guard-turned-center, Vega Ioane, had a few bad snaps in the second half as well, the A Gap became an issue again on sacks and pressures and it just wasn’t good enough up front.
Rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle called a great play for rookie Josh Cuevas early in the game where he was lined up at guard before catching a pass, but he did not get enough players involved in the run game, including Justice Hill.
The Ravens cannot push the ball downfield at all with this backup quarterback, which has always been my biggest issue with him. This was a tough assignment with him on the road in a divisional game with the Ravens compromised from a personnel standpoint, but he was shaky.
Huntley refused to use his legs as much as he should have against a defense that plays so much man coverage, especially when the Browns began selling out to eliminate running back Derrick Henry. His mobility provided no relief, his decision making suffered as the game went on and he was very lucky some lob passes in the middle of the field were not picked off, including a pass right at a Browns defender late in the fourth quarter.
Huntley averaged 5.3 yards per attempt, the Ravens screen game was highly lacking, $13M tight end Mark Andrews made absolutely no impact in the passing game whatsoever, and the combination of this quarterback and these targets was problematic.
Kyle Hamilton was a menacing figure around the line of scrimmage and seemed to have a great feel what former Monken was doing with the offense at all times.
Hamilton delivered a thumping tackle on running back Jaleel McLaughlin on a screen pass with the Browns backed up deep in the first half. He negated a Browns first down on an inside run with the game tight in the second half while engaged with a guard – yeah, a guard. And he blew up Browns talented rookie KC Concepcion on a designed screen in the third quarter for a loss at a time when the Browns were starting to gain a modicum of offensive momentum.
Hamilton was a factor stuffing the run and serving as a deterrent all day. On a second-and-short run blitz in the fourth quarter he had another stuff for a loss. It’s too bad more teammates could not come up with individual moments at critical times, but this defense has earned the chocking reputation in large part because of that.
Rookie receiver Ja’Kobi Lane has barely played this season, suffering a wrist injury in the first half of Week 1 that required a surgical procedure and landed him in Injured Reserve. Lane was an immediate sensation this summer at training camp and in the preseason, quickly establishing himself as a starter but it remained to be seen how quickly he could find his way in this offense after staccato start to his career.
No worries, as it turns out.
Lane caught his first four targets and all were critical plays; all produced first downs and he helped out Huntley on third-and-10 and was a problem working the middle of the field, where it became apparent in camp he was most comfortable. Lane came through on third-and-six on two occasions as well and also had an 11 yard gain on first down.
On a day in which the scope of the passing game was going to be limited and Andrews a shell of what he used to be and with starting receiver Rashod Bateman limited in practice all week and barely playing in this game before departing with injury, Lane being a chain mover was a big deal in an ugly, field position divisional ball game.
The Ravens have been one of the league’s premier defensive teams in the first half all season. The problems have come, consistently, after halftime.
Sunday was more of the same, and the most…

title: Four Ravens X-Factors For Clash vs. Browns
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens will continue the 2026 regular season with the second leg of a two-game road stint against the Cleveland Browns in Week 6 , and the difference in the game could come down to how an individual player performs when it matters most or over the course of the game by capitalizing on their opportunities when presented with them.
With a win, the Ravens improve to 5-1 and would further strengthen their hold on the top spot in the AFC North division standings. A loss would, at worst, tie them for second place with the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals if they both win on Sunday.
Here are four players who could wind up tilting the scales in favor of the Ravens and first-year head coach Jesse Minter.
The polarizing third-round rookie will be making his long-awaited return to the lineup after being activated from injured reserve on Saturday following a full week of practice. Lane was the unquestioned star of the Ravens' training camp and preseason, making highlight-reel catches on a daily basis by showing off his impressive hands and catch radius. His regular-season debut was cut short in Week 1 after he suffered a fractured wrist and had his first career touchdown negated by a penalty.
His size and length will make him a dangerous weapon in the red zone, a mismatch in one-on-one contested catch situations and an alluring target underneath when the Ravens need to pick up a first down and the opposing defense is too busy keying in on Zay Flowers, who is having a sensationally productive start to the season.
Even though the Browns rank in the bottom half of the league in rushing offense and top running back Quinshon Judkins is out with an ankle injury, they'll still look to establish some sort of ground game. The fifth-year veteran will be key in ensuring Todd Monken and Co. can't gash them between the tackles by taking on and defeating double teams. He did a great job helping lead that charge against one of the best rushing attacks last week and will need to do so again versus one of the worst.
The 11th-year journeyman veteran made his Ravens debut last week and played 19 offensive snaps in place of fellow blocking specialist Durham Smythe, who suffered a season-ending torn Achellies in Week 4. With fourth-round rookie Matthew Hibner out for this game due to a hand injury, Vannett will almost certainly see the field even more often in this game, especially as lead blocker on the edge or from the backfield, an area he shined in limited action against the Atlanta Falcons .
The second-year pro has been a tackling machine over the past two weeks for the Ravens defense after struggling mightily in that aspect of the game at the start of the season. He led the team with a season-high 10 tackles last week, tying his single-game career high, and it marked the first game of his career with multiple tackles for a loss. He'll help limit yards after the catch, snuff out underneath routes and can bring the heat as a blitzer.

title: The Ravens Inactives For Week 6 With Lamar Jackson Out
full_text:
The Ravens ruled out two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson (ankle) on Friday yet again but still faced numerous critical medical decision to make before Sunday’s kickoff in Cleveland.
Rookie coach Jesse Minter is facing his first AFC North opponent with an injury report that stretched to 19 names midweek. Baltimore ruled out Jackson, center Cam Jurgens (concussion), defensive lineman Broderick Washington (ankle) and rookie tight end Matthew Hibner (hand). The team has had to juggle its offensive line every week all season, Jurgens has not appeared in two games since general manager Eric DeCosta made a desperate move to land him and Baltimore was once again dealing with injuries to guards as well, with John Simpson playing through a groin problem and Andrew Vorhees (foot) and Emery Jones (ankle) both listed as questionable.
And the Ravens had to decide if third-round pick Ja’Kobi Lane (wrist) was healthy and conditioned enough to play his first game since Week 1, when the promising youngster suffered an injury in the first half and has not played since. Lane was one of the stories of the summer and the preseason and quickly worked himself into a starting role with the team, and with Baltimore dealing with injuries at tight end and with $13M “move” tight end Mark Andrews struggling mightily , having a big receiver (6-foot-4) available for backup quarterback Snoop Huntley is a big deal.
Lane was cleared to play for the first time since Week 1, while Vorhees was not.
The Ravens welcomed back $30M edge rusher Trey Hendrickson after a two-week absence due to a procedure on his finger. They are as healthy as they have been all season up front on defense – Washington is a rotational run stuffer at this point – all season. The defense in particular has been in better health than the offensive side of the ball, yet the offense has carried the team to the 4-1 start.
Undrafted rookie quarterback Joe Fagnano was once again active and serving as the primary backup to Huntley. The Ravens are hopeful that Jackson, who has yet to take the practice field since suffering the ankle injury just before halftime in Week 4, can return to practice this week with the Bengals traveling to Baltimore in Week 7, with Minter continuing to refer to him as “day-to-day” this week and Jurgens should also be cleared to begin practicing fully next week barring any setbacks with his return from concussion protocol.
Rookie receiver Elijah Sarratt was a healthy scratch as was safety K'von Wallace

title: Three Primary Reasons The Ravens Should Beat The Browns Sunday
full_text:
The Ravens were projected to compete for a Super Bowl before the season began. The Browns were projected to compete for the first-overall pick.
While the injury report may be daunting for the Ravens and no Lamar Jackson (ankle) at quarterback is certainly a big deal, this is also a football game Sunday at Cleveland that they should find a way to win. It’s the last time they are certain to be a favorite for a while with teams like the Bengals and Jaguars and Bills looming and it’s Jesse Minter’s first AFC North game and plenty of individuals on this roster realize just how difficult winning in Cleveland has been for this organization.
As always, there are a handful of critical matchups that will go a long way to deciding this football game  and, like most divisional games, this will very likely come down to which team controls the line of scrimmage. Line play will be everything and the Ravens should have the combination of $30M/year edge rusher Trey Hendrickson and $20M/year defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike on the field for longer than ever before, and at closer to full health than ever before ( they’ve played just 32 snaps together all season ).
The Ravens have, on paper, three primary advantages heading into this game that they must lean into and find a way to exploit. They provide the path to victory and explain why Baltimore is still a field-goal favorite on the road despite their injuries. Here’s how and why they should win this game.
Rookie offensive play caller Declan Doyle said Derrick Henry would see a lot of the football and didn’t back off another 300-carry season for him (he’s never done it three straight years) and, well, Henry has run the ball more times through five weeks than any age 32 RB since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger.
Guess who leads the NFL with 113 carries? You got it, with eight more than Jahmyr Gibbs (Lions). The Browns are allowing 4.5/carry and are 30th in Expected Points Added and Success Rate against the run. Their premier defensive tackle and do-everything linebacker are both on the injury report. Every reason in the world to keep this close and test them over and over with volume and multiplicity on the run game (more carries for QB Snoop Huntley, we presume HYPE GAM and some receivers as well and not necessarily just Zay Flowers).
Baltimore is as healthy up front on defense as it has been all season, Madubuike is all the way back after missing more than a year with a neck injury and they just shutdown the best running back in the NFL – Bijan Robinson – on the road in Atlanta last Sunday night.
We wonder if Browns coach Todd Monken, former Ravens offensive coordinator who knows this group well, will even mess around with establishing the run all the much and will just try to throw his way to the lead and attack a suspect secondary . Still, it’s very difficult to win games in the AFC North without being able to sustain a run game and we don’t fancy the Browns rank 30th in the NFL in EPA/designed run play (-0.22).
The Browns QB hasn’t thrown in the towel in the regular season – he certainly tried to do it in the preseason – and he’s been playing decent football. But his legs are not what they used to be, and when he holds the ball he becomes a double agent.
Watson is being sacked on 11.4% of his dropbacks , this Browns offensive line has big issues all around and this guy will turn the ball over. He is also a notoriously slow starter and if the Ravens can run their way to the lead in the first half they should have success taking the air out of the ball in the second half. Watson is in the bottom third in the NFL in air yards per attempt, pushing the ball downfield is not a forte for either QB in this game, but Huntley has the benefit of what should be a robust run game to put him in down and distances to succeed.

title: Bills' Bye Week Injury Update: Will DJ Moore, Dalton Kincaid Return Next Game?
full_text:
It sounds, and looks, as if the Buffalo Bills expect to come out of their Week 7 bye nearing full health throughout the roster.
The Bills scratched only two injured players prior to their October 18 road win over the Las Vegas Raiders. It was the second game in a row that wide receiver DJ Moore and defensive lineman Ed Oliver were inactive.
"I'd like to think that they're close [to being healthy enough to play]," said Brady as Buffalo hits its bye week.
Additionally, both tight end Dalton Kincaid and edge rusher Bradley Chubb left the Week 6 game due to rib issues, but both subsequently returned at some point.
Other than what appear to be minor issues with those four players, the Bills have no other injury concerns on the 53-man roster at the moment.
"I think we're going into it fairly healthy," said franchise quarterback Josh Allen after a 33-30 win in Las Vegas. "Bye weeks are always great for that, getting guys back, but we got to continue to grow."
Furthermore, defensive back Jordan Hancock, who has been on the shelf due to a calf strain, is eligible to come off Injured Reserve in time for the November 1 home game against the Baltimore Ravens.
Moore's issue extends back to late in the second quarter during the Week 2 game against the Detroit Lions. He came down hard on his shoulder while diving for a pass in the end zone in the September 17 primetime affair.
Having not missed a game since December 2020, when his was with the Carolina Panthers, Moore fought through the AC joint sprain to make himself available in Weeks 3 and 4. Against the New England Patriots on October 4, however, Moore reaggravated the injury while falling to the ground trying to make a catch.
For the past two weeks, Moore missed back-to-back practices before participating on a limited basis on the third day. He was questionable to appear in the last two games, but the Bills chose not to dress their WR1, presumably with the idea that giving him three uninterrupted weeks of rest and recovery will yield 100 percent health coming out of the bye.
Buffalo was likely playing the long game, out of precaution, with Oliver, too.
Oliver was also banged up during the Week 4 home loss to New England. He took a hit to the knee area on his left leg at the end of a okay near the sideline.
The Bills held Oliver out of five consecutive practices before he finally returned in a limited fashion last Friday.
Chubb was the first to leave the October 18 road game, suffering a ribs injury that sidelined the edge rusher early in the second quarter.
The Bills labeled Chubb as questionable to return. Although he did subsequently re-enter the game, he saw limited action with second-round rookie TJ Parker taking the large majority of snaps the rest of the way. Chubb was on the field for 21 of 66 defensive snaps.
Kincaid left midway through the third quarter as he was seen grabbing at his torso, in apparent discomfort, after running a route in the red zone. The Bills took him into the locker room, ruling his return questionable.
The tight end was back on the field when Buffalo took possession with 8:01 remaining in the fourth quarter. He gained 14 yards on a catch three snaps after returning.
The fact that both Chubb and Kincaid returned to action to some extent bodes well for their availability immediately following the bye.

title: What to Expect from Bills Safety Room After CJ Gardner-Johnson's Suspension
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills will already be down at least one starter for their next matchup, when they play the Baltimore Ravens in two weeks.
With safety CJ Gardner-Johnson suspended for one game , the rotation in the secondary will look different for at least one week.
We already saw how Jim Leonhard handled the loss of a starting safety mid-game against the Raiders, but the defensive coordinator now has two weeks to gameplan for it.
Here's what options Leonhard has at his disposal to deploy against an offensive in Baltimore with plenty of talnet.
When Gardner-Johnson left the game, the main beneficiary in terms of snaps was Damar Hamlin. While he doesn't provide an intruging ceiling, he does raise the flloor of the DB room and help calm the storm on the back end.
Leonhard specifically complimented his calming precense, effective communication and positional flexibility in his press conference on Monday, citing the 45 defensive snaps he played as evidence.
"He does not get the credit for the amount of things he's asked to do within a gameplan," Leonhard said.
Per PFF, Hamlin wasn't even targeted while in coverage, despite Kirk Cousins attempting 41 passes. The DB played 31 snaps at free safety, 10 in the box, three in the slot and one on the line of scrimmage, showcasing his versatility.
Fifth round rookie Jalon Kilgore finally got meaningful defensive snaps, and it was a mixed bag for the DB out of South Carolina.
Kilgore played 11 defensive snaps, one of which was a key pass break up on third down to force a punt. Later in the game, he got burned by Tre Tucker in an obvious prevent situation, where he allowed the receiver to get behind him for a touchdown to keep the Raiders alive.
The rookie is no where close to the reliable player Hamlin is, but his off the charts athleticism should intriuge the Bills enough to get him on the field more.
The safety had a 9.60 relative athletic score going into the draft, highlighted by his 4.40 40-yard dash and "elite" speed and explosion grades. For comparison, Hamlin's relative athletic score was a 7.00, with a "good" speed grade and "okay" explosion grade.
Calls have only grown for the Bills to move on from Gardner-Johnson, so Leonhard and the Bills might need to prepare for a longer-term solution that lasts them the rest of the season.
For now, with the starting safety slated to miss just one game, expect to see a majority of snaps go to the veteran in Hamlin. If Jordan Hancock is able to return from IR to back up Dee Alford in the slot, Hamlin won't need to sub into the nickel at all, meaning he'd likely see the lion's share of snaps.
However, if the team decided to move on from Gardner-Johnson, it would be beneficial to give the rookie with the higher ceiling more playing time, and implement more of a rotation between Kilgore and Hamlin before the rookie is (ideally) able to take over full-time.

title: Bills' Snap Counts in Las Vegas: Keon Coleman, Four Rookies Win Big Entering Bye Week
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills head into their Week 7 bye with a 5-1 record, but they're still not clicking on all cylinders.
"I'm not happy with how the team's playing right now," said first-year head coach Joe Brady one day after the 33-30 win over the Las Vegas Raiders.
The Bills' snap counts from that October 18 road victory are proof that the coaching staff is still trying to figure out who fits best at certain spots, especially on the defense.
Safety Cole Bishop only defensive player to see 100 percent of snaps in Week 6.
Buffalo totaled 68 offensive snaps and 66 on defense.
Here are five clear winners based upon Week 6 playtime percentages.
Official Bills' Week 6 Snap Counts [ @NFL345 ] pic.twitter.com/Fc6ZdROP55
With DJ Moore inactive , Keon Coleman was the Bills' most frequently deployed wide receiver against the Raiders.
Coleman, who is experiencing a renaissance of sorts thus far this season, recorded 58 snaps. He caught a touchdown pass for the third game in a row.
“He's where he needs to be. He's handling everything like a pro," said Brady. "There's so much trust we have for him as the player, the development. He continues to just make plays.”
In addition to his improvement as a professional , Coleman's willingness and ability to block in the run game explain why he was on the field 85 percent of the time.
Outside linebacker TJ Parker had been relatively quiet outside of a couple plays over the first five weeks of his career.
On Sunday, the Bills needed their highest drafted rookie to step up, and the No. 35 overall pick delivered. With starter Bradley Chubb temporarily unavailable due to a rib issue, Parker totaled 41 defensive snaps, which amount to 62 percent.
"I thought some guys stepped up. TJ's one. He played a great game for us. We needed him to. [Bradley] Chubb battled through some injuries," said defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard.
Second-round rookie cornerback Davison Igbinosun earned his second consecutive start over Maxwell Hairston on Sunday in Las Vegas.
The aggressive Igbinosun totaled 42 snaps on defense compared to 26 for Hairston, a 2025 first-round pick who has struggled. Igbinosun brings size and a contagious energy to the outside CB spot.
"I think what he's done the last couple weeks, he's definitely earned a high majority of the snaps at the corner position," said Leonhard. "I know what I'm getting, play in and play out. I think he's stepped in and done a great job handling more volume in this defense."
With starting safety Chauncey Gardner-Johnson's ejection as a result of repulsive behavior , veteran Damar Hamlin was called into full-time action.
Meanwhile, fifth-round rookie Jalon Kilgore picked up important reps as a dime safety. Kilgore logged a key pass breakup before surrendering a late touchdown.
It was a defensive debut for Kilgore, who saw 11 snaps with the unit in Sunday. He was active for the first time ever in the Monday Night Football win over the Los Angeles Rams, appearing exclusively on special teams.
With Brady saying he hoped to see more of fourth-round rookie linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr last week, the raw talent was part of the defensive formation 33 percent t of the game against the Raiders.
Playing a season-high 22 snaps, Elarms-Orr appeared to miss assignments in a couple of instances. He was on the field spelling Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams at different points in the game.

title: Bills' Maligned Kicker Remains Perfect on Field Goals, Nailing Four More in Week 6
full_text:
Once upon a time, Tyler Bass was looked at as a pain point for the Buffalo Bills . But in 2026, he's been their sweet 16.
Now No. 16 in your program after swapping numbers out as D.J. Moore came in this offseason, Bass has become a weapon for the Bills. In Buffalo's Week 6 win over the Las Vegas Raiders , Bass was cash, netting four field goals, including the final points for the team in the fourth quarter.
It was the first time Bass had made four field goals in a game since a win over the Jets on November 19, 2023 . It marks just the fifth time in his Bills tenure that he's made at least four FGs in a game.
Tyler Bass gives the Bills a 10-point lead in Vegas 🗣️ BUFvsLV on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/D5ur3vEDmt
Bass' season has been near-perfect, as he's made all 13 of his field goal attempts this year. His only drawback has been extra points, missing two thus far in 2026.
The Georgia Southern product has not been booting it from deep — Bass has yet to make a FG from beyond 50 yards. But he's been on his game from everywhere else, has made three or more FGs in three games this year, and has added a game-winning kick to his resume with the overtime boot he made against the Rams .
After some up-and-down moments over the years, and missing all of 2025 due to injury, Bass was looked at as a sneaky flaw for Buffalo this season. But in the Bills' pre-bye-week slate, Bass has been nearly flawless for the special teams unit.
There are a lot of contributing factors to Buffalo sitting at 5-1 heading into its Week 7 bye week. And Bass has become one of the biggest reasons for that overnight.
Tyler Bass has made 18 straight field goals dating back to 2024. He is tied for the longest streak by a Bills kicker since Rian Lindell with 18 (10/21/2007-12/09/2007). pic.twitter.com/sxfoQYH5c0
In the Bills' locker room following the 33-30 win over the Raiders, head coach Joe Brady awarded Bass with a game ball for the second week in a row.
"Love you guys, man. Love you guys. Seriously, I mean it," said Bass to his teammates .
Six days prior to going 7-for-7 on kicks against the Raiders, Bass earned a Week 5 game ball for nailing the game-ending 45-yard winner in overtime against the Los Angeles Rams.

title: Desperate Bills Finally Call Former First-Round Draft Pick For CB Help
full_text:
The door was left open all offseason, and for good reason as it turns out.
The Buffalo Bills are welcoming their 2017 first-round draft pick back home.
The Bills have reached an agreement with veteran free agent cornerback Tre'Davious White to join the practice squad with the intention of moving him onto the active roster following an re-acclimation period, according to a report from ESPN's Adam Schefter on Monday afternoon.
"We love Tre'Davious," said general manager Brandon Beane this past April . "You would never close the door on bringing a guy like Tre back to Buffalo."
Oddly enough, it was only three days ago when we advocated for Buffalo to reunite with White in an attempt to boost the undermanned CB position group. The Bills chose to keep only three true outside cornerbacks on their 53-man roster, and they've already been stretched thin there when Christian Benford was forced to miss one game due to a minor toe injury.
Furthermore, starter Maxwell Hairston, a 2025 first-round draft pick, has not met expectations thus far. His underwhelming performance has allowed second-round rookie Davison Igbinosun to see a larger share of snaps.
Behind Igbinosun, however, the Bills have no backup plan. That's where White seemingly fits in.
After all, it was White who stepped up and assumed a starting role when Hairston began the 2025 season on Injured Reserve. He proceeded to start 16 regular season games and both playoff contests.
White, who played eight of his nine season with the Bills under former head coach Sean McDermott, will have to become familiar with defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard and his 3-4 scheme prior to moving into active duty.
The well-liked White brings professionalism, experience and proven leadership qualities upon re-entering the building at One Bills Drive.
His return looks highly similar to what the Bills did last year with veteran safety Jordan Poyer, initially adding him to the practice squad before eventually inserting him in the starting lineup. Not only did Poyer perform reasonably well, he was credited with helping young safety Cole Bishop grow immensely.
In addition to being a steady locker room presence, White will almost definitely have the opportunity to help the Bills on the field. In 2025, he totaled 40 tackles, 6.0 TFL, one interception and nine pass break-ups over 16 starts. When targeted, White limited opposing passers to 5.1 yards per attempt and a 51.1 completion percentage.
There's a hope that White, a former All-Pro, can inject some life into a Bills' defense that is allowing 28.5 points per game and ranks next to last in the NFL against the pass.
It's still a mystery as to why it took this long to bring White home, so it's certainly not surprising that it's happening.

title: Punishment Handed Down to Bills Safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson For Spitting Incident
full_text:
C.J. Gardner-Johnson was ejected during the first half of the Buffalo Bills win over the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 6 after spitting in the direction of tight end Brock Bowers. Now, the league has handed down an additional punishment.
According to Tom Pelissero, the league has suspended Gardner-Johnson without pay for one game .
After the game, Gardner-Johnson gave a half-hearted apology where he refused to admit he spit at Bowers . He even tried to say he was simply being competitive, stating nothing negative was meant by the interaction. He later offered an apology on social media, and while it was better, he still didn't take full accountability. Instead of admitting to what he did, Gardner-Johnson said his "gesture" was "inappropriate."
The league released a statement shortly after the news was announced, confirming the one-game suspension. While Gardner-Johnson never admitted to spitting, the league statement said he "spit at an opponent."
"Gardner-Johnson’s suspension begins on Monday, October 26. He will be eligible to return to the Bills’ active roster on Monday, November 2, following the team’s November 1 game against the Baltimore Ravens," the statement read.
"Under the Collective Bargaining Agreement, Gardner-Johnson may appeal the suspension. Any appeal will be heard and decided upon by either Derrick Brooks, Jordy Nelson, Ron Rivera, or James Thrash, the hearing officers jointly appointed and compensated by the NFL and NFLPA to decide appeals of on-field player discipline."
Signing Gardner-Johnson was already a concern among Bills fans. His reputation is far from clean and several teams grew tired of the outspoken safety quickly. One prime example was in 2025 when the Houston Texans released Gardner-Johnson after just three games.
Now, calls for him to be released will grow louder, and one former coach says the Bills don't need him. Rex Ryan, who was the head coach of the Bills in 2015 and 2016, said playing in the NFL is a privilege, while adding no team needs Gardner-Johnson. He even called Gardner-Johnson a "punk."
"This guy, I mean, say what you want, he's a punk. I mean, that's really what he is. And, I mean, even as a practice player, I love the way he played. I really did. And then you find out about him and you're like, oh, God, nobody wants him. That's why they had six teams get rid of him. And this thing right here represents your football team. The Buffalo Bills don't need you. Guess what? No team in the league needs you," Ryan said on ESPN's Get Up .
In addition to his actions on Sunday, Gardner-Johnson missed two tackles and has struggled in coverage this season. It's still early in the year, but this signing feels like a miss from general manager Brandon Beane.

title: Buffalo Bills' Highest And Lowest Graded Players in Week 6 Win Over Raiders
full_text:
After knocking off the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 6, the Buffalo Bills are now 5-1 on the season. It was another close win as the Raiders fought back from a 10-point fourth-quarter deficit to cut the lead to 33-30. Buffalo recovered an onside kick to seal the win and they now prepare for their Week 7 bye.
There will be plenty to work on during the bye, especially for defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard whose defense has surrendered 171 points in six games. Offensively, they've been much better, but they have some issues to clean up as well, including ball security concerns.
As the Bills take a week to rest and regroup, let's look back at the win over Las Vegas and focus on the five highest-rated as well as the five lowest-rated players from Sunday.
Dorian Williams had five tackles, one pass breakup, and his first career interception in Week 6. That helped him earn the top spot above Greg Rousseau, who batted down two passes and had two quarterback hits on Kirk Cousins. Damar Hamlin was the third defender to make the top five, earning a 71.2 overall.
On offense, Alec Anderson had a strong game, earning a 78.3 . Josh Allen was second on offense and fourth overall with a 73.4 after throwing for 255 yards with two touchdown passes.
There's a real trend in the bottom five, with four of the Bills' lowest-graded players being rookies. That includes Kaleb Elarms-Orr, who was actually the highest-rated player in Week 5 with a 90.3 . He's not a full time player, recording 22 snaps, which might be why he has such major swings. Jalon Kilgore had a pass breakup late in the game, but still had a low score of 37.4 Fellow rookie defensive back Davison Igbinosun had a 43, but he stood out as a far better player than that number suggests. The only offensive player in the bottom five was Skyler Bell, who had a 47.8. He had zero receptions on two targets.
The lone veteran in the bottom five was C.J. Gardner-Johnson, who missed two tackles before being ejected from the game for spitting in the direction of Brock Bowers. Gardner-Johnson had a terrible attempt at an apology after the game, but then sent a better ( although not perfect ) apology via social media later.

title: Former Bills' Head Coach Unloads on C.J. Gardner-Johnson for Spitting Incident
full_text:
C.J. Gardner-Johnson was ejected during the Buffalo Bills' Week 6 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. Near the end of the second quarter, Gardner-Johnson and Las Vegas tight end Brock Bowers exchanged some words and Gardner-Johnson spit at the ground in the direction of Bowers.
The action happened right in front of an official, which led to Gardner-Johnson's disqualification from the game. Afterward, he offered a completely tone-deaf explanation in the locker room, claiming it " was nothing negative " from the play and said it was just being competitive. Even worse, the veteran safety refused to admit he actually spit at Bowers.
Late Sunday night, he offered a much better apology, but as Mike Moraitis of Bills On SI says, it was too little, too late . Gardner-Johnson also still refused to use the word spit, saying his "gesture" was inappropriate. Clearly, he doesn't want to take true accountability, and former Buffalo head coach Rex Ryan would surely agree.
While appearing on ESPN's Get Up, Ryan unloaded on Gardner-Johnson, calling him a punk. Ryan added that playing in the NFL is a privilege and Gardner-Johnson would do well to understand that the Bills, nor any other team in the league, needs him.
"This guy, I mean, say what you want, he's a punk. I mean, that's really what he is. And, I mean, even as a practice player, I love the way he played. I really did. And then you find out about him and you're like, oh, God, nobody wants him. That's why they had six teams get rid of him. And this thing right here represents your football team. The Buffalo Bills don't need you. Guess what? No team in the league needs you," Ryan said.
"This guys is a punk. ... The Buffalo Bills don't need you!" Rex Ryan sounds off on C.J. Gardner-Johnson. pic.twitter.com/2No91J4hai
"It's an absolute honor to play in this league. Quit being a punk. That's what, to me, that's what it is. And I like guys who have lead in their pencil. Everybody that plays on defense has lead in their pencil. But they don't have to be like this. This isn't a physical. You're not being physical. You're being a punk. That's it."
Gardner-Johnson joined the Bills this offseason and already didn't have the best reputation . Despite his obvious talent, he's now on his seventh team since being selected in the fourth round of the 2019 NFL draft. In 2025 alone, he spent time with three teams after being released by the Houston Texans after just three games. He was then signed to the Baltimore Ravens practice squad but released before playing a game. Gardner-Johnson finished the year with the Chicago Bears before signing a one-year deal in Buffalo this offseason.
At this point, there will be calls to move on from Gardner-Johnson, but at the very least, it seems impossible to picture him returning once that deal expires.

title: Joe Brady Predicts Former Penn State QB Will Be Offensive Coordinator 'Someday'
full_text:
If they're unhappy with their middling offense in Happy Valley , Penn State may be able to call one of its own home to fix it in due time.
Building his offensive staff after being promoted last winter, Buffalo Bills ' first-year head coach Joe Brady tabbed a former Nittany Lions' quarterback for an offensive assistant role.
It isn't just any former Penn State field general by the way. Trace McSorley graduated as the program record holder in wins (31), completions (720), passing yards (9,899) and TD passes (77).
"The biggest thing I was looking for was people who weren't exactly like me," said Brady on his approach.
The 36-year-old Brady knows McSorley from their shared time in State College.
"Trace, I was a GA when Trace was the quarterback and one of the greatest leaders I've been around, incredible human, incredible football player," said Brady last week with the Bills preparing to visit the Las Vegas Raiders.
Brady served as a graduate assistant for Penn State during the 2015 and 2016 seasons before moving on to spend two years as a New Orleans Saints' offensive assistant.
McSorley became the Nittany Lions' full-time starter for the 2016 season, and Brady was impressed.
"When you coach guys, you just know that, hey, whenever that guy's done playing ball, as soon as I can have an opportunity to hire him, I'm going to," said Brady.
McSorley, a 2019 sixth-round draft pick, last suited up in the 2024 NFL Preseason. He spent the 2025 season as an assistant quarterbacks coach at his alma mater.
With the Bills, he's been working primarily with the wide receivers. We wrote about Buffalo putting his arm to use during player tryouts at training camp.
"He's been outstanding with us," said Brady. "It's been great getting him in the wide receiver room and just being able to open up his eyes. Again, he's from a quarterback perspective. He's outstanding for us. I'm so glad he's here."
Brady, a former William & Mary wide receiver who went from Penn State GA to Saints offensive assistant to LSU pass game coordinator to Carolina Panthers offensive coordinator, explained how McSorley benefits from working with another position group.
"When you're coaching positions that are different than what you're used to, I think it only improves your football IQ and your understanding," said Brady.
As someone who has climbed the ladder, Brady sees serious potential for McSorley to carve out a similar career path.
"He's going to be an outstanding QB coach, someday an OC [offensive coordinator]. He's going to be, you know, Trace is an absolute stud. But I think this will be a huge time for him just doing something different right now," said Brady.
