title: C.J. Gardner-Johnson's Second Apology for Spitting Is Too Little, Too Late for Bills DB
full_text:
Buffalo Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson is in hot water, and not just because of the spitting incident on Sunday.
Of course, Gardner-Johnson got himself ejected from the Week 6 game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday after he was caught spitting at a Raiders player.
But Gardner-Johnson, who apologized to the team after the game, is also drawing ire because of the lackluster apology he offered when speaking to reporters.
While Gardner-Johnson did admit he has to "control my emotions" better, which is certainly correct, he said the incident "wasn't nothing egregious," a truly absurd statement.
Gardner-Johnson didn't just hurt his team in Week 6, he could hurt the team for its next game, also, as the NFL could very well decide to suspend him for the inexcusable act.
Gardner-Johnson apparently saw the error in his ways after that, as he took to social media to offer a much better apology for his actions.
While he did not use the word "spit" or "spitting," Gardner-Johnson did call say the "gesture" was "inappropriate" and acknowledged how disrespectful it can be toward someone.
"I want to take a moment to address my actions and sincerely apologize to my opponent, my teammates, my organization, and everyone who supports me," Gardner-Johnson said.
"My passing and competitive nature have always been a huge part of who I am, but I also understand that there is a line that should never be crossed," Gardner-Johnson adds. "The gesture I made toward my opponent was inappropriate, unnecessary, and not a reflection of the respect I have for him or this game.
"There is no excuse for my actions, and I take full accountability. No matter how emotional or intence the competition gets, I have to hold myself to a higher standard."
It's pretty clear the Bills safety got the memo that his first attempt at an apology, or whatever that was in the locker room, simply was not good enough, hence the need for what he put down on social media on Sunday night.
The fact of the matter is, Gardner-Johnson already has a bad reputation around the NFL and we don't only base that on the fact that he has been with several different teams during his career.
San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk spoke out after the spitting incident on Sunday and revealed he, too, has been spat on by Gardner-Johnson, so this isn't just a one-off. It's a pattern of behavior for the veteran safety.
"This is the least surprising thing ever. (C.J. Garder-Johnson) spit on me last year when we beat Chicago," Juszczyk wrote .
While we appreciate the attempt at a second apology, it's already too little, too late as far as we're concerned. The first apology told us everything we needed to know about the Bills' defensive back and if the team was planning on cutting him before, the second apology shouldn't change that.

title: Early Panthers-Buccaneers Odds Revealed, But There's a Big Catch
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers are coming off two straight wins (sandwiching a needed bye week) to surge into first place in the NFC South. They were favored last time out on the road against the Philadelphia Eagles, but only after some late injury updates for Philly.
This week, they're headed back home to take on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in an early-season rivalry bout. While the Buccaneers are struggling at the bottom of the division, these matchups are always tough and important.
So, what do the odds tell us this week?
The Panthers open as 3.5-point favorites at home ( FanDuel ) over the Buccaneers. One could argue that the spread is a little too small given the trajectory of the two franchises and the most recent outings for both.
Regardless, the Panthers are favored at home. They're -105 to cover the spread, while the Buccaneers are -115 to cover. That's also a little bit interesting. The Panthers have won three contests by an average of 16 points.
The Panthers are -180 on the moneyline, so they are expected to win outright. The Buccaneers are +152 to win. The over/under is set at 44.5, and the over and under are both currently set at -110.
So, based on that, the oddsmakers expect the Panthers to win a tight contest, 24-21. In other words, the Panthers are not expected to blow out a 1-5 team at home.
Now, there is a huge caveat to these odds and what they're telling us. Right now, it is totally up in the air as to which QB the Panthers will see. Jalon Daniels has been filling in for Baker Mayfield, who has been nursing a thumb injury on his throwing hand.
He's supposed to return to practice this week, and the Buccaneers may be able to start him. His moronic, stubborn need for a revenge narrative against the Panthers will probably push him to try to play at all costs.
That would change thing. Mayfield struggled before getting hurt and will be coming back from a difficult injury on his throwing hand, which will limit him. Still, he is better than Daniels at this point, and that would shift the odds.
What's telling about the current odds is that the Panthers aren't favored by more. They are clearly the best team in the NFC South. They're at home. The Buccaneers are 1-5, and right now, Daniels is in line to start again. The Panthers are getting healthier, and they're coming off two pretty substantial wins.
It's the NFL, and any team can win any game, but the odds aren't meant to reflect that. It seems Carolina is still being wildly underestimated and perhaps a little disrespected.

title: The Panthers Finally Won the Kind of Game They Usually Find a Way to Lose
full_text:
Not every win is going to look good, and Sunday's 25-14 win over Philadelphia definitely didn't. The Panthers committed 13 penalties for a franchise-record 149 yards, couldn't run the ball early, and let an Eagles team missing several key players hang around way longer than it should have.
There will be plenty for Dave Canales to complain about when they go back and watch this one, and I'm sure the penalties will be pretty high on that list.
But I'll take an ugly win like that all day.
We've watched enough Panthers football over the last few years to know what usually happens when Carolina starts piling up mistakes. One bad penalty turns into another, the other team hangs around, and eventually you're sitting there wondering how the Panthers managed to blow another one. Sunday had a few moments where I thought we might be headed there again.
The penalties were ridiculous. Carolina had eight for 105 yards in the first half alone, something I wrote about at halftime when it was hard to believe the Panthers were still winning .
They finished with 13 for 149, and Panthers.com noted that Carolina also had three good returns wiped out by penalties , including a 50-yard kickoff return from David Moore. Somehow, the Panthers still went into halftime leading 10-7.
The offense wasn't exactly lighting it up early, either. Chuba Hubbard had only 24 yards on eight carries in the first half, and while Carolina was moving the ball, it wasn't doing enough with those drives. Against an Eagles team this beat up, I thought the Panthers should've had a much bigger lead.
Carolina didn't get away from the running game in the second half, and eventually Hubbard started finding some room. He finished with 120 yards and a touchdown on 28 carries after averaging only 3.0 yards per carry in the first half. That jumped to 4.8 yards per carry after halftime , which says a lot about why Carolina kept giving him the ball.
Bryce Young missed some throws, but he still threw for 281 yards and two touchdowns without turning the ball over. Having Jalen Coker back certainly didn't hurt. He finished with 97 yards, Tetairoa McMillan had 86, and suddenly Young had two guys on the outside making plays instead of everything falling on McMillan.
I've been high on Coker for a while. I had him No. 1 in my Panthers young player power rankings , and Sunday was a pretty good reminder of why. That's something we really haven't gotten to see much of yet with Coker and McMillan healthy together.
The defense deserves some credit here, too. Philadelphia finished with only 222 total yards, which looks even better when you consider how many yards Carolina was giving away with penalties. The Eagles didn't do much offensively for most of the afternoon, but they stayed close enough to finally make things uncomfortable in the fourth quarter.
Tanner McKee found DeVonta Smith for a 19-yard touchdown to cut Carolina's lead to 19-14. After everything the Panthers had done to keep Philadelphia in the game, the Eagles were suddenly one stop away from getting the ball back with a chance to take the lead. We've watched enough Panthers games over the years to know how that can go.
This time, Carolina answered.
Tre Tyus got pressure on Philadelphia's next punt, which went only nine yards and gave the Panthers the ball in Eagles territory. Young and the offense took advantage of it, with his 19-yard touchdown pass to Tommy Tremble pushing the lead back to 25-14. Instead of giving Philadelphia another chance to make things interesting, Carolina finally put the game away.
That's probably what I liked most about Sunday. The Panthers had spent a good part of the afternoon shooting themselves in the foot, and when Philadelphia finally got close enough to make them pay for it, Carolina didn't give the game away. They made the plays they needed to make and got out of there with a win.
I'm not going to make too much out of beating this version of the Eagles. Philadelphia was without Jalen Hurts, Saquon Barkley, and several other players, while Carolina was the healthier team. This was a game the Panthers should've won, even if they made it a lot harder than it needed to be.
But that's also why I came away liking this win a little more than I thought I would. Carolina wasn't sharp, the penalties were awful, and there were a few decisions from Canales that I still don't understand. In other years, that has been more than enough for the Panthers to find a way to lose.
That doesn't mean Carolina can keep playing this way. Give away 149 yards in penalties against Tampa Bay next Sunday, and there's a pretty good chance we're having a completely different conversation afterward. The Panthers have plenty to clean up this week, and nobody should look at Sunday and think they played particularly well.
But you're not going to play well every week. Sometimes the running game takes a while to get going, the quarterback misses some throws, or you spend half the afternoon getting in your own way. There are going to be games where you just have to get out of there with a win and worry about fixing everything else later.
That's what Carolina did in Philadelphia.
It was ugly, but 3-2 looks pretty good to me.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Panthers’ Week 1 Defensive Disaster Becoming a Distant Memory
full_text:
In 2024, the Carolina Panthers fielded one of the worst defensive units in the league in recent memory. The team was dead last in total defense and rushing defense in terms of yards allowed. The team gave up 534 points, the most in a single season in NFL history. Coordinator Ejiro Evero’s unit gave up 59 offensive touchdowns, including a league-high 35 through the air.
The following offseason, general manager Dan Morgan used free agency to add defensive linemen Tershawn Wharton and Bobby Brown III, pass rusher Patrick Jones II, and physical safety Tre’von Moehrig. The draft brought edge rushers Nic Scourton (2-Texas A&M) and Princely Umanmielen (3-Mississippi). The Panthers improved to 16th in the NFL in fewest total yards allowed, and 20th vs. the run.
Now comes the 2026 offseason. Morgan opened up the checkbook in a big way. He inked edge rusher Jaelan Phillips to a four-year, $120 million deal and 2025 Pro Bowler Devin Lloyd to a three-year, $42 million contract. In August, he added New York Giants’ castoff Bobby Okereke.
Dave Canales’s team welcomed the Chicago Bears to Bank of America Stadium on the opening Sunday of the season in a clash of defending division champions. The contest produced a combined 96 points, but the Bears had 59 of those in a 22-point road victory. It was the most points allowed by the Panthers in a game in the franchise’s 32-year history.
Posting #Bears top 3 plays of every game, in the 2026 season. Week 1: Chicago Bears @ Carolina Panthers 🏈 #1: Caleb Williams with the handoff to Kyle Monangai. Monangai runs up the middle, breaks the tackle for a 61 yard rushing touchdown. THIS WAS AN AWESOME RUN!!! 🤩 🐻⬇️ pic.twitter.com/u7FmZHA5Kn
Chicago’s offense gained a whopping 552 yards —291 yards on the ground—and averaged an imposing 7.9 yards per play. Ben Johnson’s club scored at least 14 points in each quarter. All told, not a good start for Canales’ club.
1st and 10 · Philadelphia Eagles Tanner McKee ( @McKeeTmckee ) is sacked at PHI 15 for an 11-yard loss by Bobby Okereke ( @BobbyOkereke ) https://t.co/p3gaDF1CnO pic.twitter.com/NWlRQomQPK
Talk about a turnaround? Carolina apparently learned a lot after facing Chicago’s potent attack. And this has been a much different defense ever since. In their last four contests, the Panthers have allowed a combined 64 points and six offensive TDs while permitting just 304.8 yards per game. In fact, Evero’s defense has limited three of its last four opponents to fewer than 300 yards of total offense.
The run defense has gotten better on a weekly basis. In their last four contests, Canales’s team has given up 157, 132, 46, and 35 yards on the ground, respectively. And while the club hasn’t come up with a takeaway in their last two games, the Panthers have played turnover-free in those contests.
It will be interesting to see if the recent progress continues this Sunday when the NFC South leaders host the rival Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Russell S. Baxter has been writing and researching the game of football for more than 40 years, and on numerous platforms. That includes television, as he spent more than two decades at ESPN, and was part of shows that garnered five Emmy Awards. He also spent the 2015 NFL season with Thursday Night Football on CBS/NFLN.

title: 3 Panthers Who Made a Statement in Philadelphia & 1 Thing Carolina Can't Ignore
full_text:
The Panthers came out of the bye and took care of business Sunday, beating the Eagles 25-14 in Philadelphia to improve to 3-2.
It wasn't always pretty, especially with all the penalties, but Carolina was the better team for most of the afternoon. The Panthers finished with 399 yards, didn't turn the ball over, and held Philadelphia to just 222 yards on the other side. That gives us quite a few choices for Stock Up and one pretty obvious choice for Stock Down.
I was interested to see what Coker would look like in his first game back, and it didn't take long to see how much Young missed having him out there.
Coker led Carolina with six catches for 97 yards on 13 targets, including a 32-yard catch on third-and-8 in the third quarter when the Panthers were backed up at their own 10. That drive eventually went 92 yards and ended with a Chuba Hubbard touchdown, and Coker's catch was the play that really got it started.
Before Coker went down, I had him sitting at No. 1 in my Panthers young player power rankings , and Sunday was a pretty good reminder of why. McMillan finished with six catches for 86 yards, so the two combined for 183. Young doesn't have to spend the entire game looking for McMillan when Coker is on the other side, and Sunday gave us a pretty good look at what that can mean for this offense.
Coker isn't going to have 13 targets every week, but that's not really the point. Carolina got one of Young's favorite targets back, and he immediately led the team in receiving.
I'd say Young is pretty happy to have him back.
Hubbard is another one who didn't look like an obvious Stock Up at halftime. He had eight carries for only 24 yards, and Philadelphia was doing a pretty good job of keeping Carolina from getting much going on the ground.
The Panthers didn't get away from it, though, and that ended up being a big part of the second half. Hubbard finished with 28 carries for 120 yards and a touchdown, and his 19-yard run on fourth-and-1 was one of my favorite plays of the game. Carolina needed one yard, gave the ball to Hubbard, and got 19 instead.
I've written before about how Hubbard has quietly become another weapon for Young , and Sunday was another example of how much he means to this offense. We've seen him have games where he gets stronger as they go along, and that's pretty much what happened Sunday. He averaged 3.0 yards per carry in the first half and 4.8 after halftime.
Sometimes you just keep feeding Chuba.
By the fourth quarter, Carolina was able to lean on him and make Philadelphia keep tackling him. That's the kind of game Hubbard can give this offense, and it came at a good time with the Panthers trying to protect a lead on the road.
There are going to be games where Tremble does a lot for this offense, and his receiving numbers don't really show it. Sunday wasn't one of them.
He only caught four passes, but two of them went for touchdowns. The second one was the bigger of the two for me because Philadelphia had just cut Carolina's lead to 19-14 and finally had a little momentum. Young came right back and found Tremble for a 19-yard touchdown that put Carolina up 25-14.
I also liked the way Carolina used him in the running game. On Hubbard's 19-yard fourth-down run, Tremble lined up at fullback and helped lead the way. A few plays later, Carolina showed the same look on another fourth-and-1, and Young's hard count got Philadelphia to jump.
That's probably the best way to explain Tremble's value. He can catch two touchdowns, line up at fullback and block for Hubbard, and spend the rest of the afternoon doing things that aren't always going to show up in the box score. Sunday, he finally got some numbers to go along with all of it.
There really wasn't a Panthers player I wanted to force into Stock Down after this game. The penalties, on the other hand, made this one pretty easy.
I wrote at halftime about the almost unbelievable number of Carolina penalties piling up , and somehow it got worse. The Panthers finished with 13 penalties for a franchise-record 149 yards after already having eight for 105 in the first half.
That's way too much to overcome on a regular basis. Carolina got away with it because it didn't turn the ball over, held Philadelphia to 222 yards and was facing an Eagles offense already missing starting quarterback Jalen Hurts and its first three running backs, including Saquon Barkley.
I'm not going to complain too much about an 11-point road win, but Dave Canales has plenty to point to when they watch the film. The Panthers did enough good things Sunday to win despite giving away 149 yards in penalties.
Against a better or healthier offense, they might not be so lucky.

title: Dave Canales Had Two Weeks to Prepare. Did Panthers Coach Pass the Test?
full_text:
Coming out of a bye week, I expect a team to look better. It doesn't have to be perfect, but with an extra week to look at what's working and what isn't, I want to see some evidence that the time off actually helped.
I think we saw some of that from the Panthers in Sunday's 25-14 win over Philadelphia. Carolina finished with 399 yards, didn't turn the ball over, and held the Eagles to 222 yards. More importantly, the Panthers went on the road and won a game they were supposed to win.
But if we're grading Dave Canales specifically, I can't just look at the final score and give him an A. There were things I liked, especially as the game went along, but there were also a couple of decisions that I didn't understand.
The Panthers didn't have much of a running game in the first half. Chuba Hubbard had eight carries for 24 yards, and Philadelphia was doing a pretty good job of keeping him from getting anything going.
Carolina stayed with it, and eventually Hubbard started finding room. He finished with 28 carries for 120 yards and a touchdown, including a 19-yard run on fourth-and-1 in the second half. I liked that the Panthers didn't decide after a bad first half that the running game wasn't going to work.
We also finally got to see what the passing game could look like with Jalen Coker and Tetairoa McMillan out there together. Coker finished with six catches for 97 yards, McMillan had six for 86, so the two combined for 183 yards. That's something Carolina can build on because Young doesn't have to spend the entire game depending on McMillan to make every big play.
Tommy Tremble was another part of the offense I liked. He caught four passes for 46 yards and two touchdowns, but Carolina also found other ways to use him. Tremble lined up at fullback and helped lead Hubbard on that 19-yard fourth-down run, then the Panthers showed a similar look later, and Young got Philadelphia to jump with a hard count.
The fourth quarter was probably what I liked most. Philadelphia cut the lead to 19-14 and suddenly had some life, but Carolina didn't let the game get away from them. Young and the offense answered, with Tremble's 19-yard touchdown giving the Panthers some breathing room again.
That's something this team hasn't always done very well.
The penalties are the obvious place to start. Carolina finished with 13 of them for a franchise-record 149 yards, and eight of those penalties for 105 yards came in the first half.
Canales called the number "outrageous" afterward, and that's a pretty good way to describe it. He's obviously not the one committing the penalties, and some of them were more costly than others. But when your team is coming out of a bye and gives away 149 yards, I think the head coach has to own part of that.
The decision at the end of the first half bothered me even more.
Carolina faced fourth-and-1 at its own 45 with more than 30 seconds remaining and still had all three timeouts. Canales didn't want to go for it on fourth down, which I can understand, with the Panthers already leading 10-7 and getting the ball to start the second half.
What I didn't understand was letting the clock completely run out. Why not run it down, call a timeout with a few seconds left, and at least give Young a chance to throw one toward the end zone? Maybe nothing comes from it, but there wasn't much to lose by trying.
There was another decision earlier in the half that I didn't love. Canales chose not to challenge what appeared to be an incomplete pass on Philadelphia's only touchdown drive of the first half. The play stood, the drive continued and the Eagles eventually scored.
Neither decision cost Carolina the game. That's important, but it also doesn't mean I forget about them when I'm grading the head coach.
I thought there was more good than bad from Canales and the Panthers coming out of the bye. The offense stuck with the running game, found some different ways to use Tremble, got Coker and McMillan going together, and answered when Philadelphia made it a five-point game in the fourth quarter.
But I can't get to an A with 149 penalty yards and a couple of game-management decisions that could've mattered a lot more if this game had gone differently. Carolina won on the road, improved to 3-2, and did what it was supposed to do.
I'll take the B and the win.
Mark Livingston is a South Carolina native and recent Penn State graduate with a degree in Digital Media and Journalism. He previously wrote for Greenville Sports Media, where he covered various sports and teams across the Carolinas. His experience includes game coverage, feature stories and interviews.

title: Overreaction? Panthers Winning Ugly Cements Them as Playoff Contender
full_text:
Admittedly, it’s a division that has had its issues as of late as a whole. Dating back to 2022, there has been only one example, the 2024 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, of an NFC South team finishing the season with a winning record. The Bucs were a 10-7 division champion, but were one-and-done come playoff time via a home loss to the Washington Commanders.
Of course, the Buccaneers were also an 8-9 NFC South champion in 2022, just as were the Carolina Panthers this past season. These days, Dave Canales’s club is all alone in first place in the division. On Sunday, the well-rested Panthers came away with a 25-14 over the depleted Philadelphia Eagles in the City of Brotherly Love.
How did Tommy Tremble get wide open Eagles down 11 with 6:33 to go pic.twitter.com/GeJ63YyOEd
Carolina owned a 19-7 fourth-quarter lead and the Birds would make it interesting, but Bryce Young’s second TD pass of the day to tight end Tommy Tremble with 6:33 to play gave Canales’s club a comfortable cushion.
The Panthers outgained the Eagles, 399-222, in total yards, the Birds hung around in part due to some sloppy play by the defending NFC South champions. They finished the game with 13 accepted penalties for 149 yards—six of those for 72 yards in the second quarter alone.
Canales: The penalties were outrageous. Adds afterward that he didn’t have a problem with any of the calls. pic.twitter.com/0wkq5N9BVO
Yet, Carolina still managed a double-digit victory and own a two-game winning streak for the first time since posting three consecutive victories from Weeks 5-7 in 2025.
The adage of not playing your best game and still coming up with a win certainly applies here. And the fact that no other team in the NFC South has taken the proverbial bull by the horns this season to date certainly is a factor. Both the Atlanta Falcons and New Orleans Saints own 2-4 records, and the Buccaneers are all alone in the divisional basement with a 1-5 mark. Carolina hosts Todd Bowles’s club on Sunday.
Panthers RB Chubba Hubbard Week 6 🏈 28 CAR 🏈 120 YDS 🏈 1 TD Panthers defeat the Eagles 25-14 pic.twitter.com/laajx6putG
Let’s not get it twisted. There are 12 weeks remaining in the regular season. A year ago, Carolina dropped its first two games, opened 1-3 and made the playoffs. The Houston Texans were 0-3 in 2025 and reached the postseason. Every team in the NFC South has at least four divisional games remaining. The matter here is not whether the Panthers will repeat as division champions, but are they on course to reach the playoffs for a second straight season.
Young is playing the best football of his career. Running back Chuba Hubbard has once again emerged as a reliable performer and leads the team in scrimmage yards and total touchdowns. Ejiro Evero’s defense has rebounded well after the Week 1 debacle vs. the Bears. This looks like a different Panthers’ team even compared to last season, and it adds up to a lot of optimism in Carolina.
Russell S. Baxter has been writing and researching the game of football for more than 40 years, and on numerous platforms. That includes television, as he spent more than two decades at ESPN, and was part of shows that garnered five Emmy Awards. He also spent the 2015 NFL season with Thursday Night Football on CBS/NFLN.

title: An Ugly Win Couldn't Stop Bryce Young's MVP Odds From Rising Again
full_text:
Before the bye week, Carolina Panthers fans serenaded Bryce Young with MVP chants at Bank of America Stadium after a huge win over the Detroit Lions. It felt deserved, even if there wasn't much of a chance that he could win the award.
After the bye week, Young headed to Philadelphia to take on a banged-up but battle-tested Eagles team. Despite an uneven performance against a very good defense, Young played pretty well and got the win.
Fans in Lincoln Financial Stadium, not the Panthers' home stadium, sent MVP chants at the Panthers quarterback after the game. It's stunning to hear that in a place like Philadelphia, where the fans are infamous.
Fans chanting is one thing, but MVP odds are another thing. And after the ugly win, Young's odds are on the rise, too.
For the first few weeks of the season, Bryce Young was playing really well, but there was admittedly some perception that boosted how everyone felt about his performances. The bar for him had been pretty low previously, so he looked even better by comparison.
But now, after five games in which he was no worse than pretty good in all of them, it's not a perception thing. Young simply is playing like one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL, and his rising MVP odds reflect that.
Another solid outing sent Young's odds from +5000 to +4500 on DraftKings , which is a number that would've seemed impossible in the preseason.
Peter Dewey of SI wrote, "Carolina’s Bryce Young has led his team to a top-10 showing in EPA/Play this season, and he moved from +5000 to +4500 to win MVP after another win in Week 5."
He continued, "Young threw for 281 yards and two scores on Sunday, his fifth straight game with at least 280 passing yards. He has 11 touchdown passes and just two picks, and Carolina is in the driver’s seat to win the NFC South after a 3-2 start."
The Panthers are trending in the right direction, and the biggest reason for that is Young. It's fitting that his MVP case is building, too. He still faces pretty long odds, and there are a number of really good candidates ahead of him. He would not even be a finalist if the season ended today, but he'd get some down-ballot love.
Still, after what Young went through in his first three seasons, the absolute rollercoaster ride of his career, to see him in this sort of context is nothing short of incredible.
Game odds refresh periodically and are subject to change. If you or someone you know has a gambling problem and wants help, call 1-800-GAMBLER.
Zachary Roberts is a journalist with a wide variety of experience covering basketball, golf, entertainment, video games, music, football, baseball, and hockey. He currently covers Charlotte sports teams and has been featured on Sportskeeda, Yardbarker, MSN, and On SI.

title: Panthers Surge Again in Power Rankings After Convincing Win
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers are trending in the right direction . They've won two straight contests over preseason NFC playoff contenders and are leading the NFC South in the early going.
Their defense has improved every week since a Week 1 debacle, and the offense has been pretty good (at worst) every single week. They look like a formidable foe for other teams, something that hasn't been true in a while.
That is reflected in their Power Rankings placement. Once again, after another convincing win, the Panthers are moving on up.
The Carolina Panthers came into the game ranked 21st by Sporting News' Vinnie Iyer . Now, after winning an ugly one against the Philadelphia Eagles, Carolina has surged up to 17th in the league.
Iyer wrote, "The Panthers' high-volume passing offense with Bryce Young is now averaging a league-best 294 yards per game, ahead of the Rams, who are down to 284 per game. That game plan by Dave Canales has also opened up the running game and led to winning results."
Now, there is an argument to be had that the Panthers are ranked too low here. They should have come in higher than 21st after not playing and having beat the Detroit Lions the week before. The Panthers are still being underrated.
The Los Angeles Rams ranked ahead of the Panthers, and despite all their talent, there's no argument that the Rams are better than the Panthers right now. They have an ugly loss to the Arizona Cardinals and are 2-4.
The Detroit Lions, the team Carolina beat despite not having both starting cornerbacks, is also sitting ahead of the Panthers, which is frankly ridiculous since the two teams are both 3-2 right now.
You could also make an argument that the Panthers deserve to be higher than the Cincinnati Bengals, too, but that still puts the Panthers in the top half of the rankings rather than the bottom. It's hard to justify saying the Panthers are a bottom-half NFL team right now.
This is better, however, than the Panthers inexplicably dropping in Pete Prisco's rankings last week despite not even playing. The Panthers are trending up, though, no matter which way you slice it.
And in Iyer's list, they are the highest NFC South team, as they should be. Right now, they look like the class of the division, although the bar for that is still admittedly a bit low.
Zachary Roberts is a journalist with a wide variety of experience covering basketball, golf, entertainment, video games, music, football, baseball, and hockey. He currently covers Charlotte sports teams and has been featured on Sportskeeda, Yardbarker, MSN, and On SI.

title: The Panthers Edged Out the Eagles, But These 6 Things Matter
full_text:
The Carolina Panthers should've blown out the Philadelphia Eagles. With how the two teams are currently constructed, it should have never been close, even if the final score suggests there was some space between these two teams.
So, the Panthers got a much-needed win after the bye week. But what really matters?
Pass protection on Sunday was significantly better than it has been. The biggest change? Monroe Freeling for Taylor Moton. Freeling hurt his knee, and Moton was finally ready to return, and he immediately made the entire line's performance a little bit better.
The Panthers have struggled with penalties this year. It wasn't a big issue last year, but this year, it seems every single week there's a discussion to be had about the penalties. Today, they made so many brutal mistakes, and it nearly cost them . One day, it actually will cost them a win. They literally set a franchise record for penalty yards.
Dave Canales has had two major bugaboos in his tenure. Coming out of the gate ready to play in Week 1 and bye week preparation. He got the offense rolling early this season, so that wasn't an issue. But once again, the bye week wasn't as fruitful as it's supposed to be.
Two bad mistakes by the Eagles on punts helped the Panthers out a ton. But on the other side, Carolina's inability to field a punt without committing a penalty hurt the Panthers a lot. It ruined several big returns. Special teams matter a whole lot.
When the offense isn't clicking, and the defense isn't generating turnovers, or when penalties come up at the worst possible times, can the Panthers do enough to get an ugly win? Being able to do so is the mark of a good team, and the Panthers proved today that they can do it.
Overall, it was a good day for the Panthers' defense, but that was partly because the Eagles are in utter shambles. Evero was aggressive early on, and he had the Eagles on their back foot. Then, he inexplicable let off the gas, and it allowed the Eagles to crawl back into the game. That never should've happened.

title: 3 Major Takeaways from Panthers' Exceptional Win over Eagles
full_text:
Coming off a Week 5 bye, the Carolina Panthers hit the road and took care of business, beating the Philadelphia Eagles 25-14 . Carolina largely controlled the game from bell to bell, never trailing and leading by as much as 12.
This game felt like a trap spot. The Eagles are dealing with critical injuries on offense: Jalen Hurts and Saquon Barkley are both out, the offensive line is riddled with injuries, and a retirement from RT Lane Johnson.
It was a typical letdown spot for Carolina, but not on Sunday afternoon. The Panthers did what they were supposed to do against a team playing a backup QB and with multiple hurt offensive linemen.
Carolina moves to 3-2. Here are three big takeaways from the victory.
Carolina's offense was quiet at first, but ultimately put together a phenomenal performance. The Panthers totaled 399 yards of total offense; they were close to 400 before Bryce Young took a knee to close out the game.
Carolina hasn't had a game with under 340 yards of total yards this season, and now has three games with over 395 total yards.
Brad Idzik has started the season on fire as Carolina's play-caller, and it's his first year calling the game in the NFL. At this pace, Idzik will warrant consideration for head coaching vacancies throughout the league.
After an adversity-filled 2025 season, real questions arose about whether Chuba Hubbard could once again be a bell-cow back. So far, he's passed that test with flying colors.
Hubbard was a key part of Sunday's win, logging 28 carries for 120 rushing yards and a touchdown. This is Hubbard's second straight game with 120+ rushing yards and 1+ touchdowns.
In a game where Bryce Young played well but was less efficient, Hubbard kept Carolina's offense on the field, fighting for yards after contact and finding gaps to run through.
Normally, against a depleted roster on offense, the run defense wouldn't get too much credit, but this is now two straight games of improvement in that department.
Carolina surrendered just 35 rushing yards total. The defensive line did its job by stopping inside runs, and linebackers like Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke made excellent tackles throughout the game, totaling 4 TFLs.
This performance follows Week 4, when the Panthers allowed Lions RB Jahmyr Gibbs to rush for just 46 yards on 15 carries. What was seen as this team's weak point after Week 1 is building momentum as the season goes on.
Preston is an experienced sports writer focusing on NFL, College Football, NBA, and MMA topics. He is a passionate Charlotte and Oklahoma sports fan and graduated from the University of Science and Arts Oklahoma in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Communications degree with a focus in journalism.

title: Should the Bears Start Luke Newman or Jordan McFadden in Place of Jonah Jackson?
full_text:
Many feared the worst when Bears right guard Jonah Jackson went down with a hip injury in the team's Week 6 win over the Falcons on Sunday.
The 29-year-old might not get as much credit as Joe Thuney or Darnell Wright, but he's a Pro Bowl-caliber player (and legitimate road-grader) in his own right. He was immediately listed as doubtful to return, which struck fear in the hearts of the fanbase.
However, the Bears appear to have dodged a bullet with Jackson's injury timeline. ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reports the star right guard is week-to-week with a hip flexor injury.
He'll obviously miss Thursday night's clash against New England, but could have an outside chance to play (thanks to an 11-day break) for the team's Week 8 Monday night matchup with the Seahawks.
Jackson's injury will certainly hurt in the short term. To their credit, the Bears have quality interior depth that will let them survive the loss, though.
Luke Newman took over for Jackson against Atlanta, and he held his own against Atlanta's aggressive defensive front. You could make a strong case that he's not the strongest candidate to take over the job in the meantime, though.
If Jordan McFadden's name rings a bell, you probably remember him starting at left guard in the Divisional Round matchup against the Rams last season. It was a shocking decision at the time, as the Bears moved LG Joe Thuney to left tackle for an injured Ozzy Trapilo.
They felt better about having McFadden, who played two regular-season snaps and spent much of the year on the practice squad, in the lineup over Theo Benedet, who started eight games at left tackle. While Jared Verse's presence surely played a role in the decision, the Rams' interior defensive line was also far from permeable.
McFadden promptly made them look smart for showing confidence in him, too. The Bears might've left with a disappointing 20-17 loss, but their offense looked the part despite the frigid defeat. They put up 417 yards and averaged 5.1 yards per play. The former practice squad guard didn't look out of place, either.
The Bears saw enough from McFadden to reward him with a one-year extension (despite already having quality depth along the line) this offseason. They clearly liked what he put on tape.
Sure, Newman played well against the Falcons. He'd probably do the same against the Patriots' defensive front (although Milton Williams' speed could give him trouble).
However, McFadden already proved he can hold his own in a tougher test, and that's exactly what the Bears will have if Jackson isn't ready by the time they take on Seattle. He should get the first crack at the starting job for however long Jackson is out of action.

He has survived the 2010 NFC Championship Game, a career-ending injury to his favorite player (Johnny Knox), the Bears' 2013 season finale, a Double Doink, Mitchell Trubisky, Justin Fields, and Weeks 8-17 of the 2024 NFL season. Nevertheless, he still Bears Down!

title: Bears NFL Power Rankings For Week 7: Williams, Gordon Propel Chicago Into Top 10
full_text:
My, what a difference two players can make, something we saw in the Chicago Bears' Week 6 win over the Atlanta Falcons.
The Bears welcomed back Caleb Williams and Kyler Gordon on Sunday, and both made massive impacts in their respective returns to the field.
Williams completed 30-of-36 passes for 305 yards and one score, and Gordon was an absolute menace in his own right with three sacks and two forced fumbles while playing just 17 snaps.
Thanks to their performances, the Bears notched a victory and are now moving up in the NFL power rankings of experts for Week 7, going as high as into the top five of one expert's rankings.
Ranking: 5 | Last week: 13
This is the biggest leap up for the Bears in our power rankings round-up.
Orr rightly points out just how massive of a difference it made for the Bears to have Caleb Williams and Kyler Gordon back.
"Caleb Williams's return was spectacular. But so, too, was bringing Kyler Gordon back into this defense as a no-nonsense nickel blitzer that will make Chicago not only the most fun offense to watch in the NFL, but one of the most unpredictable and enjoyable defenses as well," Orr said.
Ranking: 4 | Last week: 10
Davis gets cute here and talks about the impact of "getting a key guy back," but mentions Kyler Gordon only, not Caleb Williams.
"They looked awfully good after getting a key guy back … and we're referring to DB Kyler Gordon, who had three sacks − again, he's a DB − and two forced fumbles in his 2026 debut on Sunday, all in 17 snaps. He's the first player at his position to have such a game in 26 years," Davis said.
We know Davis is trying to be funny and Gordon deserves a ton of credit for what was a historic performance in 17 snaps, but let's not forget the offense looking vastly better upon the return of QB1, who was sensational.
Ranking: 9 | Last week: 13
ESPN's Courtney Cronin was asked to list the biggest issue on the offensive side of the ball right now and she picked penalties, which is certainly a logical choice.
Chicago had 12 penalties on Sunday, including eight in the first half alone, and a lot of them were holding flags.
"One area that can stand to be cleaned up more is offensive penalties, which accounted for seven of the Bears' infractions Sunday. Those offensive penalties helped generate Chicago's most penalty yardage in a game since 2016 (133). The Bears are currently tied for the third-most offensive holding penalties (10). That's an area they'll want to fix so it doesn't derail drives," she said.
Another issue on offense is the absence of Kyle Monangai. Sure, Roschon Johnson played pretty well, but he also had a costly fumble and he just isn't as good as Monangai.
Unfortunately, the second-year back is headed toward sitting out again after he was an estimated non-participant on Monday. A short week will make it difficult for him to get back.
Ranking: 13 | Last week: 15
The Bears are still climbing their way out of the hole they landed in with Prisco after the abysmal Week 5 showing against the Green Bay Packers, with this being the lowest ranking in our round-up.
"Bouncing back from the loss to the Packers by winning on the road at Atlanta is a good look for this team," Prisco said. "Of course it helps to have Caleb Williams back."
In the three games the Bears have had Williams on the field in 2026, they've dropped 30 or more points in two of them. Not that it needed to be said, but this is a very different offense when he's under center.

title: Tory Taylor Has Developed Into A Legitimate Weapon For the Bears
full_text:
Bears punter Tory Taylor began his career with extremely high expectations after being selected in the fourth round of the 2024 NFL Draft . He became only the fifth punter to come off the board before the fifth round since 2008.
Only the special punters are that highly coveted, and Taylor fit that billing at the collegiate level. The Iowa State product was on campus during a period of significant offensive turmoil, and he was arguably the Hawkeyes' best player. He set a single-season punting yardage record with 4,479 yards on 93 punts and earned unanimous All-American honors and the Ray Guy Award for his efforts.
Expectations don't always translate to initial excitement when it comes to making the jump to the NFL, though. Many questioned Ryan Poles' decision to prioritize a punter with Chicago coming off a disappointing 7-10 campaign. They had many weaknesses, and a punter certainly wasn't going to help them develop into a contender.
Conventional wisdom says that a team coming off a rough season should prioritize positions of need on offense or defense. As it turns out, conventional wisdom isn't exactly batting a thousand when it comes to early-round punters, as the 2021 Buccaneers were the only team of the aforementioned five to have a winning record before pulling the trigger on a hopeful field-flipper.
We're starting to see why Poles prioritized Taylor, though. The Iowa State product is paying major dividends this season.
With Chicago's offense firmly among the league's best, Taylor's punting stats don't really pop off the screen. His 17 punts are tied for ninth-fewest in the league, and all but three players with fewer attempts have played fewer than six games. He's also tied for seventh in the league with 49.3 yards per punt.
However, his affinity for "banana ball" punts, which wobble sideways rather than end-over-end, makes him unique from his peers. The technique, which Taylor picked up from his Australian Rules background, makes it tough for returners to field the ball cleanly.
So far this season, Chicago has recovered two muffed punts after opponents put the ball on the ground. The first occurred in the regular season, when Panthers receiver Jimmy Horn Jr. failed to wrangle a punt in the third quarter. Falcons rookie receiver Zachariah Branch was the latest victim, muffing a punt just before halftime on Sunday. The Bears enjoyed great field position and promptly capitalized with touchdowns.
Tory Taylor best punter in the league pic.twitter.com/ZFzSt5LxdG
Taylor shed some light on the technique after the Week 1 victory. He actually said that a standard punt is more difficult for him to hit consistently than the banana ball approach.
"Americans, they didn't really grow up playing Australian Rules Football, so it's easy when you're just building it from the ground up," Taylor said. "I've had to change so many things. Get rid of so many poor habits that I've had in the past and I've got to get new ones to be able to like get consistent spirals."
Bears special teams coordinator Richard Hightower also praised Taylor for his performance to begin the season after the team's disappointing Week 5 loss against the Packers.
Richard Hightower on Tory Taylor's Performance So Far: "He made a choice to put the team in better situations, and he's doing that at a high level. We want fewer opportunities on punt return, but more production when we do get them. The protection and coverage have done a decent… pic.twitter.com/wW7UH8n8tz
It took some time, but Ryan Poles' vision finally came to fruition. Taylor has not only cemented his status as one of the league's best punters, but he's also developed into a legit weapon for Hightower's unit.

Nevertheless, he still Bears Down!

title: Bears Receiver Defended After Two Numbskull Plays Against Falcons
full_text:
Wide receiver Jahdae Walker's energy often fuels special teams and also helped the Bears offense in the past when he did get a few passing game reps.
He's testing the patience of coaches, though, when he has a Sunday like he had against the Falcons. Fortunately for Walker, the play of Bears special teams overall on Sunday was so good it overshadowed some of his foul-ups, but not entirely.  They took the ball away twice on teams, which often changes the flow of games.
One troubling mistake came when he head-butted Falcons wide receiver Chris Blair in a dead-ball situation following a kickoff in full view of the officials. Not only did the penalty cost the Bears 15 yards of field position, but it caused his ejection from the game. There was no arguing about the call as it was blatant and appeared unprovoked.
After the game, Bears coach Ben Johnson noted how much the mistakes bothered Walker, and special teams coordinator Richard Hightower seconded this after film review on Monday.
“With a player like Jahdae, I can just tell you when I got to the locker room, because obviously he had to go to the locker room (ejected), he was damn near in tears," Hightower said. "He was very remorseful because he knew what he did affected the team and it hurt the team.
Jahdae Walker screwed up with this headbutt. But he shouldn’t have been ejected. Seems a bit extreme. #DaBears pic.twitter.com/DkA0ubkEqr
"But what I will say is that Jahdae plays with a tremendous amount of passion, and I'm not going to coach the passion out of him. We want the passion, we just want it in between the whistles."
Daniel Hardy had just made tackle at the 19 on kick coverage to back up the Falcons offense and the flag put them at the 34, instead.
"He's very remorseful for that, and that's not in his personality," Hightower said. "He does not want to hurt the team. We have just got to be better going forward with that, and he knows he has to be better in that case."
Bears scoring on an outside zone run variation (Zorro). Love watching Jahdae Walker (#9) here. Hits his block with a full head of steam and is fired up after. pic.twitter.com/7U5mRonD1W
Walker had one penalty on offense last year against Cincinnati that nullified a 32-yard gain. He has three already this year, including one other costly mistake in Sunday's game. That was when he crashed into the plant leg of Falcons punter Jake Bailey. The 15-yard penalty prevented the Bears from taking possession of the ball on the punt, but their defense held up to the pressure following the gaffe.
"That one's a technique issue," Hightower said. "On that particular play, he didn't use the technique that we would like to see him use. You never really want to leave your feet there. You want to stay a sprinter so that you gain momentum, and you want to shoot your hands low and late at the block point.
Jahdae Walker runs into the punter Ben Johnson is pissed pic.twitter.com/zJGvpyLSLE
"If I shoot my hands too early, then I slow down and I'm further away from the punter. I want to stay a sprinter and shoot my hands low and late, and I don't want to leave my feet. The reason why is, when you leave your feet and you lose control of your body, then usually you can run into the plant leg, and what happens is what you guys saw happen there. The difference in running into the kicker and roughing the kicker is also something that you got to take into account because it's fourth-and-11 there."
The minor penalty wouldn't have resulted in a first down.
"So, 15-yard penalty; but credit to the defense," Hightower said. "They stood up, no-blink mentality, and they had his back. They had Jahdae’s back there.”
Now it's Walker who has to pay back some of this support with big plays on special teams or offense rather than making silly mistakes.
Walker can look forward to Saturday when the league announces its fines. He can make it up to teammates for the yardage cost on two 15-yard penalties with his play, but the ultimate cost for the head butt and ejection seems likely to come out of his wallet.
Richard Hightower on Jahdae Walker's Ejection: "He was very remorseful because he knew what he did affected the team, But Jahdae plays with a tremendous amount of passion, and I'm not going to coach the passion out of him. We want the passion, we just want it in between the… pic.twitter.com/ELjbTCn07h

title: Jonah Jackson Injury Update Leaves Bears Guard's Week 7 Status in Serious Doubt
full_text:
The Chicago Bears may not have the services of right guard Jonah Jackson for the Week 7 game against the New England Patriots on Thursday night.
According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler , Jackson is dealing with a hip flexor and is believed to be week-to-week as a result.
Fowler adds that Jackson's status for Week 7 is in doubt, but the good news is Jackson's injury is not believed to be a long-term problem.
"Bears OG Jonah Jackson has a hip flexor injury and is considered week-to-week, per source. Status for TNF in doubt but shouldn’t be long term," Fowler reported.
Jackson came down with his injury in the second half of the Week 6 win over the Atlanta Falcons. He was listed as doubtful after exiting but didn't return to the game.
The seventh-year guard was on the team's first injury report of the week and was oficially listed with a hip and quadriceps issues.
The injury report was an estimation,but Jackson was a labeled as a non-participant, which was the first sign his Week 7 status was in trouble.
Given the fact that the Bears are operating on a short week, his chances of playing are very slim.
Jackson is in the midst of a fantastic season for Chicago. He has grades of 83.9 overall, 81.5 in run-blocking and 73.7 in pass pro, ranking fifth, seventh and 18th among guards, respectively, according to Pro Football Focus .
After Jackson exited on Sunday, the Bears deployed fellow guard Luke Newman in his stead, so we'd assume that is who will get the call if Jackson is ruled out for Thursday night.
Newman played 27 snaps in place of Jackson and held up well while not giving up a single pressure and posting a solid 69.9 pass protection grade, according to Pro Football Focus . Newman also recorded a run-blocking grade of 63.0.
Jordan McFadden is another potential option, but he was listed among the team's inactives on Sunday, so it appears Newman is ahead of him on the depth chart.
Newman was a sixth-round pick of the Bears in 2025 and has 15 career games under his belt, but he has never started during his career. Newman has 54 career snaps on offense in relief duty, along with 76 snaps on special teams.
Prior to his 27 snaps in Week 6, the last time Newman saw significant playing time came in Week 12 of last season, when he appeared for 22 snaps.

title: Kyle Monangai Injury Update and More From Bears' Monday Practice Report For Week 7
full_text:
The Chicago Bears have put out their first injury report of the week ahead of the Week 7 game against the New England Patriots.
Because the Bears play on Thursday night this week, the first injury report comes out on Monday, and it's just an estimation because the Bears did not hold an actual practice and instead conducted a walkthrough.
The three biggest names we're keeping an eye on this week are running back Kyle Monangai, right guard Jonah Jackson and linebacker T.J. Edwards.
Now, a look at the Bears' full injury report for Monday
The three most important players on the list, Monangai, Edwards and Jackson, were all estimated non-participants, which leaves them in a lackluster spot to begin the week.
We know Monangai is dealing with a turf toe injury that has kept him out for two games in a row. Monangai was initially labeled as week-to-week and he has not practiced since coming down with his injury.
Edwards missed his first game of the season in Week 6 with the hamstring issue, and Jackson exited the win over the Atlanta Falcons early with his hip and quadriceps injuries.
On Monday, offensive coordinator Press Taylor did not offer an update on the Bears' right guard.
"We'll see where Jonah's at and if he's got a chance to play on Thursday night," he said . "But we're excited about the depth we have there.
We're skeptical all three will suit up in Week 7 because it is a short week, which means each player has less time to get right.
If Jackson sits, fellow guard Luke Newman figures to take over for him after the former sixth-round pick was called into duty when Jackson got injured on Sunday.
The Bears will likely continue to roll with running back Roschon Johnson if Monangai is absent again, and linebacker D'Marco Jackson will start in place of Edwards.
Linebacker Jack Sanborn is a new addition to the injury report. There was no news from the team during the game about his concussion, so he amounts to a surprise.
After sitting out in Week 6, both cornerback Tyrique Stevenson and rookie linebacker Keyshaun Elliott were both upgraded, which puts them on track to return. Stevenson logged only limited practices last week, while Elliott did not practice at all.
The Bears will drop their second injury report of the week on Tuesday, and it won't be an estimate because the Bears will conduct a regular practice.

title: Bears Facing Patriots Roster With Even Worse Injury Luck This Week on 'TNF'
full_text:
The Chicago Bears didn't escape a 31-23 win over the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium unscathed. Starting right guard Jonah Jackson left the game with a hip injury and may not be back in time for the team's Thursday Night Football matchup with the New England Patriots.
New England may be even worse for wear after a 26-19 win over the New York Jets , though.
The Patriots lost receiver Romeo Doubs (shoulder), right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle), left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring), and backup interior offensive lineman Ben Brown (knee) against the Jets.
New England head coach Mike Vrabel didn't sound overly optimistic that he'd get the majority of them back with just four days to recover.
"I mean, again, listen, we are all smart people here, some smarter than others. But it's a short week," Vrabel said postgame . "So whether they can make it back or not, I don't know. They don't finish the game. We'll have to see. But I don't know any other thing other than that. And we'll just have to figure out who we have available and find 48 to put out there. So it's just hard to say, but it's a short week. And if you don't finish the game, that's a quick turnaround."
The Patriots got a solid efforts from the fill-in offensive line. Doubs is the leading receiver by catches, though. He may be significantly harder to replace as Drake Maye's favorite target this season by volume.
Chicago got key contributors back from injury against Atlanta.
Quarterback Caleb Williams was the most important returning star, and he delivered a masterclass performance. Williams completed 30-of-36 passes for 305 yards and one score in his first game in a month.
Nickel Kyler Gordon also made his return. Gordon had not played a game since the NFC Divisional Round in January, but it was hard to tell. He had three sacks, four tackles total, and two forced fumbles against the Falcons.
Last but not least, left tackle Ozzy Trapilo made his long-awaited return, playing mostly special teams snaps but rotating in behind fill-in starter Theo Benedet on the blindside.
The Bears probably won't get running back Kyle Monangai back, but they'll still be in good shape heading into "TNF," all things considered.
Let's not pretend that New England will be the only team dealing with significant wounds and key absences.
The Patriots' offensive line will be facing a Chicago defensive front that's lacking key difference-makers like linebacker T.J. Edwards, and edge rushers Dayo Odeyingbo and Montez Sweat.
Edwards and Odeyingbo are injured, while Sweat is serving the second game of a two-game suspension over PED use on Thursday Night Football.
All in all, the Bears' issues aren't as fresh as New England's, and there's enough good injury news to leave those issues on the backburner.
Still, Chicago isn't anywhere close to 100% and won't be for a while.

title: Chicago Bears Reunite With Defensive Back Ahead of Week 7 Game vs. Patriots
full_text:
The Chicago Bears are making an addition to their practice squad ahead of the Week 7 game against the New England Patriots on Thursday night.
The Bears announced on Monday that they have signed defensive back KC Eziomume to the practice squad.
Eziomume was with the Bears during the offseason before he came down with an injury that led to him being waived with an injury designation on Aug. 8.
Eziomume was one of the Bears' initial 2026 undrafted free-agent signings. He played his final season of college ball at Tulane and tallied one pass break-up in seven contests.
Prior to his stint at Tulane, the 6-foot-1, 198-pound defensive back appeared in four games with Alabama A&M, totaling five tackles.
If Eziomume is able to get into a game for the Bears, he will be making his NFL debut. He did not play a snap during the preseason, as his injury occurred before Week 1.
Eziomume will be taking the practice squad spot of cornerback Nick McCloud, who was promoted to the active roster over the weekend on the same day veteran safety Xavier Woods was waived.
It was surprising to see the Bears cut Woods loose. After all, he had started in two games this season and was playing a key role with the Bears dealing with injuries in the secondary. Woods was waived on the same day slot cornerback Kyler Gordon was activated off the physically unable to perform list.
The Bears are also dealing with an injury in their cornerbacks room with Tyrique Stevenson, who is battling a hip issue . Stevenson was able to practice on a limited basis throughout last week and had a questionable tag but was ultimately inactive for Sunday's game.
Given the fact that Stevenson practiced on a limited basis last week tells us he has a decent chance to return in Week 7, but playing on a short week might complicate things.
We'll know more about Stevenson's status on Monday and over the next few days, when the Bears put out their injury reports.
Even when he returns, Stevenson isn't going to have much of a role. Gordon's return puts him back in the slot, and that moves Malik Muhammad to the boundary opposite Jaylon Johnson.
The Bears are still going to need some snaps from Muhammad in the slot until Gordon is fully ramped up, something defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said could take more time .

title: Kyler Gordon's Playing Time and Other Bears Snap Count Observations From Week 6 Win
full_text:
The Chicago Bears came away with an impressive 31-23 win over the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday.
The final score doesn't paint an accurate picture of the contest, as Chicago controlled the tempo of the game for the first 49 (and final four) minutes. They had a few strong contributors on both offense and defense, including incredible performances by two returning franchise cornerstones on both sides of the ball.
This was another game with a lopsided time-of-possession difference, as they had 77 snaps on offense compared to 55 on defense. Chicago actually rested some key defensive starters for one drive at the start of the fourth quarter (a fact that almost came back to bite them).
The most impressive aspect of the offensive snap count was the fact that Luther Burden III blew up the stat sheets (he led the team with eight catches for 95 yards) despite playing only 39% of the snaps. He was heavily involved in the gameplan and could explode with more playing time.
Meanwhile, Rome Odunze 's stat line (three catches, 39 yards) looks a bit empty with him being on the field for 74 plays, but he did have a 24-yard catch-and-run taken away due to a penalty.
Jahdae Walker and Zavion Thomas both played ten snaps, and their roles are becoming clearly defined as the season progresses. Walker didn't see any targets, but made a few key blocks in the running game. Meanwhile, Thomas caught three passes for 25 yards despite seeing limited action. It felt like a concerted effort to get him involved.
Sam Roush continues to play a healthy dose of snaps, as Ben Johnson has no interest in throwing in the towel on that experiment anytime soon.
The Bears also had three backup offensive linemen get into the action against Atlanta. We knew Ozzy Trapilo would be out there, and it was good to see them actually rotate him in at left tackle rather than letting him get his feet wet in jumbo personnel. They'll eventually expect him to take over for Theo Benedet there once he's ready to play a full complement of snaps.
Jonah Jackson going down with a hip injury was hugely disappointing, as he's arguably been their most underrated offensive lineman this season. However, they didn't skip a beat with Luke Newman taking over for him for 27 snaps. Second-round selection Logan Jones also got his first taste of regular-season NFL action late in the contest for a resting Garrett Bradbury.
Kyler Gordon getting three sacks and forcing two fumbles despite playing only 17 snaps is not only the biggest story for the Bears , but it's the biggest story across the entire league this week. That's ridiculous production in limited playing time. Unsurprisingly, he leads all defensive backs in sacks this season despite debuting yesterday.
Devin Bush and Noah Sewell deserve a world of credit for keeping Bijan Robinson in check this week. As expected, the Bears were in their base defense more often this week, and they finished first and second on the team in tackles (Sewell getting six tackles and one TFL despite playing half the snaps is especially impressive). That's the type of output you want to see from the guys in the middle.
Austin Booker was a bit quieter this week, but their added attention to him might've been a factor that led to Gordon and Daniel Hardy eating on the other side. To Hardy's credit, he also had a strong performance in relief of Montez Sweat, finishing with two QB hits and one sack.
Defensive tackle James Lynch also saw by far his heaviest snap count of the season. While he didn't finish the contest with any tackles, he did do a great job of getting his hands on a pass on fourth down.
It was also good to see cornerback Clark Phillips III finally get into the action on the defensive side of the ball against his former team. While he wasn't nearly as flashy as Gordon, he also got some heat on Penix coming off the edge a few times. The Falcons had no answer for Chicago's aggressive gameplan.
Meanwhile, defensive lineman Shemar Turner didn't play nearly as much as some expected in his season debut. They'll probably ease the 2025 second-round pick into the lineup slowly, and he'll have to make some big plays to secure more playing time.
Jerry Markarian has been an avid Chicago Bears fan since 2010 and has been writing about the team since  2022.  He has survived the 2010 NFC Championship Game, a career-ending injury to his favorite player (Johnny Knox), the Bears' 2013 season finale, a Double Doink, Mitchell Trubisky, Justin Fields, and Weeks 8-17 of the 2024 NFL season. Nevertheless, he still Bears Down!

title: Why the Bears Must Trade for Colts' Star DT After Chris Ballard Firing
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts made waves on Monday morning, giving the NFL world its first firing of the 2026 season. General manager Chris Ballard has been fired after 10 years with the Colts, following a disastrous loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans. Head coach Shane Steichen has not been fired, but this only fuels speculations that the Colts are about to undergo the kind of fire-sale that the Miami Dolphins did a year ago when they fired Chris Grier but retained head coach Mike McDaniel.
In many ways, the Colts would be better off trading away their best players before the deadline, and the Chicago Bears should stand ready to benefit from their chaos. Specifically, the general manager Ryan Poles ought to make a phone call to gauge the trade value of one player in particular: two-time All-Pro defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.
Buckner is currently experiencing something of a renaissance season. Despite turning 32-years-old in March, he's already up to four sacks through six weeks this season. He's the third-highest ranked defensive tackle according to Pro Football Network , earning a 92.8 impact grade. He missed some time in each of the last two seasons, but over the previous three years, Buckner had racked up 23 total sacks without missing a game.
This is exactly the kind of player the Bears should be targeting as they continue their march towards the playoffs. Though they've had their moments, the defensive line play has not been up to snuff, and it's not likely to get better with Montez Sweat suspended for one more game and Dayo Odeyingbo currently on Injured Reserve. That is, unless they make a trade for a player like Buckner.
Big No. 99 would immediately slot into Chicago's starting lineup alongside Grady Jarrett. This would push Kentavius Street back into a rotational backup role, which is where he can do his best work.
Despite his impressive resume, Buckner is well past being the kind of trade target that would be deemed a 'blockbuster move'. As aforementioned, he's 32 years old and is playing on the last year of his contract. Any trade for Buckner at this point would most likely be a one-year rental with potential for a small, two-year contract extension.
With that in mind, and considering the Colts' desperate position, I would imagine that the Bears could send Indianapolis the fifth-round pick they acquired by trading Gervon Dexter Sr. to the Falcons , and that might be sufficient to bring on Buckner. Remember, the Bears got future Hall of Fame guard Joe Thuney for only a fourth-round pick, so a fifth-rounder is a reasonable price for both sides.
In this mock trade, the Bears would score a serious upgrade along their defensive line, the Colts would free up some salary cap space and add a draft pick to their war chest, and Buckner could finally play for a legit contender. Pick up the phone, Ryan Poles, before someone else does.
A former Marine and Purdue Boilermaker, Pete has been covering the Chicago Bears since 2022 as a senior contributor on BearsTalk. He lives with his wife, two kids and loyal dog.

title: Bengals Fill 53-Man Roster Entering Ravens Matchup, Add LB to Practice Squad
full_text:
The Bengals made a couple of back-end roster moves on Tuesday. Cincinnati announced practice squad shuffling, with safety Russ Yeast signed to the active roster.
On the practice squad, Cincinnati released safety Isaiah Nwokobia and signed tight end Josh Kattus. The latter had been with the team this summer and went unsigned to start the season.
They also added a linebacker to the practice squad in Emany Johnson, who spent time with Dallas in 2024. He tallied his rookie season on the practice squads of the Cowboys and L.A. Chargers. Johnson played the entire 2025 campaign on the Chargers’ practice squad. He did not suit up for any team in practice or on the playing field to start this season.
Johnson notched a 49.8 defensive Pro Football Focus grade on 86 preseason snaps this year and a 74.5 grade on 149 snaps last year.
It's a minor shakeup for a pretty locked-in roster entering Week 7. Cincinnati should be getting Jalen Davis and Andrei Iosivas back from injured reserve in the coming weeks, while the only injury to monitor is a week-to-week Kyle Dugger (quad).
The pass-catching group has to pick up a little more slack without depth tight end Tanner Hudson for the rest of the season. He's out for months with a torn pec.
"I think we'll call on the whole room in the receiver room. We're getting healthy at the receiver room too, so I think just combining both those rooms and dispersing how those roles will play out is something we're always open to week to week," Bengals head coach Zac Taylor said on Monday. "We feel like we've got a lot of people with a lot of different strengths that can all play at a high level in both those rooms, and just finding ways to game plan for those guys, get them involved, is important for us."
Cincinnati has Tuesday off before returning to practice on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. They are in a tight AFC North race with a massive road game on deck under the sun in Baltimore this weekend.
That contest kicks off at 1 p.m. ET on Sunday.

title: Blockbuster Trade Idea Gives Bengals Final Piece on Offense
full_text:
Week 6 of the NFL offered more clarity on who could compete for the playoffs this season. After Sunday's conclusion, almost half of the AFC have a record of .500 or worse, including the Indianapolis Colts, who lost to the formerly 0-5 Titans. This led the Colts to fire general manager Chris Ballard and sparked speculation that they could offload veteran talent as they sit at 2-4.
This should prompt the Bengals to strike a deal with the Colts for a difference-maker in Jonathan Taylor to bolster their run game and remain competitive in the AFC North.
Taylor would immediately skyrocket the Bengals running back room to the stratosphere, as the unit has dramatically underwhelmed to start the season.
Taylor has routinely excelled on runs from under center throughout his career. This season he has averaged 4.4 yards per carry when under center compared to 3.4 yards per carry out of shotgun. He would allow Zac Taylor and the offense to continue building their offense from under center.
While his total 3.9 YPC this season may cause some to worry, the situation with the Colts is much different than it would be in Cincinnati . Daniel Jones and the Indianapolis receivers are less than half of what Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins are. Because the passing game poses little threat, opposing defenses have focused heavily on stacking the box to stop Taylor. That focus intensified last week when the Colts lost to the Steelers, who stopped Taylor by stacking the box with eight defenders on 80% of his runs.
With Chase and Higgins at receiver, and given Burrow's ability to dissect defenses, Taylor would arguably have the most open space of his career if he lands with the Bengals.
Taylor has maintained his dominant level of play through six games this season despite his lower numbers and is currently on pace for 1,394 rushing yards and 20 touchdowns. Adding that level of talent to a running back unit that has consistently handicapped the offense in the Burrow era would add another dynamic layer to an already dangerous offense.
Acquiring Taylor would require trading away a premium asset and more, as the closest comparison is likely what the 49ers gave up to acquire Christian McCaffrey from the Panthers in 2022. The 49ers traded a second, third, and fourth-round pick in the 2023 draft, along with a 2024 fifth-round pick, to get McCaffrey.
That is the ceiling on what Taylor's cost likely is. The realistic package for him would likely be somewhere in the middle in the form of a 2027 second-round pick, along with a Day 3 pick. He signed a two-year, $44 million extension before the season; however, the Bengals would only pay his remaining $6.98 million in base salary and incentives this season, since the Colts have already paid his signing bonus.
What could make a hypothetical deal more interesting is what the Bengals can offer alongside draft compensation compared to other teams. The team could make negotiations with Indianapolis more interesting by including underutilized players in the deal, such as Shemar Stewart.
Stewart's played just 17 snaps over the first six weeks of the season. He is a former first-round pick, and those players typically command solid compensation, as the Cardinals got a second- and sixth-round pick for Marvin Harrison Jr.
Including Stewart in a deal for Taylor could shrink the draft assets the Bengals give up.
Acquiring Taylor is a move the front office must consider after they acquired Dexter Lawrence in a blockbuster deal to transform the defense this offseason. Six months later, they have another chance to add a proven superstar to the team. The trade deadline is in three weeks on November 10th at 4 PM EST.

title: Revenge Game? Orlando Brown Jr. Weighs In on Bengals Facing Trey Hendrickson
full_text:
The Cincinnati Bengals are gearing up for a very important early season game against the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday.
Not only is this game a massive meeting for AFC North supremacy, but it's also the first time the Bengals will face former defensive end Trey Hendrickson.
Hendrickson moved on from the Bengals and joined one of the three teams this fan base would have preferred he not sign with. The former Bengals star may have a pep in his step when he takes the field in Week 7.
On Monday, Ben Baby spoke with Orlando Brown Jr. about the matchup with his former teammate. The Bengals are definitely expecting more spark from their former teammate.
"Just the way things ended here, from a personal and player perspective, I get it. I've been in that position before as well," Brown said when asked if Hendrickson would have extra motivation on Sunday. "I imagine he will have a little something extra to play for."
Brown also went on to say that he expects Hendrickson's best on Sunday because every time he has went up against the former Bengals star, he has gotten his best.
Hendrickson has missed two games this season with the Ravens, but returned on Sunday in the team's 13-10 loss to the Cleveland Browns in Week 6.
The Ravens pass rusher earned his second sack of the season against the Browns. Hendrickson has been dealing with issues with his finger after having a surgery, but it seems like there's no chance in this world he will miss the opportunity to go after Joe Burrow this week.
"He's a good player," Bengals head coach Zac Taylor said. "They got a lot of good players on their defense and we got to put together a great plan and be able to execute it to give ourselves the best chance to win."
Bragging rights will be on the line Sunday, but there's more than that at stake. With the bye week, the Bengals fell to last place in the AFC North at 3-2, while the other teams are 4-2. A win on Sunday will put the Bengals back in a good spot in the division race. A loss means the Bengals will move to 0-2 in the division, putting them a lot further behind than they would like.
The talk leading up to this game will be about Hendrickson, and rightfully so. All four of his Pro Bowl selections and his First-Team All-Pro honors came with the Bengals. But even he knows this game is more than earning bragging rights over his former home. This game has major postseason ties to it. The Bengals will need to bring their A game.
