title: No. 8 Is Coming Back; Eight Reasons Why Josh Jacobs Must Save Run Game
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs will get a “full week of practice” this week and could play at the Detroit Lions on Sunday, coach Matt LaFleur said on Monday.
Goodness knows, they need him.
Jacobs spent the first six games of the season on the exempt list following an off-the-field incident with a female over Memorial Day Weekend. He was removed from the exempt list on Monday but isn’t necessarily in the clear.
While Jacobs hasn’t practiced since the end of training camp, he’s been working out with the training staff and participating in team meetings, so he shouldn’t need a ramp-up like a player coming off a significant injury.
“Well, that’s to be determined,” LaFleur said of Jacobs’ readiness. “We feel like he’s in a pretty good spot. He’s been training, but he’s missed the exposure to football.”
The Packers don’t just need Jacobs. They desperately need him. Just look at the numbers.
Green Bay’s rushing attack is the worst in the NFL by a considerable margin. Here are eight statistics that show the complete ineptitude.
One: The Packers are 32nd in the NFL with 59.8 rushing yards per game and 2.87 yards per carry. They are last in both categories by considerable margins: 16.2 yards per game behind Dallas and 0.14 yards per carry behind the Raiders.
The Chargers in 2000 averaged a record-low 66.4 rushing yards per game.
Two: The Packers’ best rushing day this season was their 86 yards against Tampa Bay in Week 4. There have been 45 individual games of more than 86 rushing yards this season.
The Packers’ best rushing day in terms of efficiency was their 3.5 yards per carry against the Jets in Week 2. That best day would rank 30th in the NFL over the course of the season.
Three: On first-down running plays, the Packers are averaging a worst-in-the-league 2.25 yards per carry. The Raiders are 31st with a 2.81-yard average. A total of 26 teams are averaging at least one more yard per carry. Against Dallas, the Packers’ first-down average plunged to 1.47 yards per carry.
Four: Yards before contact can be an offensive line stat, but it obviously can be swayed by a player’s ability to get through a hole or make someone miss. According to Stathead, the Packers have a league-low 239 yards before contact. Their 1.9-yard average is 31st.
With Jacobs, the Packers were 26th with 2.2 yards before contact per carry in 2025 and 17th with 2.4 yards before contact per carry in 2024.
Five: Yards after contact is almost totally a running back stat, though speed through a hole and getting to the second level with the offensive line matters. The Packers are last with 120 yards after contact and 31st with 1.0 yards after contract per carry, according to Stathead.
With Jacobs, the Packers were 13th with 1.9 yards after contact per carry in 2025 and third with 2.4 yards after contact per carry in 2024.
Six: Green Bay’s rushing success this season is 34.3 percent, which ranks 30th. A “successful” play gains at least 40 percent of the required yards on first down (a 4-yard run on first-and-10 would be a success), 60 percent of the required yards on second down and 100 percent of the required yards on third and fourth down. Jacobs had individual success rates of 52.2 percent in 2024 and 49.1 percent in 2025.
Seven: A “stuff” is a run that gains 0 yards or worse. The Packers are 31st in stuff percentage, with a drive-killing 29.0 percent of their runs failing to gain yardage. With Jacobs, the Packers ranked second in stuff percentage in 2024 (17.6) and 12th in 2025 (19.3).
Eight: MarShawn Lloyd leads the Packers with 122 rushing yards. That’s a 17-game pace of 346 yards. That projected total would rank 16th in the league through Week 6.
Lloyd is averaging 2.54 yards per carry. It would require him to carry the ball 394 times to reach 1,000 yards. That would be the seventh-most rushing attempts in NFL history.
So, Jacobs could be a season-changing addition. The Packers have won three games in a row with no running game whatsoever.
“Well, I think he’s an elite-level back,” LaFleur said. “He’s certainly not going to hurt it. I think he can provide a spark.”
Is it the backs? Is it the blocking? LaFleur deflected the blame when asked about the running game on Monday, instead choosing to credit the Cowboys, who had the worst run defense in the NFL entering Week 6 but were coming off their mini-bye.
“I think there were some moments where it was good and then there were some moments where it wasn’t as good,” he said. “And then there were some moments where, quite frankly, the concepts had no chance based on different front structures they were presenting to us.
“They did a good job. I think any time that you go into a game and the opposition has a little longer to prepare for that, I think there’s some unscouted looks that can come up. Certainly, they caught us in a couple of those looks, where we didn’t have good plays for what they were showing.”
The Packers will play at the Lions on Sunday. They rank 20th in rushing yards allowed per attempt and 15th in rushing yards allowed per game. Then, they’ll host the Panthers, who are last in the league in yards allowed per attempt. Back-to-back games against the Patriots and Vikings, who boast top-10 run defenses, will follow.
Jacobs, even if it’s turning runs blocked for 1 yard into gains of 3 yards, could be a season-changing addition, perhaps as soon as Sunday.
“Yeah, absolutely,” LaFleur said when asked if Jacobs can hit the ground running. “I think that’s possible but we’ve got to go through the week and see where he’s at.”

title: New Packers Defensive Tackle Will Have Micah Parsons’ Seal of Approval
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – There might be nobody happier about the Green Bay Packers’ decision to sign Mazi Smith to the practice squad on Monday than his former-turned-current teammate, Micah Parsons.
As reported by ESPN.com’s Rob Demovsky , the Packers signed Smith to the practice squad following a Monday workout.
“Let’s go!” Parsons screamed when the Cowboys drafted Smith in the first round in 2023.
Parsons with the Packers has been the hype man for Lukas Van Ness, among others. He was the same way with Smith during their time together. More on that in a moment.
“NO MORE QB SNEAKS AJ!” @MicahhParsons11 told Cowboys DC Dan Quinn to pick Michigan's Mazi Smith earlier today and IT HAPPENED 😂 pic.twitter.com/nGm62CAnDK
Smith was a bust for the Cowboys and represents a Hail Mary of sorts for the Packers on a talented player who could fill a need. The Packers have been hammered by injuries at defensive tackle, with Warren Brinson, Javon Hargrave and Jonathan Ford on injured reserve. They beat the Cowboys with only four defensive tackles on the active roster. Plus, they have only one player on the practice squad, undrafted rookie David Blay Jr.
So, maybe the Packers will catch lightning in a bottle with Smith, who was the 26th pick of the 2023 draft.
"It's like Christmas," then-Cowboys coach Mike McCarthy said after Smith was selected. “When you look at all the work that goes into it, going back to his 30 visit, and just what a great fit he is for us … I just want him to be himself. He is a great fit for us.”
During the predraft process, Smith gained a big supporter in Parsons. He even texted his defensive coordinator at the time, Dan Quinn, hoping the Cowboys would draft Smith.
“It’s not what I think he can be, it’s what Mazi has to be,” Parsons said at the start of training camp in 2024 . “When you get to this business, there is no more of a choice or a can, it’s either you will or you won’t. They usually try to find someone else to do it if you can’t. It’s what Mazi has to be. He has to be dominant. He has to be a force. He has to be that guy for us.
“That’s why they drafted him in the first round. You’re not getting drafted in the first round not to be a productive talent, not to be on the sidelines. We drafted him to be in the game and that’s how much confidence you have (to have). I don’t expect Mazi to do anything. It’s what Mazi has to do at this point.
“That’s why I’m in his corner, I’m rooting for him and hoping to get him better every day. Pushing his conditioning, pushing his limits, because we need Mazi to be strong. We need Mazi to be that great force. He can be a dominant player, it’s just a will and mindset. That’s why we’re all here.”
Responded Smith : “I don’t really set goals. Everybody want to be an All-Pro, everybody wants to be a top five. I want to be the best me I can be and I know what that can get me. It’s got to this point so, I ain’t worried about accolades or that type.”
Smith played in 17 games with three starts as a rookie and started all 17 games in 2024, when he set career highs with 41 tackles and four tackles for losses.
“You can see it in his face that he loves ball, he loves everything about it,” Cowboys executive vice president and director of player personnel Stephen Jones said. “All the coaches that met with him agree that he'd be a great fit in this organization, and for him to fall down there to us and for us to have the opportunity to pick him, I feel like Mike. I feel like it's Christmas."
Last year, the Cowboys traded him to the Jets in the midseason blockbuster for Quinnen Williams, so he played in a total of eight games between the teams. He failed to make the Jets’ roster in training camp this year and signed to the Dolphins’ practice squad. He played in one game with Miami and was released last week.
Added together, Smith is in his fourth season. He’s played in 43 games with 20 starts. He has 57 tackles, including two sacks and seven for losses.
“I'm excited to get pointed in the right direction," he said after he was drafted, a quote that perhaps fits today. “To climb this big ole' mountain, they'll tell me where to start. I'm excited to get into the heavy duty [part] of things. I'm ready to put this work in and feel what my first offensive lineman feels like in the NFL.”
The native of Grand Rapids, Mich., was a consensus first-team all-Big Ten selection at Michigan in 2022, when he was the Wolverines’ defensive player of the year with 48 tackles in 14 games.
He was the No. 1 player on Bruce Feldman’s prestigious Freaks List before the 2022 season. He measured 6-foot-3 and 323 pounds at the 2023 Scouting Combine. He skipped most of the testing but put up 34 reps on the 225-pound bench press.
“A dog. A big dog, you know what I’m saying, he said after he was drafted. “A big fella; a big, physical guy. I’ve never been afraid of contact. I’ve never been afraid to ball. A guy that’s going to get in somebody’s face. A guy that isn’t going to make it easy.”
He used that size in college to be a premier run-stopping tackle.
“Man, I’m like 325 pounds. I’ve got real power in my hands. I’ve been strong my whole life. I came out of the womb looking like I did pushups. I was doing pushups in there, so I’ve just been strong my whole life. I’ve figured out how to use it on the field, figured out the right techniques, figured out the right stance to get into and just started striking blocks and making sure they went backwards.”
Parsons hoped that would improve Dallas’ run defense. It did not, but maybe that from-the-womb strength will be an asset with Parsons in Green Bay.
“You got to give him attention,” Parsons said after the 2023 draft . “He’s going to push guys back. He’s powerful. He’s strong. He’s going to get under people’s pads. And he’s great in the run and we’re going to develop him in the pass.”

title: Three Overreactions After Packers Beat Cowboys: Collapse Like House of Cards?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – A win is a win. The Green Bay Packers earned a big one against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday night. It was a surprisingly easy victory considering the number of self-inflicted wounds that prevented the Packers from winning by30.
Here are this week’s Overreactions
If ever there were a chance for Green Bay’s slumbering running game to at least crack open its eyes, yawn, stretch and shift positions, it was this game.
On offense, the Packers entered the game ranked last in the NFL with 60.4 rushing yards per game – almost 20 yards worse than any other team – and next-to-last with 3.05 yards per carry. On defense, the Cowboys entered the game ranked last with 168.4 rushing yards allowed per game and 29th with 5.10 yards allowed per carry.
Instead, the Cowboys looked like the Tom Landra-era Doomsday Defense and the Packers looked, well, exactly like they have all season.
The Packers ran the ball 26 times for 57 yards. Even with Jordan Love’s 13-yard run putting some cologne on a swine, they averaged 2.2 yards per carry. The 20 handoffs to running backs generated 36 yards, or 1.8 yards per carry.
The offensive line didn’t provide many openings. When there was a crack of daylight, the backs acted as if they were blindfolded in a cave trying to find a lost black sock.
The Packers’ run game almost impossibly went from worst to more worst – the intentional butchering of the English language a perfect fit for the butchering of the building block of offensive football. Green Bay is down to 59.8 rushing yards per game (Dallas is next with 76.0) and 2.87 yards per carry (Las Vegas is next with 3.03).
The 2000 Chargers set the dubious NFL record with 66.4 rushing yards per game. Over the past 70 seasons, only the 1994 Patriots’ 2.79 average was worse.
The Packers have 359 rushing yards in six games. Thirteen individuals have more rushing yards.
“Certainly, there’s some stuff that we can clean up where we’re maybe not winning a block or whatever it is, or we miss a cut,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “But we got to keep hammering it because it is critical in today’s football to be able to run the football at a decent level.”
A “decent level.” What a damning statement. Not a top-10 level. Not a winning level. The Packers, who are so far down the rankings that they have to reach up to touch bottom, would settle for decent.
A decent running game would open a world of possibilities. Against Chicago last week, Love in the play-action game was 12-of-14 passing for 245 yards and one touchdown. Against Dallas, those play-action fakes elicited giggles, with Love going 1-of-6 for 7 yards and getting pressured four times.
Maybe the vision and power of Josh Jacobs will be the salvation. If nothing else, he’ll fight for a gain of 3 yards rather than running sideways for a loss of 3.
MarShawn Lloyd think he's got 4.30 speed and he's going against some West Coast college's defense. He does not have 4.30 speed and this is not a college defense. pic.twitter.com/hOrNm6DC8Z
“I think that definitely hurts a little bit, especially when we’re trying to sell run action and they’re just sitting there waiting for you to do the passes off of it,” LaFleur said. “You’ve got to get the run game going.”
The Cowboys showed the rest of the league how to beat the Packers. Blow off the play-action game and attack the quarterback. The Packers had better figure it out fast, or the offense will fall like a house off cards.
The big reason why I predicted the Packers would finish 8-9 is that I didn’t think they had a snowball’s chance in a broiler to earn a win or two against the likes of the Bears, Cowboys and Lions without Micah Parsons.
The Packers beat the Bears, but they didn’t have Caleb Williams at quarterback. So, whatever. The game against Dallas would be an infinitely more difficult challenge. Dak Prescott is an elite quarterback. CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens might be the best receiver duo in the NFL. Jake Ferguson is a quality tight end and Javonte Williams is a quality running back.
Without Parsons to protect the secondary, how on earth would the Packers be able to beat teams with real quarterbacks?
That, to me, was the season-defining question. Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon delivered an emphatic answer on Sunday.
It’s a shame a phantom roughing-the-passer penalty on Lukas Van Ness led to the Packers giving up a meaningless touchdown in the final minute, because they entered the final drive having given up seven points and less than 200 yards. It was a defensive masterpiece for a team that entered the season with suspect cornerback and a suspect pass rush.
Green Bay’s cornerbacks helped limit Lamb and Pickens to a combined 4.9 yards per target. The traditional four-man rush was feeble, but Gannon created enough of a pass rush to make Prescott uneasy. The confusion created by Gannon led to two more interceptions.
“I was really happy just overall with our whole defensive performance, especially against that offense,” LaFleur said. “If you told me going into this game that you’re going to score 23 points, I was like, ‘Ah, we need to score 30-plus.’”
As it turns out, the 17 points in the first half were more than enough.
Through six games, LaFleur’s hiring of Gannon looks genius. The problem with hiring a good coordinator is he eventually becomes a head coach, as was the case with Jeff Hafley. Gannon bombed in his three-year run of coach of the Cardinals, but any team needing a coach at the end of this season should be smart enough to acknowledge that his tenure was torpedoed by the lack of a quarterback.
“I definitely think he’s doing a good job mixing it up,” said safety Xavier McKinney. “Putting guys in different positions, placing guys in different spots on the field, whether that’s deep zone, whether that’s in the half, blitzing, so it’s kind of mixing everything up. It’s hard for the opponents when they’re watching film and trying to figure who’s going to be doing what. So, I think it’s been a good mix of all of us kind of doing different things.”
The Packers are showing signs of being a pretty good team. But this is unsustainable.
The Packers have been penalized a league-high 57 times for a league-high 465 yards. They are first with six roughing-the-passer penalties, tied for second with four unnecessary roughness and tied for third with 10 offensive holding.
The Packers are No. 1 in dropped passes. According to Pro Football Focus, Jordan Love has had 19 passes dropped; no other quarterback has more than 11. All of the other NFC North quarterbacks have had 15 passes dropped.
They cleaned up their act against the Cowboys, but they’re still tied for the second-most fumbles per game.
They seemingly had cleaned up their act in terms of pass protection, but Love faced pressure on 45.5 percent of his dropbacks against Dallas – the fourth-highest of his career, according to Next Gen Stats.
The Packers have the second-highest stuff rate, with 29.0 percent of their running plays gaining 0 yards or worse. Their first-down rushing average is 2.25 yards – more than a half-yard worse than any other team. It was an even more feeble 1.47 yards against Dallas.
Green Bay’s offense is almost fully dependent on Love. It’s up to Love to navigate dirty pockets. It’s up to Love to make the offense work without a running game. It’s up to Love to follow up a perfect pass that was dropped with another perfect pass. It’s up to Love to pick up the slack by the first-down ineptitude.
Love has been tremendous for most of the season. It’s true for almost every team, obviously, that the season will go only as far as the quarterback can take it. It’s especially true for the Packers because of all the surrounding problems that continue to fester.

title: One Sequence Shows Jonathan Gannon’s Winning Formula for Packers’ Defense
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Flashback to January. Matt LaFleur is looking for a defensive coordinator after Jeff Hafley left Green Bay to become the coach of the Miami Dolphins.
It’s OK to admit it. You wanted Jim Leonhard to return to Wisconsin, where he starred as a college football player and defensive coordinator, to push the Green Bay Packers’ defense to new heights.
LaFleur had other ideas once he met with former Arizona Cardinals coach Jonathan Gannon.
After meeting with Gannon for more than a day, LaFleur offered Gannon the job and he accepted.
Gannon has been on the job for only six games. There is a lot that can change between now and the end of the season, but LaFleur’s decision looks like a home run.
One of the biggest reasons for Gannon’s success in Green Bay is something he said when he was hired in Arizona.
“I don't believe in a scheme. I believe in putting players we have in positions to be successful," Gannon said. "We will look different week to week. … We’re going to use guys’ skill-sets to present matchup problems.”
The Packers have had to look different out of necessity. Edgerrin Cooper and Micah Parsons, Gannon’s two best players, have played a total of 14 quarters of football. Parsons has yet to return from an ACL injury he suffered in December, and Cooper was lost for the season with an Achilles injury he suffered in Tampa Bay a couple weeks ago.
All the while, Gannon and his group have soldiered on. They hit their stride after the Week 3 disaster against the Atlanta Falcons, but Sunday night’s game against the Dallas Cowboys represented a different test. It’s easier to look good against backup quarterbacks and low-level starters. The Packers were facing Dak Prescott and the high powered Cowboys offense with CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens as two star receivers.
Sure, the Packers came in rolling. They gave up 21 points, tallied seven sacks and seven takeaways the last two games. This test, however, was going to be much more challenging. A veteran quarterback like Dak Prescott was going to have all the answers for Gannon’s defense.
The Cowboys threw for 258 yards on 54 dropbacks. Prescott was only sacked once, but never looked comfortable throughout the night. He threw two interceptions, including one by Evan Williams that was brought on by a brilliant disguise and play sequencing from Gannon.
On Dallas’ first two series, Gannon tipped his hand. He was going to show and bring pressure to keep Prescott guessing and uncomfortable.
We often talk about play sequencing from an offensive coach, but what Gannon did on Dallas’ third possession was an example of a defensive coordinator setting up a call in a big spot.
Dallas had the ball after Jordan Love threw an interception and was facing a third-and-8 from Green Bay’s 17 with a chance to tie the score.
Gannon showed pressure. Williams was in the box and Prescott accounted for him.
When the ball was snapped, however, Williams was nowhere to be found. Prescott never found him as he fired a pass toward the end zone to his favorite target, Lamb.
Evan Williams is on the far left side as this video starts. pic.twitter.com/g7EdlGPzqa
“I was showing around the line of scrimmage and got the quarterback to count me into the blitz pickup, which was a good sign,” Williams said. “When you see a quarterback acknowledge you, that’s probably a good sign he’s probably not picking you up in the coverage aspect of things.”
So what happened? Did the Packers trick Prescott on the play due to the pressure they sent before that?
“Yeah, absolutely,” Williams said. “Anytime you can speed a quarterback process up, anytime you can do that, it’s going to lead to some good things regardless of whether you’re bringing it or whether you’re not. I feel like we did a good job of sending some pressure early, establishing some physicality.”
Sending pressure is nothing new for this year’s Packers. Last year, things were different. They finished 28th with a blitz rate of 29.7 percent , choosing to trust a front four that included Parsons for most of the season.
The idea is good in theory. Parsons is one of the best players in the sport. The Packers’ cornerbacks were suspect a season ago. Leaving as many people in coverage as possible seemed like a good idea but, ultimately, the results were not there. The defense was often subject to long drives, keeping their offense on the sideline and tiring their defense out by the end of the game.
“I think we were more floaty last year, passing things off,” cornerback Keisean Nixon said. “I think this year, we’re more man-man, more sticky. It’s a little different.”
A little is underselling it. Entering Sunday, the Packers were 12th in blitz rate at 33.9 percent. So, what’s the difference?
“I think it’s just a little bit more of an aggressive mindset,” Williams said. “Us dictating the tone and dictating what the offense is going to do, they have to react off of us instead of playing passive and let the game come to us.  We’re trying to dictate pressures, dictate where the line is going to slide to or where the ball is going to go. It feels good to be on the offensive side on defense.”
The aggression and dictation of terms to an opposing offense that Williams speaks of stood out on Sunday.
Gannon is not like some defensive coordinators who have made a name for themselves. He’s not calling quarterbacks overrated and pompous, while demanding they need to hit the ground hard. He’s not outspoken.
He’s more reserved. Especially in the public eye. When he’s coaching? His intensity shines through with how he is calling his defense. He has earned the trust of his players in a short period of time. He’s found his best players in Xavier McKinney, Williams and Javon Bullard and turned them into weapons.
“Yes. Not even close,” Bullard said when asked if he was blitzing more this year than last year. “The trust that the coaches have in me, I’m so grateful for that. We come to practice, we work every day, we put things on tape that coaches notice. Some coaches have the guts to dial them. up, some coaches don’t. You respect the ones that do.”
Respect is one word. Love is another. Williams could hardly contain his joy when asked about how much he likes being sent as a blitzer more often this season.
“Love it, love it,” Williams said. “Anytime we get a chance to be around the line of scrimmage, be around the ball and affect the QB, those are game-changing plays when you get around the QB and affect things around the line of scrimmage.
“I’m looking to get me a couple more sacks this year. It feels good to have the trust from a DC to understand that he trusts you to run your blitz path, show the look to where you can get free instead of just wasting rushers.”
Six weeks into the season, Gannon has his team playing fast and is controlling games for their offense that is still finding its way at times early in the year. Now, the return of his best player is looming as Parsons is set to return to the practice field sooner than later.
Do the Packers have to fight the urge to play safer like they did a season ago when he gets back? Not if his players have anything to say about it.
“I don’t like the word safe when you’re talking about defense,” Bullard said. “We play with an edge, we play gritty. If you’re playing safe, you’re playing timid. I truly believe that. When 1 [Parsons] gets back it’s only going to up our play style with a player like that you know the ball is coming out quick, they don’t have much more time to get it out.”
Trust, aggression, and the players executing at a high level. The recipe is working for Gannon and his defense. With another big test on the horizon, how can the Packers slow down the Detroit Lions?
“Rush and coverage, baby,” Xavier McKinney said. “When that rush is getting there and you add that disguise game in there, I think it’s everybody. I don’t think it’s just one group. The defensive line rushing and making him uncomfortable. Linebackers, Z [Zaire Franklin] communicating and…

title: Snaps, Studs and Duds: Analysis of Packers’ Win Over Cowboys
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers beat the Dallas Cowboys 23-13 on Sunday night for their third consecutive win. They’ve allowed 14 or fewer points in each of those games, a first since the 2016 season.
Here is our weekly analysis of the snap counts, along with some studs and duds from their 10th consecutive October win.
The Packers played 75 snaps on offense.
Quarterback: For the fifth time in six games, Jordan Love played every snap. PFF charged his receivers with four drops. That’s 18 on the season for Love; no other quarterback has been saddled with more than 11. The other NFC North quarterbacks have been victimized by 15.
It’s not just drops. PFF had his targets going 2-of-9 on contested catches. With a little help from his friends, Love would have had a monster night and the Packers would have scored a blowout victory.
Running backs: Pierre Strong didn’t start but he is the Packers’ best running back. After spending the first four games on the practice squad, Strong played a unit-high 41 snaps. MarShawn Lloyd played 30 snaps and Kaleb Johnson played only four. You’ve got to wonder what his future will be if Josh Jacobs returns this week.
Strong led the team with 11 carries for 25 yards, a 2.5-yard average. Lloyd lost 5 yards on his first two carries and finished with eight attempts for 10 yards, a 1.3-yard average. Johnson’s only carry lost 2 yards. That’s a combined 20 carries for 36 yards. By our count, they had 39 yards after contact. At least Strong manufactured a couple first downs with YAC in the passing game.
Receivers: Christian Watson played 66 snaps and Matthew Golden played 63. Those are huge workloads at a position in which an incredible amount of running is required. That’s especially true for Watson and Golden, who run a lot of deep routes.
Golden caught six passes for 104 yards, including the opening touchdown. It was a great game on paper, though one emoji says a thousand words.
Savion Williams went from injured reserve to getting 40 snaps – almost double the combined number of Bo Melton (18) and J. Michael Sturdivant (four). Williams had a 15-yard catch on the opening series and finished with six touches for 41 yards.
“I thought Savion Williams came in and provided a huge spark for us,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “He made a lot of critical plays on that first drive. He was balling out. It was great to have him back out on the field. He’s a big, tough, physical receiver that can provide a spark, which he did, not only in the pass game but in the run game, as well, just giving him some of those jet sweeps. We’ve got to find ways to get him the ball.”
Tight ends: It was a largely forgettable night for Tucker Kraft, who played 58 snaps. Trusted blocker Mark Redman played 25. Jonnu Smith, who had been averaging 20 snaps per game, played a season-low nine; Josh Whyle, who played zero snaps against the Jets and one snap against the Falcons, played a season-high 17.
Kraft caught five passes for 37 yards. The big play was a fourth-and-3 conversion that gained 14 yards and looked like vintage Kraft with the missed tackle and YAC.
Offensive line: When Jordan Love was intercepted in the first quarter, Sean Rhyan wound up in the blue medical tent. He wound up playing every snap, though, along with the rest of the starting offensive line.
Rhyan was charged with two sacks, and right tackle Anthony Belton and right guard Travis Glover were each deemed responsible for three pressures and one penalty. Belton had a good block on Pierre Strong’s 5-yard run to the 1 in the fourth quarter and left tackle Jordan Morgan leveled his man on the fourth-down pass that Christian Watson dropped in the end zone.
The Packers played 78 snaps on defense.
Defensive tackles: The Packers lined up with only four defensive tackles because Warren Brinson, Javon Hargrave and Jonathan Ford are on injured reserve. How would the Packers make up for the loss of Hargrave, who played about 31 snaps a game? Everyone did just a little bit more.
Karl Brooks, as usual, led the way with 47 snaps and Devonte Wyatt played a season-high 46. Chris McClellan hit 40 for the first time in his career and Anthony Campbell, who missed the last three games, played 32. Brooks had two of the three solo tackles and the only tackle for loss. Coming off a big game, Wyatt had one assisted tackle and zero pressures.
Edges: It was a balanced approach, with Lukas Van Ness playing a unit-high 43 snaps and Dani Dennis-Sutton playing a unit-low 36 snaps. In between were Barryn Sorrell’s 40 snaps and Brenton Cox’s 39. The Packers elevated Arron Mosby from the practice squad so he could play 11 snaps on special teams.
Van Ness had the only sack and a team-high six pressures, according to PFF. Next Gen Stats credited Dennis-Sutton with a team-high six pressures and Van Ness with five. Cox had a couple chances at sacks but couldn’t finish the play. Sorrell officially led the team with two quarterback hits and was in on two tackles for losses.
Linebackers: Zaire Franklin played every snap. At the other position, Isaiah McDuffie played 43 snaps and Ty’Ron Hopper played 33. Last week, Hopper had a slight advantage. The rotation is allowing them to maintain key roles on special teams, with McDuffie playing 14 and Hopper 12. Hopper took advantage with four tackles.
Speaking of special teams, Nick Niemann played 16 snaps and Kristian Welch logged 11.
This is wild: McDuffie (four), Franklin (three) and Hopper (one) combined for eight tackles on defense. Edgerrin Cooper had halves with that many.
Cornerbacks: Keisean Nixon went the distance and Brandon Cisse dropped out with a stinger after 54 snaps. That meant Carrington Valentine played a season-high 26 snaps.
Nixon was the target for Prescott. According to PFF, he targeted him 13 times and completed nine passes but for only 55 yards. It wasn’t much better against Cisse (3-of-8 for 30 yards) and his first career interception.
Valentine was excellent off the bench. The first two targets resulted in an interception (overturned by a penalty) and pass breakup.
Safeties: Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams played every snap and Javon Bullard played 67 – the third-most of his career. They were among the three best players on the field. Williams is the only player on defense to have played all 420 snaps.
A week after McKinney picked off two passes in the win against Chicago, Williams grabbed a big one against Dallas. Bullard was tremendous with three pass breakups, including one on fourth down, and two pressures, one of which produced a holding penalty.
CBs Keisean Nixon, Brandon Cisse: In last season’s 40-40 tie at Dallas, CeeDee Lamb was inactive but George Pickens caught 8-of-11 for 134 yards and two touchdowns. A couple weeks ago against Houston’s vaunted defense, Lamb caught 17-of-21 targets for 189 yards and one touchdown.
So, the Packers know what they’re capable of doing against any opponent. On Sunday, the Packers limited them to 15 catches (out of 29 targets) for 143 yards. The Cowboys kept testing Nixon but never really beat him. Cisse had one interception and was mad he didn’t have a second.
“Felt good but should’ve had two,” he said. “That’s what I’m frustrated about, the one at the back pylon. Read the double-move and knew it was coming. Just got to execute on that one, but I felt good. Hopefully, we get many more. That’s the mindset.”
S Javon Bullard: Yeah, Bullard gave up the touchdown at the end of the game. Whatever. Bullard has gone from solid to good to really good in his three seasons. He had six tackles, three passes defensed and two pressures. One of the PBUs came on a fourth-down pass to Lamb in the fourth quarter and essentially clinched the game.
S Evan Williams: It was just another day at the office for Williams, who had six tackles, one interception and one quarterback hit.
“I was showing up around the line of scrimmage pretty early,” he said of the interception. “I think I saw Dak point at me, which typically is a tell that either the…

title: Packers Report Card: Gold-Star Performance Highlights Grades vs. Cowboys
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The grades are in after the Green Bay Packers defeated the Dallas Cowboys 23-13 on Sunday night, and the highest marks were attached to the defense.
One year after giving up 40 points to the Cowboys, they held them to seven points before a garbage-time touchdown got them into double-digits.
The task in front of them was not a small one. The Cowboys have largely the same cast of characters. Dak Prescott is still their quarterback. George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb were healthy and on the field.
It didn’t matter. The Packers never allowed Prescott to get comfortable.
“Rush and coverage, baby,” safety Xavier McKinney said. He was right. When defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon was not dialing up blitzes, Green Bay had Prescott guessing on what coverage they were playing.
They get the highest mark in our weekly report card following the team’s third consecutive victory.
Jordan Love was three plays away from throwing four touchdown passes and topping 350 passing yards. That was not to be as the Packers’ struggles with drops reared their ugly head again.
Matthew Golden and Christian Watson dropped one touchdown apiece. Golden had another that could be called a drop or a pass breakup by Joey Porter Jr. Tucker Kraft continued to struggle with one drop and another play that could have been a reception but he did not drag his foot at the sideline.
Love, despite what the box score numbers say, was excellent save for two plays. He had one interception that he threw to linebacker Dee Winters on a telegraphed pass to Golden. He almost threw another interception that turned into an instant-replay debacle before ultimately being ruled an incompletion.
He did all that despite having little protection, zero run game and receivers that continued to let him down throughout the night.
Is it perfect? No, but the Packers’ quarterback has played very well the last two weeks.
The group in front of him left a little to be desired. Dallas’ pass rush has been largely ineffective this season, ranking 29th in sack percentage. Love was sacked three times and hit on eight occasions, according to the official stats. He was pressured on 40 percent of his dropbacks, according to Pro Football Focus. Rashan Gary had 10 pressures.
The guard combination of Laken Tomlinson and Travis Glover struggled for the first time since becoming starters against Tampa Bay earlier in the month.
With four full weeks of practice under his belt, will next week be the time for Kevin Zeitler to make his debut at right guard? That remains to be seen, but this group was not as good on Sunday as it had been. The line will face better defenses during this next stretch of games, starting with a date next week with the Lions led by the mighty Aidan Hutchinson.
If there is a way to sum up the Packers’ run game to start this season, it came on their first possession of the game.
Dallas was the 32nd-ranked defense against the run coming into play. The Packers’ first three runs had a long gain of 0 yards. Yes, 0. MarShawn Lloyd continues to try to bounce runs outside that are designed to stay between the tackles. Pierre Strong and Kaleb Johnson don’t offer much juice in the run game, either, though Strong wound up getting most of the run and made some things happen as a receiver.
Josh Jacobs is expected to return to practice on Wednesday, but will he have any room to roam if he plays on Sunday at Detroit?
In the battle of the very stoppable force against a movable object, the movable object looked like the Steel Curtain from the 1970s.
The Packers had 40 rushing yards in the first half on 15 carries, with 14 of those yards coming from Jordan Love. Lloyd, the team’s starting running back, had minus-2 yards on three carries.
The atrocity of the run game cannot be understated. The failure falls on the offensive line and the guys being asked to carry the ball.
Perhaps inserting Kevin Zeitler into the lineup with Jacobs will give them a boost next week against Detroit.
Take a bow, Jonathan Gannon.
Last season, the Packers’ defense had no answers for Dak Prescott and his group of receivers. Those same players were on the field on Sunday night. The Cowboys even added CeeDee Lamb, who missed last year’s matchup. Prescott rang up 319 passing yards and three touchdowns in a 40-40 tie, with George Pickens catching eight passes for 134 yards and two touchdowns.
Sunday night? Not even close.
In 54 pass attempts, Prescott threw for 258 yards. His only touchdown pass came after the game had largely been decided. He was only sacked once but under duress most of the night, which led to two interceptions and a third wiped away by a questionable roughing-the-passer penalty.
Pickens had six catches on 11 targets for 73 yards. Lamb had nine catches on 18 targets for 70 yards.
“Did they score?” cornerback Keisean Nixon asked.
The answer was no. The Packers held one of the top receiver duos in football out of the end zone with a cornerback group that entered the season shrouded in questions.
The difference in play style from 2025 to 2026 is prevalent. The Packers are not willing to just wait around for one of their defensive linemen to make plays. Gannon is more than willing to force the issue.
He forced the issue on Sunday, and the Packers’ defense is rolling ahead of another big test next week against the Lions.
“Yeah, I thought JG was aggressive, getting pressure on the quarterback,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “It’s hard to throw when you’ve got stuff in your face, and I thought the coverage was outstanding. Our guys challenged them. They did a great job.”
Evan Williams and Brandon Cisse had interceptions, and Carrington Valentine had a pick that was eliminated by Lukas Van Ness’s dubious roughing penalty. Javon Bullard broke up three passes, including one on fourth down.
“I was really happy just overall with our whole defensive performance, especially against that offense,” LaFleur said. “If you told me going into this game that you’re going to score 23 points, I was like, ‘Ah, we need to score 30-plus.’ But our defense, they did their job. They got one (touchdown) late in the game and I thought for the entire game our defense really balled out.”
The run game was not much of a factor for Dallas. It wants to throw the ball, first and foremost. With the Packers leading by two scores for most of the game after opening up a 10-0 lead, the run game became even more of an afterthought.
Overall, the Cowboys ran for 48 yards on 15 carries. Their longest run was 8 yards.
Not bad for a group that was shorthanded on the defensive line and is still working on replacing linebacker Edgerrin Cooper.
Green Bay has been excellent against the run each of the last two weeks but will face a well-rested Jahmyr Gibbs next week as the Lions are coming off a bye. Will they hold him to 48 yards rushing on 15 carries? Probably not, but a similar effort is going to be needed.
How was Trey Smack going to rebound after missing three kicks last week? That was a big storyline coming into a game in which it felt like points were going to be precious to each team with a shootout in the forecast.
A shootout did not break out, but the Packers’ rookie kicker was clean. He made both extra points and three field goals for a perfect night at the office. His last field goal all but iced the game in the fourth quarter.
Coleman Owen, who was elevated from the practice squad , returned punts in place of Skyy Moore and had a 16-yard-return. J. Michael Sturdivant looked comfortable returning kickoffs, as well. Daniel Whelan averaged 50.3 yards per punt. Ultimately the special teams did not make any egregious mistakes. A clean game was a welcome sight after last week’s debacle.
Forget about Matt LaFleur and Cam Achord for a minute. LaFleur had his team ready, and it built on last week’s win over the Bears in a spot that could have been prime for a letdown. LaFleur gets credit for that. Achord’s special teams were fine.
The star of the show, however, was defensive…

title: With 4-2 Record, How Have Packers Gone From Staggering to Streaking?
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Twenty-four days earlier, the Green Bay Packers were embarrassed in front of a national television audience and booed off the field in a blowout loss to the Atlanta Falcons.
The vultures were circling coach Matt LaFleur’s team after a 1-2 start. They seemed like a team ready to sink under the weight of their fatal flaws, undisciplined play and numerous injuries. They couldn’t run the ball, couldn’t protect the passer and couldn’t get out of their own way.
Incredibly, with their 23-13 victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday night, the Packers have won three consecutive games. They still are a team with fatal flaws, and they certainly haven’t gotten any healthier. They can’t run the ball, they struggle to protect the passer and they can’t get out of their own way at times on either side of the ball.
And yet, the Packers have the fourth-longest winning streak in the NFL.
LaFleur wasn’t proud of the way his team played but he is proud of its mental toughness.
“I think it feels pretty good right now. But once tonight’s over, you watch the tape, you learn from it, you move onto the next,” LaFleur said. “It’s not like our schedule is going to get any easier here. So, it truly is a week-to-week league, and you’ve got to take it one game at a time – really, one day at a time. You’ve got to put in the work, first and foremost. And I love that locker room, I love those guys, they come to battle, they come to work, got a great attitude.”
The victory over Dallas serves as a decent summary for the season.
The rushing attack produced a woeful 57 yards on 26 carries. That’s 2.2 yards per carry. That’s pretty terrible. And yet, when you limit it to the running backs, 20 handoffs were turned into 36 yards. That’s 1.8 yards per carry. You could do better by face-planting.
“We got to find a way to get this run game going because it’s too inconsistent,” LaFleur said.
Later, he added: “We got to keep hammering it because it is critical in today’s football to be able to run the football at a decent level.”
Jordan Love according to the official stats was sacked three times and hit on five other occasions. According to PFF’s early grading, he was pressured on 40 percent of his dropbacks and threw the third-most under-pressure passes in Week 6.
“The goal is to not get hit,” Love said. “The O-line, that is their job, and they take pride in that. And I think we’ll look at what we can continue to clean up. But for me, that’s my job. I’ve got to be able to stand in there.”
The Packers were flagged 11 times for 96 yards. There were three penalties for roughing the passer and two for taunting.
“You can only control how you respond to all that stuff and we’ve got to do a better job of making sure, whether we feel it was justified or not, it doesn’t matter,” LaFleur said. “You got to control your emotions to the best of your ability, and you’ve got to move on and play the next play and go beat him between the whistles.”
The dynamic duo of Christian Watson and Matthew Golden made some big-time plays but also looked like they had traded their receiver gloves for oven mitts at times. Drops have been a problem all season, with Love victimized by a league-high 14 through the first five games. Watson and Love each flubbed touchdown passes against Dallas.
Nonetheless, with no rushing attack, no discipline and shoddy execution, the Packers won with relative ease. They led 17-0 at halftime and more or less cruised over the finish line.
The Packers are 4-2 and in fifth place in the NFC. It’s an unthinkable achievement, really, given how they looked like an understaffed and underfunded semipro team for the first quarter of the season.
“We’ve had some ups and downs, obviously, but most teams do in the National Football League, and it’s truly how you respond to the adversity and if you can face it head on,” LaFleur said. “One thing I love about those guys, even through it all, there’s been any finger pointing.
“Everybody’s looking inward and trying to look at what they can improve upon as an individual, because we know that’s going to help the collective. That’s the way it needs to be, and those guys are selfless guys. Certainly, we’ve got some guys that aren’t playing that probably are deserving of playing. But they just keep coming to work with a great attitude and keep battling, and that’s the mark of a good team.”
For all the warts, they found a way.
Offensively, the Packers – the worst third-down team in the league through five games – went 11-of-18 against Dallas.
“Definitely feels good to get rolling with some wins,” Love said. “That’s what we talk about as a team. The mindset is take it one week at a time. We’ve got to stack wins. Obviously, a little adversity early on in the season with a couple of losses, but it’s all about how you respond, and I think we’re responding well right now.
“It definitely feels good, but we’ve just got to keep building upon it, keep stacking, keep taking it one week at a time.”
Defensively, Jonathan Gannon put together a winning game plan and the players executed it to perfection. Cornerbacks Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse won their matchup against Cowboys receivers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. With some late-game fluff, they caught 15-of-29 targets for 143 yards.
“I think we’re right where we need to be,” Nixon said. “We got them losses out of the way, and I think it’s full throttle nowadays. We’ve just got to keep stacking. One-week-at-a-time mentality.”
The Packers are going to have to play better, to state the obvious. And quickly.
The Packers will play next week at the Lions, who are 3-2 and coming off their bye. Then, they will host the NFC South-leading Panthers, who are 3-2. After that, it’s a road trip to New England to face the defending AFC-champion Panthers, who are 4-2 with three consecutive wins. Finally, in the last game before the bye, the Packers will host the undefeated Vikings.
At some point, their fatal flaws will be just that. Fatal. But they are 4-2 and will be getting Josh Jacobs and Micah Parsons back at some point.
“That’s life in this league, right? Everybody’s going to have some flaws and you just got to find a way to go 1-0 every week,” LaFleur said. “I think the process is a big part of that in terms of what you’re doing from Monday to Saturday.
“I know we’re all judged on that 3-hour window of what the final product is, but I’m a big believer in the process. You’ve got to have a routine and you’ve got to come in with the right mindset and put in the work, because there’s no hiding from it.”
It wasn’t perfect on the field, though the final score showed another win. It wasn’t perfect in LaFleur’s postgame news conference, either, as he almost fumbled his closing thoughts on the final question.
“Proud of our guys. I think they do sh … stuff the right way. I almost slipped there,” he said with a laugh. “They do things the right way and I feel fortunate to be around a group of men like that that are willing to uphold a standard and do things the right way.”

title: Winners and Losers: Jonathan Gannon Leads Packers’ Victory Over Cowboys
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers entered their Week 6 matchup on Sunday Night Football against the Dallas Cowboys in a situation that could swing their season.
A win would give them a three-game winning streak and helped build on last week’s win over the Chicago Bears. A 4-2 record in their first six games, considering how the season started, could not be considered anything other than a significant achievement for the team.
A loss would drop them to 3-3 with a date against a Detroit Lions team that will be well rested off their bye week.
They started with a bang, riding a 17-0 lead to a 23-13 victory. There was a lot of meat left on the bone for the offense, but the defense was the star of this show. They lead off our list of winners and losers.
Evan Williams said earlier in the week that he was licking his chops facing an offense like Dallas, which wants to put the ball in the air as much as it can.
Williams was the first of two Packers defensive backs to get an interception in the first half. More on that in a little bit, as Williams was in perfect position to make the play.
Evan Williams dropped from the line of scrimmage into a deep quarter — a ton of ground to cover — and still got into position for the INT. Dak Prescott never saw the rotation coming. Brilliant angle here. pic.twitter.com/Z2bMHBG6rp https://t.co/z8hoqXSDfa
Williams made plays at multiple levels of the defense on Sunday night. In the third quarter, he was sent on a blitz that got immediate pressure, forcing Prescott to get rid of the ball early. The pass fell incomplete and the Cowboys had to punt.
The Packers’ defense has not had its top two players for most of the season, and it appears that Williams has been weaponized by his defensive coordinator.
Jonathan Gannon may not have been the most popular choice to be the Packers’ defensive coordinator. It appeared that the most popular choice would have been former Wisconsin Badger Jim Leonhard, who ultimately landed with the Buffalo Bills.
Gannon was dealt a bad hand to start the season as his best player, Micah Parsons was out for the start of the season thanks to an ACL injury he suffered before Gannon was in town.
Just three games and one half into Gannon’s tenure, he lost his second best player when Edgerrin Cooper went down for the year with an achilles injury.
Gannon has simply soldiered on and helped captain Green Bay’s defense that has given up 20 points, which in the last two weeks against two powerful offenses
A year ago, the same Dallas offense with largely the same cast of characters scored 40 on the Packers.
They scored seven while the game was in the balance.
He weaponizes his best players. He keeps opposing quarterbacks guessing. We often talk about play sequencing for an offensive play caller, but Green Bay’s first takeaway of the night was the result of Gannon sequencing plays early in the game.
Gannon was not waiting around to allow Dak Prescott to find a rhythm. He was sending pressure early and often at Dallas’ quarterback.
With the Packers’ defense facing a third down following a Jordan Love interception nursing a seven point lead, Gannon tricked Prescott. He showed pressure with Evan Williams, but Williams dropped at the last second. Prescott never saw him as he fired the ball toward the end zone, and Williams had an interception.
Gannon, unlike some of his predecessors, does not wait around hoping for his front four to win. If they’re not getting pressure, he’s going to send more guys to try and make the quarterback uncomfortable.
Whenever the Cowboys had a chance to snatch some momentum, the Packers’ defense had an answer. More importantly, Gannon had an answer.
One of Jordan Love’s strengths is his ability to keep an even keel even as everything else around him continues to unravel.
Limited protection? That’s fine. No run game? No big deal. Receivers dropping passes? Love keeps putting the ball where it needs to be.
Love had one touchdown pass in the first three quarters of play, but easily could have had four. Matthew Golden dropped two. Christian Watson dropped one. Love’s game on Sunday was a case where the final stat line is not going to show how well he played.
Jordan Love Just Threw It Right Over The Cowboys Defender’s Head. What An Amazing Throw From The Packers Quarterback. Unreal. 🔥 pic.twitter.com/2WxMKSDWcx
Save for one poor decision on an interception that he threw to Dee Winters, Love was excellent on a night where his team needed him to be. If he can get a little bit of help from his supporting cast, the Packers’ offense could be really dangerous down the stretch.
Yes, it was a gift, but sometimes gifts are what it takes when you play cornerback. With the Cowboys’ offense driving and threatening to cut into Green Bay’s 10-0 lead, Dak Prescott tried to find his top target, CeeDee Lamb.
Lamb fell out of his break on his route and Prescott hit Cisse right in the numbers.
Charles Woodson used to always say that if a cornerback catches the passes that are thrown to him, he’ll lead the league.
Cisse may not lead the league, but he’ll never forget his first career interception.
Matthew Golden was so close to having a first half for the ages. He caught a touchdown pass on Green Bay’s first series of the game to open the scoring. He also converted a key third down on Green Bay’s final possession of the first half which led to a touchdown to give the Packers a 17-0 lead.
That was the good news. The bad news was the rest of the first half.
Golden was two plays away from having three touchdowns in the first half, and well over 100 yards receiving. Two separate passes from Jordan Love hit Golden in the hands, but he was unable to corral either of them.
He was also flagged for taunting on the first drive of the game. Quibble with whether the flag was weak or not, but it did happen.
His first target in the second half also resulted in a drop. It was a poor throw, but both hands touched the ball on the play.
Maybe it was the bright lights of Sunday Night Football. Maybe it was the prospect of playing the team from his home state.
Either way, the drops are uncharacteristic from Golden, but those are the types of plays that separate a good receiver from a great one.
Dennis-Sutton had a gift of a sack when he came free on a rush at Dak Prescott in the first half, but left his feet, allowing Prescott to escape.
Later in the game, he gave the Cowboys a gift of his own. Prescott threw the ball out of bounds on third-and-6 with mere seconds remaining in the third quarter. The Packers thought they were off the field, but Dennis-Sutton had extra things to say to Tyler Guyton, which resulted in a taunting penalty.
The taunting penalty was part of an offsetting foul thanks to a holding call against Dallas, but it gave the Cowboys a mulligan. They would convert on a completion to George Pickens.
Javon Bullard deflects the 4th down pass away! DALvsGB on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/yAXwn9jtgN
Matt LaFleur was livid with Dennis-Sutton, as he was immediately pulled off the field following the play.
The Cowboys’ drive that should have ended in a punt, resulted in a failed fourth down thanks to Javon Bullard’s heroics.  Still, it’s a play that should not have happened at all. It’s a play that will hurt them against the league’s better teams.
The idea coming into the offseason was that the Packers’ passing game was going to be better because it had fewer bodies to take away targets from the likes of Matthew Golden, Christian Watson, Jayden Reed, and Tucker Kraft.
The Packers were almost stretched to their limit in the first half. Tucker Kraft caught a pass on the sideline before taking a seat there. Kraft did not return for the rest of the first half, before making his return after halftime.
The point is more in what could have happened had Kraft not been able to return to the game. The Packers’ quartet of pass catchers would have been down to just a duo with Golden and Watson the only healthy…

title: Streaking Packers Start Fast, Earn Mistake-Filled Win Over Cowboys
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Was the Green Bay Packers’ blowout victory over the Chicago Bears last week real or was it a byproduct of circumstances, including facing a backup quarterback?
The Packers kicked themselves in the shins repeatedly but outclassed the Dallas Cowboys 23-13 on Sunday night at Lambeau Field. It was Green Bay’s third consecutive win. After a sputtering start to the season, it is 4-2 headed into next week’s game at the Detroit Lions.
The running game was horrendous. The pass protection was faulty. They dropped touchdown passes. They hit double-digits on penalties.
None of if mattered, though, as Jonathan Gannon’s defense was dominant.
This wasn’t against Tyson Bagent, Rome Odunze and Luther Burden, as was the case last week. It was against Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens.
Not until the final drive of the night, when the Cowboys (2-4) scored a meaningless touchdown, did Prescott get past 200 passing yards. At the 2-minute warning, Lamb and Pickens combined for 12 catches out of 26 targets for 108 yards.
Jordan Love was 23-of-41 passing for 276 yards with one touchdown and his first-ever interception on a Sunday night start. He would have had about 340 yards and three touchdowns if not for dropped touchdown passes by Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. Golden, though, caught six passes for 104 yards and the opening touchdown as Green Bay rolled to a 17-0 halftime lead.
With the Packers leading 23-7, the Cowboys embarked on the most tedious drive imaginable. On third-and-20, Ty’Ron Hopper was flagged for illegal contact to give the Cowboys a first down.
Next, Carrington Valentine – who had just entered the game after Brandon Cisse sustained a stinger – intercepted Dak Prescott but Lukas Van Ness was flagged for roughing the passer for shoving Prescott.
After the Cowboys converted on fourth-and-5, Karl Brooks was flagged for roughing the passer.
Finally, the Packers made a play that held up. Van Ness sacked Prescott on first down to set the stage for fourth-and-11, when Zaire Franklin and Van Ness converged on Prescott, who flung a pass toward the goalposts, where there were no Cowboys receivers located.
That gave Green Bay the ball with 5 minutes to go and essentially ended the game. With 4 minutes to go following a first-down conversion by Tucker Kraft, a “Let’s Go Brewers!” chant rang out; it was shut down by public-address announcer Bill Jartz, who told the fans it wasn’t the right time.
With the Vikings and Lions having their byes and the Packers winning their third in a row, here are the NFC North standings through Week 6:
The Cowboys pulled within 17-7 to start the second half but Jordan Love had the response.
First, Love on fourth-and-3 found Tucker Kraft in the flat for a tackle-breaking gain of 14. One play later, Love bought time to his left – left tackle Jordan Morgan pancaked his defender – and unleashed a missile to Christian Watson for what should have been a 26-yard touchdown. The reliable Watson, who is having a second-to-none season , dropped the pass in the end zone.
Trey Smack, who missed three kicks last week, booted a 44-yard field goal to make it 20-7 with 5:02 left in the third quarter.
The Packers forced a punt, with Evan Williams coming free on a blitz to force an incompletion. However, Green Bay started at the 6 and couldn’t move the ball, with former Packers Pro Bowler Kenny Clark smoking center Sean Rhyan for a third-down sack.
The Packers appeared to get off the field but blew that opportunity when, on third-and-6, Dani Dennis-Sutton was flagged for taunting on an incomplete pass. The Cowboys were flagged for holding, meaning there were offsetting penalties. Given a reprieve, Prescott hit George Pickens for 7 and a first down on the final play of the third quarter.
Moments later, the Cowboys faced a third-and-2. Isaiah McDuffie was unblocked on a blitz and forced an incompletion. On fourth down, Prescott booted to his left and tried to hit CeeDee Lamb at the sideline, but Javon Bullard made a leaping breakup to give the Packers the ball at Dallas’ 49.
The Packers turned that into a 29-yard field goal. Love connected with Golden for 20 yards before getting hit into the middle of next week by Caleb Downs and Golden again for 12 yards on third-and-5 before getting hit by Rashan Gary. That made it 23-7 with 10:06 remaining.
At that point, Dallas’ feeble defense, which ranked at or near the bottom of the league in practically every category, including sacks, had three sacks, seven tackles for losses and eight quarterback hits in a step-backward performance by the line.
Green Bay led 17-0 at halftime. Even with some dropped passes, no running game whatsoever and a feeble first-down attack, it was total domination.
The Packers forced a punt to start the game, then marched 90 yards for a touchdown. Love was 6-of-8 passing for 109 yards – yes, 109 yards on a 90-yard scoring drive – because of two penalties for 20 yards and two rushing plays that lost 5 yards. After a pair of third-and-13 conversions, Love hit Matthew Golden on third-and-6 for the score.
After Green Bay forced a three-and-out punt, a key moment followed. After Love was sacked on first down, he threw an out to Golden. Linebacker Dee Winters saw it coming, jumped the route and made a tumbling interception. Winters got up, ran through a couple would-be tacklers and scored on a 43-yard pick-six.
A replay review, though, showed Golden touched Winters down at the 43. It was maybe the biggest tackle of the game. The Cowboys drove into the red zone but Prescott was picked off near the goal line by Evan Williams.
The Packers turned the turnover into a chip-shot field goal to lead 10-0. Golden dropped a 43-yard touchdown pass, but the Packers moved it to second-and-goal at the 1. However, Pierre Strong was stuffed on a run and Tucker Kraft couldn’t get his shoulders upfield on a catch in the flat.
After Brandon Cisse’s first career interception, the Packers extended their lead to 17-0 just before halftime. Bo Melton drew a 37-yard penalty for interference and Golden had a 21-yard catch to set up Love’s 1-yard sneak.
The Packers, the worst third-down offense in the league, went 9-of-10 in the first half. It was a remarkable achievement, considering Green Bay averaged less than 1.5 yards per play on first down.

title: Studs and Duds With Packers Routing Cowboys 17-0 at Halftime
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – Could the Green Bay Packers build upon last week’s blowout win over the Chicago Bears by doing it again against the Dallas Cowboys? Or was it merely the fool’s gold that tends to sparkle against a backup quarterback?
Through the first 30 minutes, the Packers’ rout of the Bears was no fluke. With Jordan Love contributing 190 passing yards and one touchdown and 14 rushing yards and another touchdown, Green Bay is clobbering the Cowboys 17-0.
The Packers are 9-of-10 on third down. They entered the game ranked last in the NFL with a 27.6 percent conversion rate while Dallas’ defense was last with an opponent conversion rate of 52.6 percent.
Here are some first-half studs and duds.
On the opening touchdown drive, Jordan Love was 6-of-8 for 109 yards. That’s only possible in Canada, but the Packers were guilty of 20 yards worth of penalties and a pair of negative-yardage runs to help Love eclipse 100 yards on a 90-yard touchdown drive.
Love completed a pair of third-and-13s before hitting Matthew Golden for a 9-yard touchdown on third-and-6.
It was a strong start for Matthew Golden – literally and figuratively. On the opening drive, he beat Shavon Revel deep for 37 yards to the 9. Golden was flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct for flexing in front of Revel; whether he said something, only the officials know. So, that moved the ball back to the 24. Another penalty moved it back to the 29. But the Packers scored, anyway, when Golden beat Ameer Speed on a post for a 9-yard touchdown.
AGENT 0 📺: NBC pic.twitter.com/g9gZwas6JN
Midway through the second quarter, Jordan Love threw one of his majestic deep balls. It should have been a 43-yard touchdown but Golden, who was 2 yards in front of Ameer Speed, dropped the pass.  It was a four-point play, as the Packers settled for a field goal.
Late in the first half, Golden almost made an incredible, twisting touchdown catch but couldn’t hang onto the ball while falling to the turf. The first few notes of "Bang on the Drum" were played and some fireworks were set off.
He made up for it a moment later with a leaping, 21-yard catch on an extended play to give Green Bay a first-and-goal at the 2. On the next play, Golden drew a pass-interference flag on DaRon Bland. Love scored on a sneak on the next play to make it 17-0 with 23 seconds left in the half.
On the second play of the second quarter, Zaire Franklin blitzed up the middle and clobbered Dak Prescott. The floating pass was almost intercepted by Brandon Cisse and Prescott was slow to get up.
On the next play, with the Cowboys facing third-and-8 from Green Bay’s 17, Dak Prescott had a solid pocket as he muscled one over the middle to CeeDee Lamb. Lamb had position on Xavier McKinney at the goal line, but maybe it was all a trap as Evan Williams jumped in front of the pass for the interception.
EVAN. WILLIAMS. 📺: NBC pic.twitter.com/H2dBumCPkg
“For sure. For sure. You got to attack these opportunities,” Williams said this week of the challenge of facing the high-powered Cowboys. “If you’re hesitant in any facet, that’s when you get exploited as a defense. When you’re unsure or questionable about what you’re going to do, that’s when explosives start to show up and things can go downhill in a hurry.
“As a back end, you’re licking your chops for opportunities like this when you know the ball’s going to be in the air, and it’s up to you to stop it. That’s what we look forward to on any Sunday. It’s our job to shut down receivers like this, and when you get those opportunities, can’t shy away from it.”
As we wrote before the game , this was the classic case of the stoppable force squaring off against the movable object. The Packers entered the game ranked 32nd with 60.4 rushing yards per game and 31st with 3.05 yards per carry. The Cowboys were 32nd with 168.4 rushing yards allowed per game and 29th with 5.10 yards allowed per carry.
Green Bay’s running game was horrendous. Nine handoffs to running backs gained 11 yards. Even Jordan Love’s 13-yard scramble didn’t put much lipstick on the pig.
The Packers’ best running back? Until Josh Jacobs returns, it’s probably Pierre Strong. On the opening possession, Jordan Love didn’t have any options on third-and-13, so he checked it down to Strong, who broke Ameer Speed’s tackle and gained 14 yards. Later, after Evan Williams’ interception, Love on third-and-8 checked it down to Strong again. He split two defenders for a gain of 10 and another first down. Those plays led to both of their first-half scores for a 10-0 lead.
The Packers entered the game ranked 17th with 5.42 yards per first-down play. It certainly wasn’t because of the running game, which was last in the NFL with 2.47 yards per carry – 0.36 yards worse than No. 31 Las Vegas and 0.89 yards worse than No. 30 Miami.
During the first half, Green Bay ran the ball eight times or 7 yards – the last of those was Jordan Love’s 1-yard quarterback sneak – and attempted seven passes that gained 11 yards.
The Cowboys have one of the best passing attacks in the league with Dak Prescott throwing to CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. Prescott finished the half 11-of-15 passing for 86 yards and two interceptions. Lamb caught 2-of-6 passes for 22 yards and Pickens caught his only target for 16.

title: Texans Injury Update: Another Starting DB Banged Up Before Week 7
full_text:
The Houston Texans were already dealing with a couple of key injuries heading into their Week 6 battle against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
On the offensive side of the ball, Houston was forced to go without running back David Montgomery with a groin injury he suffered back in Week 5 . Defensively, they were without their versatile nickel/safety Jalen Pitre, who suffered a shoulder injury in that same game .
And it turns out, after the events of the Texans' Week 6 game in London against Jacksonville, the secondary is dealing with another injury that could lead to an absence this weekend facing the New York Giants.
According to DeMeco Ryans in his Monday press conference, Texans safety Reed Blankenship is in the concussion protocol after leaving in the middle of Houston's Week 6 game against the Jaguars.
Ryans did also have some good news on the status of Pro Bowl linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair, who left in the middle of the game with a groin injury, but would eventually return and be described as "fine" heading into Week 7.
Being without Blankenship, though, is a notable loss for this Texans defense, who signed the veteran safety to be a weekly starter in the back-end of their secondary, and he's continued to fill that role since the season started.
While Blankenship's play has been up-and-down overall, he's combined for 45 tackles, three passes defended, one tackle for loss, and one interception in the six games he's played this season. And if without him in the secondary for any stretch of time, Houston will be forced to make another pivot for their starting defense as they already had to do last weekend without Pitre.
We won't know for certain if this Texans secondary will be without Blankenship heading into Week 7, though the concussion protocol for any player can tend to result in at least a one-game absence. So his status will be one to monitor over the course of this week at practice.
If Blankenship is forced to miss a game, the most obvious fill-in Houston could call up as their second safety next to Calen Bullock is veteran safety M.J. Stewart.
The 32-year-old is officially healthy after missing the first four games of the season due to a quad injury, but has appeared in the Texans' last two games with three total tackles. games with three total tackles.
Stewart was a frequent starter for the Texans in 2025 before he went down with what would be a season-ending quad injury, ultimately playing in nine games while starting in four of them for 25 tackles and two passes defended.
We'll certainly know more about the defensive plans for Houston once we get closer to Week 7's kickoff against the Giants. However, don't be surprised if the Texans are forced to be without both Blankenship and Pitre in their secondary as they were down the stretch in their last game against Jacksonville .

title: What to Expect From Texans WR Tank Dell in His Return vs. Giants
full_text:
The Houston Texans made a major announcement heading into their Week 7 matchup against the New York Giants, revealing that wide receiver Tank Dell would be making his return to the field for the first time in over 650 days since suffering his devastating knee injury in 2024.
It's been a long time coming for both Dell and Texans fans . The fan-favorite wideout first suffered his knee injury back in Week 15 of the 2024 NFL season against the Kansas City Chiefs, and has been diligently rehabbing and working back from it ever since.
Now, he'll finally get to see his hard work pay off this weekend in a key matchup for the Texans that could take them to their third win in a row.
But what exactly could Dell's first game back with the Texans look like? How often will he be able to get onto the field, and how involved in the offensive game plan will he be?
It probably goes without saying, but it'd be hard to expect Dell to get back into the mix for the Texans as an every-down receiver who's on the field for a lion's share of their offensive looks.
And those likely limited snaps come for two reasons: one being the obvious in that Dell hasn't played in a live, in-game setting since 2024. While he has been busy in team practice with pads on, playing in an NFL game with tackling and heavy contact is a different animal .
Houston, in all likelihood, will give Dell a few weeks of limited snaps for the first couple of games that he's back in the action, rather than simply throwing him into the fire, then continue to ramp up his workload the longer he's on the field.
Head coach DeMeco Ryans made it clear during his Monday press conference that he won't have any huge expectations for Dell in his first game back, and simply just wants to see him back out there and "be himself."
"I expect Tank just to be himself, and just play the offense the right way," Ryans said. "No huge expectations for what he needs to do. We're all just going to be excited... I'm just thankful, grateful for him to have this opportunity to return."
"I don't have any expectations, I'm just happy to see him out there. And that's the only thing that matters."
The Texans also don't have to feel an overwhelming need to get Dell quickly adjusted because of the talent they already have around him in the wide receiver room.
Of course, having Dell on the field and at 100% makes this passing attack even more potent than it already looked last week. But when he's also surrounded by other pass-catchers like Nico Collins, Marvin Harrison, and Jaylin Noel among others, the Texans can instead deploy Dell situationally and allow for an overall smoother transition to be a higher-usage player down the line.
And based on what DeMeco Ryans has seen in practice the past two weeks, he's confident that Dell can still be the explosive, playmaking talent he was when he was last on the field for the Texans.
"Tank is an explosive player. Still quick as ever. Ask our defenders who's been covering him the past couple of weeks," Ryans said. "He's been putting us in some tough matchups in practice the past two weeks. So I expect him to go out on Sunday and do the same thing; really stress defenders."
"And you add him in the mix with all the other guys we have, we just have a really good group of guys; a lot of guys who are capable of making big-time, explosive plays for us."
If there were a snap count projection to place on Dell heading into Week 7 against the Giants, think around 10-15 looks on the offense throughout the day.
We just saw last weekend against the Jacksonville Jaguars how the Texans wanted to limit Marvin Harrison Jr.'s integration into the offense in his first game back, where he was held to just 11 total offensive looks, though he saw four targets in the time he was out there.
Harrison Jr. and Dell are in two vastly different situations, sure: Harrison Jr. is getting integrated into a brand-new offense, while Dell has been in the building for the past three seasons and is just getting back on the field for the first time in nearly two years.
But in terms of how the Texans might deploy those two in their first games of the season, the results could be relatively similar: get Dell slowly integrated with a limited snap share, get him involved when he's out there for three to four targets, and both numbers will continue to increase with each passing week.
