Drake Wally is a Senior Writer for the Indianapolis Colts On SI. His works have also appeared on Bleacher Report, MSN, Yahoo, and SBNation. He also co-hosts the Horseshoe Huddle Podcast.

title: 5 Colts Players Most Impacted by Chris Ballard Firing
full_text:
Monday morning, the Indianapolis Colts made a long-overdue change at the top of the organization, firing general manager Chris Ballard after nearly a decade on the job . The decision marks the end of an era in Indianapolis and opens the door for a new voice to reshape the franchise's future .
Ballard may not be the only major departure this season. Head coach Shane Steichen's job is far from safe, while the upcoming trade deadline and a new-look front office could put several veteran players' futures in question .
Longtime assistant general manager Ed Dodds has been tasked with serving as interim general manager for the remainder of the 2026 season , leading the team's personnel department, while Steichen and non-personnel staff will report to ownership.
With the Colts entering a period of uncertainty, here are five players whose futures could be most affected by Ballard's departure.
When Ballard decided to bring Daniel Jones back on a two-year, $88 million contract extension, he essentially put his own fate in the quarterback’s hands.
Jones has looked nothing like the player the Colts had before his Achilles injury, and it's not all on him, but with Ballard already out of the picture, the quarterback's days in Indianapolis feel numbered.
The next general manager will inherit Jones’ contract and have to decide whether he is still the right man to lead the franchise. Either way, his status as the Colts’ long-term starter is in serious doubt.
Jonathan Taylor has established himself as the centerpiece of the Colts' rushing attack, but a change in the front office could eventually influence how Indianapolis approaches his future.
Taylor signed a two-year extension in August, keeping him under contract through the 2029 season and making him one of the NFL's highest-paid running backs. The new general manager will inherit that commitment while determining how best to build around the team's offensive stars.
If Indianapolis believes it can remain competitive with its current core, Taylor should continue to play a major role. But if the new regime takes a different approach to roster construction, it will have to weigh the value of keeping a high-paid running back against other needs.
Taylor isn't necessarily on the way out, but his future is one worth watching as the Colts enter a new era. Especially if playoff contenders come calling at the deadline.
DeForest Buckner was one of the most frustrated players after the embarrassing 26-20 loss to the then-winless Tennessee Titans on Sunday, vocalizing his exhaustion with the organization’s continued malpractice.
“I’m sick and tired of the same song and dance every year.”
#Colts DT DeForest Buckner’s postgame presser. “I’m sick and tired of the same song and dance every year.” pic.twitter.com/0lwXhKDpVS
It’s clear that a change of scenery is what’s best for Buckner. After fighting so hard to return from a scary neck injury ,only to continue the same story as the last ten seasons, he’s worked too hard to spend what remains of his prime on an uncompetitive roster.
San Francisco has been thrown out as a popular trade destination for Buckner. Of course, the Colts acquired Buckner from the 49ers in 2020, so a return back to the Bay to join the currently unbeaten 49ers on a Super Bowl run would make a ton of sense for Buckner.
If San Francisco general manager John Lynch is interested, I don’t think it would take very long for a deal to come together.
At then-owner Jim Irsay’s insistence, Ballard took a big swing for the fences by drafting an unproven and inexperienced Anrthony Richardson Sr. with the 4th-overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft. The idea was that Richardson would be the franchise quarterback Indianapolis had been missing since Andrew Luck.
Richardson’s story in Indianapolis is a long one with many twists and turns. I’ll spare you the details and get to the point: the organization failed Richardson so badly that his NFL future is now up in the air.
The fourth-year quarterback didn't hold up his end of the bargain either; however, as Vikings' head coach Kevin O'Connell so famously said, "I believe organizations fail young quarterbacks before young quarterbacks fail organizations."
Indianapolis declined Richardson’s fifth-year option, meaning he’ll be a free agent following this season. Depending on the new general manager’s opinion on him, the 24-year-old could be searching for a new home this spring.
But if he thinks that Richardson is the future of the franchise or at least a viable backup, then the Colts could absolutely bring him back.
Simply put, Richardson’s future is now in the hands of Ballard's successor. Whoever that may be.
When Chris Ballard traded two first-round picks and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell to acquire Sauce Gardner, he made one of the biggest bets of his tenure as Colts general manager.
The move brought a two-time All-Pro cornerback to Indianapolis, but it also cost the franchise valuable draft capital that could have helped address other roster needs.
It was one of the moves that ultimately sent him packing.
Now that Ballard is gone, the next general manager will inherit the responsibility of making that investment worthwhile.
Gardner remains a cornerstone of the defense, but the new regime will have to determine how to build around him and whether the rest of the roster is good enough to capitalize on his presence. They may think moving on is in both parties’ best interests.
The Colts' cornerback tweaked his calf against the Tennessee Titans in Week 6 and is now week-to-week, so don't be surprised if Indianapolis shuts him down through the trade deadline as they look to recoup as many assets as possible for the future.
With Indianapolis already sacrificing its 2026 and 2027 first-round picks, the pressure to get the most out of Gardner will only grow. It may be worth biting the bullet and taking whatever you can get just to move the next era forward.

title: Ed Dodds Has a Chance to Shape the Colts' Future
full_text:
Ed Dodds has spent years being viewed as one of the NFL's next general managers. Now, after nearly a decade as Chris Ballard's right-hand man, he finally gets his opportunity in Indianapolis.
According to Tom Pelissero, Dodds will lead the Colts' personnel department for the remainder of the season after Ballard was fired Monday morning. He takes over a 2-4 roster with 22 days until the Nov. 10 trade deadline.
And interestingly enough, whoever eventually becomes the full-time GM will inherit a foundation Dodds is about to help shape.
The Ballard era had plenty of highs from a talent-acquisition standpoint, but the results were never good enough.
Indianapolis went 72-82-1 under Ballard, made the playoffs twice, won one postseason game and never captured the AFC South. As Colts On SI's Noah Compton detailed Sunday night , the same shortcomings followed this organization year after year until Sunday's 26-20 loss to the previously winless Titans finally forced ownership's hand.
Carlie Irsay-Gordon can’t be blamed for taking a wait-and-see approach entering this season. The Colts were 8-2 last year before everything completely fell apart, and giving Ballard and Shane Steichen one more chance was understandable.
But after a full year running the organization, this feels like Irsay-Gordon starting to assert herself. I'd imagine her frustration with the franchise had been building long before she made that public on Monday.
Her statement Monday made that clear.
"Making this change during the season was a deliberate decision. Waiting would only delay the important work that needs to begin now."
Dodds joined Indianapolis in 2017, became assistant general manager in 2018 and has since interviewed for several GM openings, including jobs with the Chargers and Titans.
Now he gets his first real chance to run a personnel department.
That does not mean Dodds suddenly controls every football decision. As Pelissero reported, "Coach Shane Steichen and the football staff outside of personnel will report to ownership."
Still, with the season trending in the wrong direction, everything should be on the table. That includes giving Anthony Richardson Sr. another opportunity if Daniel Jones continues to struggle.
The bigger question for Dodds comes at the trade deadline.
Colts On SI's Peter Miller laid out several names Indianapolis should consider moving, with DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson standing out because both are on expiring contracts. Jonathan Taylor, Sauce Gardner and Laiatu Latu should at least draw conversations if another team is willing to pay a serious price.
Will Dodds actually dismantle a roster he helped Ballard build? Probably not.
But if he handles the next three weeks well and this team shows something down the stretch, he could do enough to earn legitimate consideration for the full-time job.
For years, Dodds has waited for his shot at running an NFL franchise. Now, with the Colts entering a new era, he has a chance to prove he deserves the job permanently.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Colts Reportedly Reach Out to Peyton Manning About GM Opening
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts could be looking to a franchise legend to help lead the organization into its next chapter.
Following the firing of general manager Chris Ballard on Monday, a report on The Dan Patrick Show says Indianapolis will contact former quarterback Peyton Manning as it searches for a replacement. The conversation would reportedly go beyond seeking recommendations and explore whether Manning himself is interested in the job, potentially with ownership interest involved.
“The Colts first call will be/has been to Peyton Manning,” Patrick said, reading a message from a league source. “The call will not only get names/suggestions, it will explore whether or not Peyton is interested in being a GM for Colts.”
"The Colts' first call will be/has been to Peyton Manning." — DP shares what his source has told him. pic.twitter.com/MgTbuJIxhW
The report has not been independently confirmed, and it remains unclear whether Manning has been contacted or would consider the position.
Indianapolis began its search for a new general manager Monday after dismissing Ballard following a 26-20 loss to the Tennessee Titans. Owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon said the Colts would conduct a thorough search for the right leader and emphasized that making the change during the season allowed the organization to begin immediately.
We have relieved Chris Ballard of his duties as General Manager. pic.twitter.com/BleD6bfTsG
According to the report, a conversation with Manning would serve two purposes: identifying potential candidates and determining whether he might want the job himself.
However, the report does not establish that Manning has agreed to interview, expressed interest or received a formal offer.
Manning spent 14 seasons in Indianapolis, leading the Colts to two Super Bowl appearances and a victory in Super Bowl XLI. He also won four NFL MVP awards with the franchise and became one of the most recognizable figures in team history.
His football knowledge and understanding of the organization could be valuable as Indianapolis looks to return to contention. Especially considering he lead the team through the most dominant era in its history.
But playing quarterback and running an NFL front office require different skill sets. A general manager must evaluate talent, manage the salary cap and oversee the personnel operation for the long term.
Manning's playing career alone does not establish that he can handle those responsibilities. Whether he would want the job and how the Colts would structure a potential role remain open questions.
Manning's name surfaced during Indianapolis' previous general manager search in 2017, when the Colts fired Ryan Grigson. Then-owner Jim Irsay acknowledged speaking with Manning but said there had been no serious negotiations for him to become general manager. Irsay did leave open the possibility of Manning eventually taking a role with the organization.
The Colts hired Ballard instead.
Nearly a decade later, they are again searching for a leader who can address roster construction, the quarterback situation and the franchise's long-term direction.
Manning's involvement could range from recommending candidates to pursuing a leadership role himself, but the current report does not establish which possibility is being considered most seriously.
The Colts should explore bringing Manning back, but they do not necessarily need to make him general manager. Indianapolis could consider a structure similar to the Atlanta Falcons' approach with Matt Ryan, who became president of football in January, with the head coach and general manager reporting to him.
A similar role could give Manning a meaningful voice in the team's direction while leaving day-to-day personnel decisions to experienced football executives. His knowledge of the Colts and stature within the organization could help restore confidence, but his reputation should not outweigh the qualifications needed to build a winning roster.
Manning's judgment should also be evaluated like anyone else's. He vouched for Adam Gase during his head coaching searches, and Gase went 32-48 over five seasons as a head coach, reaching the playoffs once.
If Manning wants a leadership role, Indianapolis could consider making him president of football and placing a qualified general manager and personnel staff beneath him. Assistant general manager Ed Dodds, currently overseeing the personnel department on an interim basis, should be considered, though the Colts should also conduct a serious external search.
The Matt Ryan model offers a potential middle ground: bring in a franchise legend to help shape the organization's direction while experienced executives handle roster construction. Any potential ownership stake would need to be evaluated separately.
Manning's return would be an intriguing story, but the Colts' priority must be finding the right leadership structure, not simply the most appealing name.

title: 5 GM Candidates the Colts Must Target After Firing Chris Ballard
full_text:
Losing at home to a 0-5 Tennessee Titans team was the final straw for the Indianapolis Colts - as it should have been.
On Monday, Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon officially fired general manager Chris Ballard following Sunday's embarrassing 26-20 loss, dropping Indianapolis to 2-4.
I've defended Ballard plenty over the years, and I still believe he's brought some exceptional talent to this roster. But after nearly a decade of mediocrity, two playoff appearances, and zero division titles, it was time to move on.
Now, Irsay-Gordon faces arguably her biggest decision since taking ownership of the franchise.
The Indianapolis Colts need a fresh perspective, and finding someone who can combine strong player evaluation with a modern, analytics-driven approach should be a priority.
Here are five candidates Indianapolis should immediately consider.
If Indianapolis wants to prioritize analytics, Adam Berry might be the most intriguing name on this list.
Philadelphia promoted Berry to assistant general manager in May after he spent 14 years at Goldman Sachs before entering the NFL in 2023.
His responsibilities include player evaluation, salary-cap management, contract negotiations and integrating analytics into roster construction.
There's also a fascinating Indianapolis connection. Berry's twin brother, Browns GM Andrew Berry, previously worked for the Colts and helped Irsay-Gordon learn the game during his tenure.
That familiarity, combined with Adam's analytical background, makes him someone I'd seriously consider.
Cook is another candidate with Indianapolis ties, having started his NFL career as a Colts scouting assistant in 2011.
Now serving as Cleveland's assistant GM and vice president of player personnel, Cook works alongside Andrew Berry and helps oversee free agency, the draft and roster construction.
He's been involved in Cleveland's personnel operation for a decade, gaining valuable experience in both scouting and front-office leadership.
For an organization seeking someone familiar with Indianapolis but capable of bringing a different perspective, Cook makes plenty of sense.
Few candidates on this list have a more impressive recent scouting résumé than Liipfert.
Houston's assistant GM previously directed college scouting and was part of the organization that drafted C.J. Stroud, Will Anderson Jr. and Derek Stingley Jr.
He also spent nine seasons with New England, winning two Super Bowls, and received a second interview for Atlanta's GM vacancy earlier this year.
That's the type of personnel background Indianapolis should be targeting.
McKay has spent 11 seasons with the Rams, working his way from scouting assistant to assistant general manager.
His responsibilities include evaluating NFL rosters, managing player movement and assisting with college evaluations.
Los Angeles has consistently developed front-office talent under Les Snead, and McKay is another executive worth watching.
Agnew has been Detroit's assistant GM since 2021, helping Brad Holmes build one of the NFL's stronger rosters.
Before arriving in Detroit, he spent years in the Rams' personnel department and played 11 NFL seasons as a defensive lineman.
He's helped oversee a remarkable turnaround in Detroit, and that experience could be particularly valuable for Indianapolis.
Now, here's a name that could completely change the direction of this franchise.
According to Dan Patrick, the Colts' first call following Ballard's dismissal will be, or may have already been, to franchise legend Peyton Manning.
Patrick reported that the conversation would go beyond simply asking Manning for recommendations, potentially exploring his interest in becoming Indianapolis' next general manager, with an ownership stake also part of the discussion.
Although nothing has been confirmed by Manning or the Colts, his football knowledge, leadership and connection to this organization are difficult to ignore.
Would I trust Manning to immediately take over every aspect of roster construction? That's a different conversation.
But bringing one of the greatest players in franchise history back to Indianapolis in a leadership role would certainly be an intriguing way to begin a new era.
Bottom line: Ballard assembled plenty of talented rosters, but the results never matched the expectations.
Whoever takes over needs to change that. The Colts can't afford another decade of coming up short.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: The Colts Were Right to Fire Chris Ballard
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have finally decided that enough is enough.
Following Sunday's embarrassing 26-20 loss to the Tennessee Titans, the franchise fired general manager Chris Ballard, ending a decade-long tenure that produced far more disappointment than success.
“Our standard is to compete for championships, and I believe a change in leadership is necessary to achieve that standard,” owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon said in a statement.
We have relieved Chris Ballard of his duties as General Manager. pic.twitter.com/BleD6bfTsG
The move was long overdue. Ballard found talented players and made several shrewd personnel moves, but he never turned that talent into sustained success. Indianapolis repeatedly waited for a breakthrough that never came, giving Ballard more opportunities even as the same problems persisted.
The Colts were right to make a change . The bigger question is why it took so long.
2021: A Collapse That Should Have Ended His Tenure
Indianapolis entered the 2021 season with legitimate playoff aspirations after winning 11 games the previous year. The team acquired quarterback Carson Wentz to provide stability at the position and appeared capable of making a deep postseason run.
Instead, the season ended in one of the most embarrassing losses in franchise history.
The Colts needed to beat the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 18 to secure a playoff berth. Jacksonville entered at 2-14 and had already been eliminated from contention.
The collapse exposed a team that could not deliver when the stakes were highest. Ballard also deserved scrutiny for the Wentz trade, which cost the Colts a first-round pick and left them searching for another quarterback after just one season.
That should have been the final nail in the coffin for Ballard's tenure. A general manager must be judged by more than the talent on his roster. He must also be accountable when his team repeatedly falls short.
Instead, Ballard remained in place. The following season made that decision even harder to justify.
2022: Another Failed Gamble
If the 2021 collapse did not convince Indianapolis to make a change, the 2022 season should have removed any remaining doubt.
The Colts finished 4-12-1, fired head coach Frank Reich during the season and turned to former Indianapolis center Jeff Saturday as interim coach despite his lack of NFL coaching experience. The team struggled on both sides of the ball as its season unraveled.
The quarterback situation deteriorated as well. Indianapolis had acquired Matt Ryan to provide stability after the Wentz experiment, but that move failed, too.
Ballard had now overseen two failed veteran quarterback acquisitions and a midseason coaching change. The Colts were heading toward a top-five draft pick and needed a new head coach and a long-term answer at quarterback.
Yet ownership gave Ballard another chance.
Indianapolis hired Shane Steichen in 2023 and selected Anthony Richardson fourth overall, effectively giving its general manager a fresh start with a new coaching staff and a premium draft asset.
It was another gamble that bought Ballard more time. It did not solve the franchise's problems.
A New Coach and Quarterback Didn't Do the Trick
Steichen and Richardson gave Indianapolis a fresh start, but Richardson's development quickly became complicated. A shoulder injury ended his rookie season after four starts, and he started 11 games in 2024 before struggling with consistency and losing the job to veteran Joe Flacco. Richardson eventually reclaimed the starting role, but questions about his readiness remained.
Those concerns carried into 2025. Richardson had not established himself as a dependable franchise quarterback, and injuries further complicated his development. The Colts eventually turned to Daniel Jones, who provided a different path forward and helped raise expectations entering 2026.
For a stretch, the change appeared to be working. But Jones' arrival underscored a larger problem: years after spending a top-four pick on Richardson, Indianapolis was still searching for a sustainable answer at quarterback.
By the time the Colts fell to 2-4 in 2026, the Steichen era had produced no playoff appearances. Richardson's injuries and development, coaching decisions and other factors all contributed, but Ballard was responsible for building a roster with a viable path forward at its most important position.
The problems extended beyond quarterback. Indianapolis continued to show glaring weaknesses in the passing game and along the defensive front.
The result was a team capable of flashes without establishing itself as a legitimate contender. After the 2021 collapse, the Colts needed accountability. After the 2022 disaster, they needed a new direction. Instead, they kept giving Ballard more time and hoping the next decision would fix the previous one.
The Numbers Tell the Story
Ballard finished his Indianapolis tenure with a 72-82-1 regular-season record, two playoff appearances and one postseason victory.
Since 1980, he is one of only two general managers to remain in the job for at least 10 seasons while overseeing fewer than three playoff appearances. The other is Rod Graves, who served as Arizona's general manager from 2003-12.
But Graves' Cardinals reached Super Bowl XLIII and won four postseason games. Ballard's Colts won just once in the playoffs.
Last month @RomeovilleKid looked at Chris Ballard's track record in Indy and compared it to other GMs with comparable tenure https://t.co/8WUebTjROW pic.twitter.com/BtRxPVaqNZ
That makes Ballard the only general manager in that 45-year span to remain in the job for at least a decade while recording fewer than three playoff appearances and fewer than two playoff victories.
The Colts reached the postseason in 2018 and 2020, but never built on those appearances. They failed to win the AFC South during Ballard's tenure and went six consecutive seasons without making the playoffs.
The NFL offers teams opportunities to turn things around through the draft, free agency and coaching changes. Ballard had nearly a decade to take advantage of those opportunities. Instead, Indianapolis remained stuck between rebuilding and competing, never fully committing to either path.
Eventually, a franchise has to judge its general manager by what the team accomplishes. By that standard, Ballard fell short.
The Colts Need a New Voice
Firing Ballard does not guarantee Indianapolis will become a contender. In fact, the Colts' general manager opening could be one of the least desirable jobs in the league.
The next executive inherits years of mediocrity, aging veterans on large contracts and immediate pressure to deliver results. The quarterback situation remains unsettled despite years of investment, the defense needs answers along the defensive front and difficult decisions loom regarding the roster's long-term direction.
There is talent to work with, but the next general manager cannot simply add a few pieces and expect a contender to emerge. He must determine whether the current roster can realistically compete, identify which players fit the next competitive window and build a plan that avoids repeating the previous regime's mistakes.
That could mean moving established players to recoup draft capital , particularly DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson, whose contracts expire after the 2026 season. Indianapolis should also evaluate the trade value of other key players rather than treating the current roster as untouchable.
The next GM will need patience from ownership while facing pressure to win. Ballard received nearly a decade to build a contender and still fell short. His successor must fix the same problems while convincing the organization that a different approach can finally work.
In other words, it'll likely get worse before it gets better.
That makes the hire especially important. Indianapolis cannot afford to replace Ballard with someone who simply continues the same roster-building philosophy and hopes for…

title: Colts Would Be Better Off Trading Away Their Best Players
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts ' 26-20 loss to the Tennessee Titans on Sunday was more than another disappointing result in a season that has quickly gone off the rails. It was another reminder that the organization has spent years living in a constant state of mediocrity under general manager Chris Ballard .
Indianapolis entered the season with expectations of competing for a playoff spot. Instead, the Colts fell to 2-4 after surrendering a 13-point halftime lead to a Titans team that had yet to win a game. The loss exposed familiar problems, from a defense that struggled to pressure the quarterback to an offense that could not protect the football when it mattered most.
Ballard's tenure has run its course . He's had ample time to build a contender, yet Indy continues to fall short.
The Colts need a new direction, and that requires more than replacing the general manager. The organization must also be willing to move on from some of the players most closely associated with the current regime and give its next leadership group the resources to build a team of its own.
One of the biggest obstacles to a genuine rebuild is the temptation to preserve the core of the current roster. Indianapolis has several talented players who have earned their reputations around the league, but their individual accomplishments have not translated into the sustained team success the organization needs.
A new general manager should not be expected to inherit the same roster construction philosophy or feel obligated to preserve Ballard's most significant personnel investments. The next regime needs the freedom to determine which players fit its vision and which assets would be better used elsewhere.
Keeping the same core together simply because those players are talented would risk prolonging the very cycle the Colts need to escape. Ownership must recognize that continuity is not inherently valuable when it continues to produce the same disappointing results.
The frustration inside the locker room is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Following Sunday's loss, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner expressed his exhaustion with the team's recurring shortcomings.
"I'm sick and tired of the same song and dance every year."
Buckner's words capture the frustration of not just a player, but a fanbase that has experienced the highs and lows of the Colts' recent seasons without seeing the organization take a meaningful step forward. Players like Buckner have invested years of their careers into trying to make Indianapolis a contender. They shouldn't have to waste the rest of their playing days waiting for the organization to figure out how to get there.
#Colts DT DeForest Buckner’s postgame presser. “I’m sick and tired of the same song and dance every year.” pic.twitter.com/0lwXhKDpVS
The Colts need to stop treating the current roster as something that must be preserved at all costs. A new regime deserves the opportunity to evaluate the team on its own terms, and several of Indianapolis' best players could be better served by continuing their careers elsewhere.
Recouping draft capital should be one of Indianapolis' top priorities moving forward . The franchise needs more opportunities to add young talent, address roster weaknesses and give its next general manager the resources to build a sustainable contender.
Buckner and Quenton Nelson are the clearest candidates to move. Both are foundational players who have spent years establishing themselves among the league's best at their respective positions. Both are also playing on contracts that expire after the 2026 season, putting the Colts at risk of losing two valuable assets without receiving anything in return, but that also gives Indy's trade partner the freedom to sign their new addition to a fresh contract instead of inheriting one they did not negotiate.
If the organization is ready to move on from Ballard and acknowledge that the current roster has not delivered, holding onto two veteran stars on expiring deals makes little sense. Indianapolis can recoup draft capital, give the next regime additional resources and allow two accomplished players to join teams with clearer paths to contention.
The Colts should not stop there, though the decisions become more complicated and difficult.
Jonathan Taylor remains one of the most important pieces of the offense. Cornerback Sauce Gardner is a young, established talent in the secondary, while defensive end Laiatu Latu still has room to develop into a cornerstone of the pass rush. All three could help establish a competitive floor for the next regime, giving a new coaching staff a foundation to build around rather than forcing it to restart from scratch.
A reset doesn't have to become a full teardown, and Indianapolis should not sacrifice every established player for the sole purpose of accruing draft capital---that would be reckless. A new general manager needs talented players who can contribute while younger prospects develop.
But Taylor, Gardner and Latu should not be untouchable. Taylor's contract and the market for running backs would factor into any potential deal. Gardner's age and established reputation, plus consideration to the fact he hasn't been a Colt for very long, could attract a contender looking for a top cornerback. Latu's youth and potential could appeal to a team seeking a long-term answer off the edge.
The Colts need to actively explore the market for all three. If they receive a trade package that would meaningfully improve its long-term outlook, the organization shouldn't hesitate make the deal.
Keeping a player simply because he is talented or was acquired through a significant investment would repeat the same mistake of prioritizing past decisions over future needs.
The distinction is straightforward: Buckner and Nelson should be moved because of their contract situations. Taylor, Gardner and Latu can help provide a foundation for the new regime, but their value in a trade must be weighed against what they could contribute to a rebuilt roster.
The goal  is simple: give the next regime as much flexibility as possible to build a winner .
Trading away established talent is not an easy path forward. Draft picks are uncertain, rebuilding takes time and a new general manager could make mistakes of their own. Indianapolis would also have to replace the production and leadership of players who have been central to the roster for years.
But the alternative is to keep trying the same approach year after year and hope the results eventually change. And we've already seen how that story goes.
Indianapolis has spent years trying to find its way back to the postseason and establish itself as a consistent contender. Sunday's loss to Tennessee was another painful indication that the franchise has not reached that standard. The organization can't keep asking its players and fans for patience while making the same decisions that have left it in this position.
Buckner and Nelson deserve the opportunity to compete for something meaningful during what remains of their primes. The same is true of Taylor, Gardner and Latu if the Colts cannot offer them a credible path toward winning football. These players have invested their careers in Indianapolis, and the organization owes them an honest assessment of where the franchise is headed.
Moving on from Ballard and trading Buckner and Nelson would give the Colts a clear starting point. Exploring the market for Taylor, Gardner and Latu would give the next regime additional options without requiring a complete teardown.
The Colts have reached a point where preserving the status quo is the greater risk. A new-look front office needs the authority to shape its own roster, the draft capital to address its weaknesses and the freedom to make decisions based on the future, not the past.
Indianapolis can't change what happened on Sunday, but it can control how they react. By making big decisions, ownership can indicate they're willing to do…

title: Colts Reach Rock Bottom in Chris Ballard's Magnum Opus
full_text:
The sense of urgency for head coach Shane Steichen and longtime general manager Chris Ballard has never been higher - or at least that's what Indianapolis Colts ' Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon said ahead of the 2026 regular season.
But after six weeks of play, the Colts look like the same uninspired team that's served as a revolving door of mediocrity under Chris Ballard's reign.
The Indianapolis Colts have posted new lows each season under Ballard and Co., but their Week 6 loss to the winless Tennessee Titans was so inexcusable that it should be the final nail in this regime's coffin.
This roster is likely beyond saving, but there's still a chance the season can be salvaged. The only way that hypothetical becomes feasible is if wholesale changes are made before the season concludes.
The Indianapolis Colts were up 13-0 against the Tennessee Titans at halftime, but 20 unanswered points opened the door for the worst team in the league to rebound, and Shane Steichen's team refused to close it shut.
This loss in question could be viewed as a one-off performance that a playoff contender just needs to shake off, but the optics around Indy's already bleak outlook suggest the opposite: the Colts may have lost to the team with the worst record in the NFL, but they themselves are closer to being the worst team.
The Colts allowed just 189 total yards of offense, and more than doubled up with offensive production of their own with 399 yards produced, but they still managed to leave their home field with a loss.
Shane Steichen's Colts offense is thoroughly broken.
Quarterback Daniel Jones has officially reverted to his New York Giants self, one of the league's top offensive lines looks uncharacteristically lost more often than not, the run game cannot be relied on to save the day, and the passing attack is nonexistent.
The offense's firepower is lacking, especially from its passcatchers, but there's no excuse worthy of absolving Steichen and Co. of their offensive sins.
But Lou Anarumo's Colts defense has not been much better, either.
The Colts have the worst pass rush in the entire NFL, their secondary has solid coverage defenders but lacks playmakers, and their linebacker room is littered with subpar options.
No matter how you shake it, the Indianapolis Colts are officially a dumpster fire.
Even more so, they very well may be the league's new laughingstock.
There are unfortunately plenty of examples to compare this loss to, but considering they are supposed to serve as lessons to his reign, Indianapolis' Week 6 loss to the Titans looks to be Chris Ballard's Magnum Opus.
Entering the 2025 regular season, a poll done by The Athletic showed that Indianapolis Colts fans are the least excited fanbase among all teams in the NFL.
An unforeseen historic start to that season briefly changed everyone's tune, but a mid-season implosion reminded folks that Chris Ballard's Colts may just be destined for mediocrity after all.
Fast forward one calendar year, and things looked even bleaker entering a new season.
Chris Ballard, Shane Steichen, and Co. hitched their wagon to an Achilles-torn Daniel Jones, banked on DeForest Buckner returning to form despite suffering a serious neck injury, and looked to replicate their offensive success from the season prior by signing an ankle-recovering Alec Pierce to a historic free agent deal.
The outlook remained uninspired; therefore, Colts fans checked out as they awaited the inevitable demise of the Ballard era.
But what we've witnessed through six weeks is grounds for a mid-season fire sale.
As long as fans keep showing up, the Colts have no problem staying the course, but that's not the case anymore.
Not only are Colts fans not filling up Lucas Oil Stadium anymore, they're booing more consistently and loudly than ever before, and season ticket holders are actively trying to encourage fellow members to forego renewals for the foreseeable future.
This fanbase has become numb to such disappointment, and can you blame them?
There's an incredibly fair reason that Indianapolis Colts fans were caught chanting "Fire Ballard!" at the tail end of the team's embarrassing loss at home to the 0-5 Tennessee Titans.
The Colts should have parted ways with Chris Ballard at numerous stops throughout his tenure, but if there's been any time to do so during the middle of a season, it's now.
We've predicted this season will finally be Ballard's last stand, but perhaps now's the best time to rip off the band-aid.
Ridding oneself of the mediocrity that the Ballard era has normalized is a good start for changing one's own scenery, but an exodus of the roster's top players should be the next step.
The Colts need to set up their next regime as best they can, so dealing assets to recoup for the incoming era is the top priority.
Indianapolis is already without a first-round pick for the upcoming NFL Draft after new ownership allowed Ballard to dish out multiple top draft selections for cornerback Sauce Gardner at the 2025 trade deadline.
The Colts would benefit from parting ways with key players Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, and Sauce Gardner, but moving on from the man who's tied to them is the first order of business.
Parting ways with Chris Ballard would allow the Colts to begin their rebuild early, while also giving them an (albeit unlikely) chance to rebound in the ongoing season.
In theory, immediately shipping out your best players would make the current outlook even bleaker; however, the Colts have proven time and time again that no matter what the roster looks like, success is impossible so long as Chris Ballard lurks behind the scenes.
The pillars of the Colts' roster have not gotten the job done, so there's no reason to believe they'll unlock a new version of themselves anytime soon.
If parting ways with Chris Ballard is not an option at this point in time, doing so with head coach Shane Steichen would be the next best thing.
Someone needs to be held accountable, so if it's not Ballard, then the man leading the charge on the field should be the one to go.
Both Steichen and Ballard experiments have run their course in Indianapolis, so ideally both are let go; however, if a full-blown fire sale and/or Ballard's departure isn't in the cards, Steichen should see the door.
Special teams coordinator Brian Mason and Assistant General Manager Ed Dodds feel like the ideal interim replacements, but we'll have to see if any changes are even on the table first.
One playoff victory, zero divisional titles, and countless examples of redefining what it means to hit rock bottom across an entire decade have become what's expected of Chris Ballard's reign.
When will enough be enough?
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Why Colts Should (Finally) Part Ways With GM Chris Ballard
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts find themselves in a rare opportunity where it makes sense to part ways with their general manager mid-season.
After a decade of disappointment, Colts ownership decided to run it back once and for all, suggesting that this time, Chris Ballard and Co. must win the AFC South and/or make the playoffs to right the ship.
Just six weeks into the 2026 regular season, it's evident that this sinking ship cannot be saved. Even more, the ship has already sunk to the bottom of the sea.
The Colts sit at a lowly 2-4 record after losing to the 0-5 Tennessee Titans at home, and this unforgivable loss should be enough to take the keys from the man who is responsible for constructing such an unacceptable, near-disrespectful product year in and year out.
The staff and rosters have not held up their end of the bargain throughout the years, but each shortcoming can be attributed to and traced back to general manager Chris Ballard's decision-making.
Furthermore, this most recent implosion is the perfect culmination of what the Ballard era has been: a revolving door of mediocrity.
But if Colts ownership has already planned to cut ties with this regime following the season if they cannot produce results, why would they jump the gun and do so now?
The Colts should have ended the Ballard era on numerous occasions throughout his tenure, most recently, ahead of this season, but there's no longer any reason to keep this regime around.
The current coaching staff, led by head coach Shane Steichen, defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo, offensive coordinator Jim Bob Cooter, and special teams coordinator Brian Mason, will also likely see the door after the season, but there's an argument to be made that you'd rather keep them around and part ways with Chris Ballard, as opposed to having a full-blown fire sale.
The roster and staff are what they are. There's more than likely no chance any version of this team rebounds this season, but seeing what a Colts team looks like without Chris Ballard lurking behind the scenes could be enough to inspire some confidence moving forward, at least as far as this season goes.
Eliminating the common denominator could very well be enough to get the Colts' swagger back, but there's a more important factor at play.
Parting ways with general manager Chris Ballard not only allows the Colts to get a brief audition period of what they've got, but more importantly, it also gives them a golden opportunity to sell off their best assets as they prepare for the next era.
Ideally, both Ballard and head coach Shane Steichen are relieved of their duties and we get a truly fresh look at what this roster can do, but if nothing else, the former should see the door.
The product we've gotten after a decade of roster construction is not only not good enough, but it's destroyed the fanbase's will to live.
With one playoff victory, zero divisional titles, and no future to look forward to after a decade of disappointment, how can you blame them?
The apathy is loud, so ridding oneself of this normalized mediocrity should be step one in the pursuit of earning the fanbase's trust back, and that starts with ripping off the band-aid that Chris Ballard has so regularly replaced.
The Indianapolis Colts would likely turn to longtime assistant general manager Ed Dodds in the scenario that Chris Ballard is fired mid-season.
While most may view Ballard's and Dodds' inherent ties as a reason to part ways with the entire front office, Dodds has been regarded as one of the NFL's top general manager candidates for quite some time now, and it's been shocking that he's stuck around to remain Ballard's right-hand man after going through numerous interviews with interested teams across the league.
Dodds would likely jump at the opportunity to become a first-time general manager, even if that means in an interim capacity.
Ideally, the Colts ownership trio of Carlie Irsay-Gordon, Kalen Jackson, and Casey Foyt turns to Dodds mid-season, and they instruct him to deal any assets they have remaining in an attempt to recoup as much draft capital as possible for the next regime.
Of course, Dodds may not appreciate the notion that he's to take his friend's job and rectify the damage they've done so that the next guy can benefit from it, but again, it's one of 32 jobs in the world.
I'm sure even Ballard would tell Dodds to jump at the opportunity, but that aside, the top priority moving forward is to set up the next era with the best possible situation.
The Colts are famously without their 2027 first-round pick after Chris Ballard traded away a blockbuster haul for cornerback Sauce Gardner at the 2025 trade deadline, so Indianapolis is already set for an uphill climb when it comes to attracting top general manager candidates.
Maximizing their outlook for 2027 and beyond is what should be the primary focus moving forward.
The Colts' 2026 season is already lost. They'll need a miracle to suggest otherwise.
Given how unlikely it is that Indianapolis rebounds and makes any noise in the playoffs, the best course of action from here on out is to think of the future.
Every decision from this point on should be trying to answer the question, "Does this make future us better?"
To do that, the Colts must focus on adding as much top draft capital as possible, and that begins with shopping their best players ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline, which is scheduled for Tuesday, November 10th at 4:00 PM EST.
There are no untouchable players on the roster anymore. Some definitely deserve the designation; however, this regime has made it impossible to consider anyone as a long-term option.
Whoever ends up calling the shots in the post-Ballard hypothetical should entertain any call that comes asking about Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Sauce Gardner, or Laiatu Latu.
Taylor, Gardner, and Latu are all under contract for 2027 and/or beyond, so the Colts could very well choose to keep them around to become the next regime's pillar players, though that should only happen if strong deals aren't offered.
However, when it comes to Nelson and Buckner, it'd almost be malpractice not to trade them elsewhere.
Both players are on expiring deals and will become unrestricted free agents this coming offseason. This added layer would do wonders come negotiation time, given that a true Super Bowl contender would jump at the opportunity to go all-in by trading draft capital for a one-year rental.
Legitimate contenders are worried about the present, while the Colts should be focused on the future.
The Colts have an opportunity to sell their best players to the highest bidder, and the fact that interested suitors could use this to not only bolster their current roster, but also figure out a long-term extension to get ahead of free agency and lock down their newcomer for the long haul would favor the Colts in negotiations.
Again, not a single player on the Colts' roster should be deemed untouchable moving forward.
This team has featured these talented players for each of their annual implosions, so there's no reason to believe they'll figure it out anytime soon.
It's clear the 2026 Colts won't be making the noise come postseason play, so ensuring a healthy transition should be the top priority from here on out.
This season may not be salvageable, but the future is.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: The Biggest Decision Jaguars' Liam Coen Got Wrong Against the Texans
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Hindsight is always 20/20, especially after a loss in the NFL.
With that said, it didn't take the benefit of hindsight to dive into one of Liam Coen's biggest decisions in the Jaguars' 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans in Week 6. Coen and the Jaguars had a chance to put themselves in a position to beat the Texans and improve to 5-1, but that was before this critical decision.
Coen has bgeen an aggressive coach when it comes to fourth-down decisions since he was hired, and it has helped the Jaguars more than a few times. He was even aggressive against the Texans in the first-half, passing up a potential field goal for a fourth-down attempt that would end in an incompletion.
That is what made his decision to kick a 60-yard field goal with 1:55 left a difficult one to understand in the moment. The Jaguars were down by three and had the ball at the Texans' 42-yard line, facing a 4th-and-4 with the game on the line. Going for it would have meant risking the chance of giving the Texans the ball back near midfield, but it also would have given the Jaguars their only real chance to win the game considering the performance C.J. Stroud had.
The math, though, was clear. There were four potential scenarios with the decision, and only one of them would have led to a likely Jaguars win; kick it and make it, and the Texans get the ball back with three timeouts and nearly two minutes to kick a field goal and likely lose, which is what happened; kick it and miss it, and lose; go for it and do not get it, and likely lose; go for it and get the first down, which would have likely led to, at worst, overtime.
For the Jaguars to win this game, they needed to be aggressive one more time instead of trusting their kicker. But they didn't, and the Texans drove down the field and won the game as a result.
"Look, every decision like that, it's a coach's decision. I ended up doing that and there's always hindsight. And you look, alright, if we don't get it, we're going to need a stop either way," Coen said on Monday. "If we go down and you're down by six points, now we have got to go score a touchdown. I felt like we had just got the turnover, maybe we put a little pressure on them on the other side of the ball."
Little, of course, made the 60-yard field goal. The Texans then drove into field goal range in six plays, finishing the drive with a 49-yard field goal as time expired to give themselves the win -- a win that the Jaguars could have had with a different decision and, of course, the proper execution.
But having Little's big leg plays a factor. The Jaguars knew he could make the field goal, and that is exactly what he ended up doing.
"But he gives you so much confidence to be able to be in those moments regardless of end of game, end of half, you feel like he got a shot and that's why we were able to be aggressive at the end of the half was to try to put us in a position to get points and he's such a weapon," Coen said. "Sometimes it makes some of these decisions challenging when you have a guy that's so dynamic that he can make kicks from so many different spots on the field, but very proud of Cam in the last few weeks that he's had, just continues to give us a chance to win.”

title: 2 Jaguars Foes Have Suddenly Emerged as Logical Brian Thomas Jr. Landing Spots
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jagyars are clearly heading in one certain direction with third-year wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. and now a few more teams have emerged as logical landing spots.
With the trade deadline still several weeks away, a lot can change around the NFL to shift the wide receiver market. We saw that over the last two days, with the Los Angeles Rams and Washington Commanders each suddenly having significant receiver injuries pop up over the course of Week 6.
As a result, there is a case to be made for both franchises as landing spots for the embattled former Jaguars' first-round pick , and here is why.
The Rams are in serious trouble at 2-4, with their Super Bowl and dream team aspirations from the offseason looking like a distant memory. The Rams need to quickly rebound over the next 11 games,and the reality is they can likely only afford to sustain three or so losses during that time. To make matters worse, the Rams have now have gotten the injury bug in a big way.
Amongst the injuries the Rams are now facing is one to star wide receiver Davante Adams, who Rams head coach Sean McVay said would be out for the next 6-to-10 weeks after sustaining a lower-body injury in their woeful loss to the Arizona Cardinals in Week 6. Adams has 30 catches for 480 yards and four touchdowns already this season, and he has a high target share of 20.2%, behind only Puka Nacua amongst the Rams' targets.
With Adams out for potentially most of the rest of the season, the Rams will have to rely on a receiver room made up of Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, Jordan Whittington, and Xavier Smith. Outside of Nacua, this is one of the worst wide receiver depth charts in the NFL, and they could use a big boost.
Naturally, Thomas could be that boost. He has had serious issues with drops with the Jaguars over the last two seasons and it seems like the only logical solution is to let him hit the reset button somewhere else while the Jaguars get draft picks in exchange. The Rams need a big-play threat to help the offense get by until Adams returns, and Thomas could certainly be that since he would have more opportunity in the Rams' receiver room than he does in the Jaguars' deep one.
There is a question of whether the Rams would be interested in Thomas since they already gave up picks for Myles Garrett and since they have close ties with a Jaguars' staff that has had their own issues making it work with Thomas. But the Rams need receiver help now to turn around their season and get them to the playoffs, and Thomas would certainly give them a dangerous weapon to pair Nacua with for the long-term.
The next team that suddenly has a massive wide receiver need is the Washington Commanders, who saw wide receiver Terry McLaurin sustain a serious injury on Monday Night Football that NFL Network's Ian Rapoport said is likely a season-ending injury that will sideline him for the rest of the 2026 season. The Commanders are a bad team that is sitting at 1-4-1 and does not have much going for them, but this still makes sense for a few reasons.
#Commanders WR Terry McLaurin, who was carted off in an air cast last night against the #49ers , is feared to have suffered a serious and season-ending knee injury. He’ll have an MRI today. pic.twitter.com/TOs0bxGoNu
While Commanders head coach Dan Quinn will likely be fired this year, it does not feel like the Commanders will dump general manager Adam Peters. The easiest way for Peters to keep his job in the long-term is via Jayden Daniels -- if Daniels can improve his play and get back to his rookie year form, that will look pretty good for the general manager who drafted him a few years ago.
So Thomas is not a trade that would make a ton of sense for a Commanders team that might be losing a ton of games and needs their picks to rebuild ... but it would make sense for a general manager who needs to keep his job to give his quarterback a familiar and talented target. Daniels was Thomas' quarterback during their final seasons at LSU, and the connection between the two could go a long-way toward solving some of Washington's long-term issues at the wide receiver position.
If the Jaguars truly are comfortable with moving on from Thomas this season, there should be no shortage of potential suitors. Two more have hit the radar this week, and more could join as the season goes on.

title: 3 Things We Learned From Jaguars' Week 6 Loss to Texans: C.J. Stroud is a Problem
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are 4-2 entering their bye week thanks to a tough loss to the Houston Texans on Sunday, but the loss did reveal quite a few things.
So, what did we learn about the Jaguars after their 34-31 loss to the Texans, and what does it all mean for the franchise moving forward? We break it down below.
Sometimes, the game is the game. The Jaguars ran into a buzzsaw in the form of a red-hot C.J. Stroud on Sunday and it felt like there were more than a few times that there was nothing they could do. The deep balls to Nico Collins and Jaylin Noel and the second touchdown pass to Foster Moreau were just outrageous passes. And when the Jaguars did get pressure on Stroud, he carved them up with the best EPA/dropback against pressure of any quarterback this week.
The Texans' defense seems human again, which is a good thing. But their passing game also looks very dangerous right now, and the Jaguars might have to see the Texans two more times depending on how things play out. There are quite a few other AFC quarterbacks a team would rather face in an important late-season game than Stroud right now.
Travis Hunter was certainly special against the Texans on Sunday, and the scary thing is he did it without even playing that much on offense. Hunter made major contributions to both sides of the ball , ranging from his red-zone interception to his four catches for 59 yards and a touchdown against the Texans on offense. It was the first game this year Hunter received multiple targets, and he responded with a significant uptick in production.
The rub, of course, is that Hunter still only ran seven routes. That is four more than he did against the Eagles a week before and three more than his previous season-high of four against the Patriots. The difference is that instead of being targeted one or zero times, like he had been in his previous four games on offense, he saw the ball come his way four times. The Jaguars need Hunter to be a part of the offense for it to be at its best, and they should start to expand his route tree and snap count while continuing with the recent increased volume.
Cam Little was absolutely stellar on his 60-yard field goal , and having a weapon like him is a big, big advantage for the Jaguars in nearly all cases. With that said, it almost felt like the confidence in Little to make the 60-yard kick with under two minutes left against the Texans forced the Jaguars into making a decision that didn't help them win the game. If the Jaguars had a kicker they did not have as much faith in, they likely would have just gone for it on 4th-and-4 from the Houston 42.
There is no telling if the Jaguars would have gotten it, of course. They had gained just six yards on three pass plays ahead of the fourth-down, there were a few drops, and perhaps Liam Coen had confidence in his defense getting one stop to keep the Jaguars in the game with three timeouts left. But the Jaguars' best chance to win this game was always to get that first down. Kicking it back to the Texans with two minutes left felt inevitable, but so did Little making his kick. Little is a special player, but this was a glimpse into how he can impact the flow of the game and critical decisions, even indirectly.

title: Jaguars' Biggest Need Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline Is Painfully Obvious
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are sitting in a perfectly good spot at 4-2 entering their Week 7 bye week, but things could always be better, and they could always improve.
The trade deadline is the most obvious avenue for a team to find in-season improvement, as we saw last year with the Jaguars' trade for Jakobi Meyers. And just like the Jaguars needed receiver help a year ago, it has become clear that there is one position they must target this year.
The Jaguars have all that they need at a few positions: they should be very happy with their linebacker play, and they clearly have the depth required, and then some, at wide receiver, tight end, running back, and quarterback. That does beg the question of a few other positions, though, and namely on the defensive side of the ball.
Jacksonville was one of the NFL's top-ranked defenses entering Sunday, but they got absolutely lit up against the Texans and their passing game in Week 6. Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud had several high-level throws and found plenty of deep and red-zone success against Jacksonville, burning them for explosive plays, efficient gains, and everything in between.
The defensive line is one position that will draw a lot of attention ahead of the deadline, especially after a day in which the Jaguars hardly pressured Stroud without sending the house on blitzes ... that Stroud then picked apart. The Jaguars' biggest issue with the defensive line appears to be the ceiling when it comes to their backups, with most of the Jaguars' backup spots consisting of cheap journeyman or young former undrafted free agents.
With that said, I think the loss to the Texans exposed the cornerback position more than the defensive line. As Coen noted after the game, and as you could see as players slipped all day, the surface was not one that exactly helped a pass-rush unit.
"The surface, obviously, I didn't feel like we were under a ton of duress, either. I think that venue benefits the offense in a lot of ways in terms of the pass rush. If we weren't feeling them, they probably didn't feel us," Coen said.
The cornerback group can't say the same thing, however. Jarrian Jones and Jourdan Lewis each struggled and allowed big plays at times against the Texans, with Lewis allowing a red-zone touchdown and Jones allowing an explosive play to set the Texans up in the red-zone before the end of the half. Travis Hunter was beat by Nico Collins twice, too, but he also managed to intercept Stroud and proved to be a more effective coverman than anyone else in the cornerback room on Sunday.
But then you have to consider the Hunter experience. Hunter also starred on offense in limited snaps on Sunday, and with Brian Thomas Jr.'s recent struggles it would make sense for Hunter to start getting more and more snaps on offense eventually. It is hard to afford to do that when dealing with injuries and up-and-down play at the cornerback position, though.
I mean, the Jaguars added two cornerbacks to the active roster two weeks ago for a reason in Jaylon Jones and 
Alijah Huzzie, but those are special teams and depth options. The Jaguars need someone who can step in and play, and they can't just hope Montaric Brown's hamstring suddenly heals and he reverts back to his 2025 form.
The Jaguars need at least one more solid cornerback to be the complete team they want to be. This was clear in Week 2 when they gave up too many explosives. It was clear in Week 5 when the same thing happened. Then more explosives have hit over the last two weeks, and the need has started to become a screaming red flag.

title: Shipley's Dozen: What the Jaguars' Loss to Texans Means and Travis Hunter's Next Step
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- That was a tough one.
The Jaguars left London with a Week 6 loss to the Houston Texans, and we break it all down in this week's Shipley's Dozen column, with 12 takes on where the Jaguars must go next.
Travis Hunter is starting to prove himself. Had the Jaguars won on Sunday, the entire story from the game would have been all about Travis Hunter and his two-way impact. Hunter's fourth-quarter touchdown drive and his red-zone interception were two of the biggest moments of the game, and the fact that they came from the same player is mind-boggling. Now that the Jaguars have seen a taste of what Hunter can do in one game, the question is where do they go from here. Hunter, naturally, should see more and more snaps and chances on offense in the weeks ahead, but that also could mean changes for a defensive role that he is clearly key in.
The Jaguars are certainly in a good spot entering the bye week. They are 4-2, hold a two-game lead in the AFC South, and have an easy second-half schedule. With that said, the Jaguars are still not in a great spot. They would have been with a win since they would have held a three-game lead over Houston, but the Texans have the ability to make up a two-game gap, and the Jaguars know that. The Jaguars' playoff chances are still very, very healthy. They are still a very good team. But a win would have gone a much longer way than the loss.
Yes, the Jaguars have gotten jobbed out of several touchdowns by bad calls -- four over the last three games, somehow. But I still do not think one can pin this game on the refs. The Jaguars are still the team that gets in their own way too often, whether it be drops, red-zone turnovers, false starts, whatever you want to call it. Same on defense with missed tackles and penalties. The Jaguars have gotten a really bad hand with officials in recent weeks, but it isn't why the Jaguars lost Sunday. The Jaguars lost because of their own self-inflicted mistakes, which is why they have lost in Week 2, and to Buffalo last year, and so on and so forth.
After the Jaguars benched Brian Thomas Jr. against the Texans in the second-half, they more or less closed the door on him ever becoming a factor in the offense. It seems like the Jaguars' only real option is to shop him on the trade market over the next few weeks, but which teams would make sense as potential trade partners?
Las Vegas Raiders: Tre Tucker has turned it on and Brock Bowers is a beast, but those are the only NFL pass-catchers on that roster. The Raiders have a ton of picks and a young franchise quarterback they need to surround with talent. They seem like a team that would swing big on Thomas.
Atlanta Falcons: The Atlanta Falcons already have a few explosive play-makers, but their offense could use another pass-catcher opposite of Drake London. Thomas would bring a different element that could fit within their scheme and with their quarterback room, too.
Seattle Seahawks: The Seahawks' offense looks like a mess, and they can not just keep spamming the JSN button without giving him support. They do not have real wide receiver depth behind him, and they need to make a big move to ensure they can make the playoffs in a tight NFC.
The trade deadline is still a month away , but the Jaguars should spend the bye week thinking about how they can add to the roster and improve it. The Jaguars have the draft picks and the ammo to make moves happen, but what are the needs they would have to hit? After the Texans game, I think a few are clear.
Cornerback: The Jaguars clearly need to play Travis Hunter both ways, so more cornerback depth is needed ... especially with Montaric Brown injured. I do not think the cornerbacks are as bad as some of the yardage numbers say, but they could use some reinforcements.
Defensive Tackle: The Jaguars might have the least amount of resources allocated to their backups on the defensive line in the entire NFL, and defensive tackle is a big part of that. Taking a swing for a starting-level player would make a big difference.
EDGE: The Jaguars are getting very, very little from their backup defensive ends such as Danny Striggow and Bryan Thomas Jr. Dennis Gardeck is a nice change of pace situational pass-rusher, but the Jaguars need to start winning by rushing four, and they can't rely on Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen every snap.
Sunday was a classic quarterback duel between Trevor Lawrence and C.J. Stroud. Stroud was throwing dots drive after drive against the Jaguars' defense, while Lawrence led the Jaguars to a 10-point comeback in the fourth-quarter after some terrific throws to all levels of the field. Lawrence and Stroud have had some great battles over the years, and I think this game rivaled the 2023 duel they had in Houston. This is the best quarterback rivalry in the AFC South, and one of the very best in the entire NFL. It isn't Mahomes/Allen, but there are not many better than it in the NFL today.
The Jaguars had just four drops on the season entering Week 6, but they collected five in Week 6: two from Brian Thomas Jr., two from Parker Washington, and one from Jakobi Meyers. The Jaguars had not had many, if any, drops during the first few weeks of the season but they have seven over the last three games. The Jaguars have gotten into their own way far too many times during the 2026 season, and this was one of the biggest reasons they lost on Sunday. If the drops linger on post-bye week, then the Jaguars should consider it a serious issue.
How well the Texans ran the ball. The Jaguars allowed their longest rush of the season, their most rushing yards allowed all season, their highest average yards allowed per carry, and their highest yards after contact allowed per rush. The Texans running game has genuinely stunk against every other defense in the NFL the last two seasons but the Jaguars'. This is the second meeting in a row in which they have ripped off big plays on the ground against the Jaguars, so it seems like a real-deal concern for the next matchup.
C.J. Stroud's success. I figured this would be a shootout, but I didn't factor in the turf making it a 7-on-7 game. Still, Stroud has been a top-10 quarterback this season who has been able to hunt explosives while still being efficient as a quick-passer, which was always bound to be a bad matchup for the Jaguars' defense. This wasn't a great matchup on paper to begin with, and Stroud proved why this was the case.
This one is obvious, no? Hunter became the third player since at least the 1970 merger to have an interception and a receiving touchdown in a regular season game, joining HOF S Brian Dawkins (Week 4 of 2002) and Cardinals WR Roy Green (Week 3 of 1981). He also became the first player since 2014 to record 50-plus receiving yards, two tackles and a touchdown in a game. He is truly a unicorn.
The Jaguars now hold a two-game lead in the AFC South leaving Week 6, which saw two different AFC South divisional battles take place. The Texans improved to 2-4, while the Indianapolis Colts had a woeful performance at home in a loss to the winless Tennessee Titans to also fall to 2-4. The Colts seem like they are teetering on implosion, while the Titans won a sloppy game that saw their quarterback fail to hit 110 passing yards.
As usual, that leaves the Jaguars and the Texans. The Jaguars' post-bye schedule has them playing the Colts, New York Giants, and Tennessee Titans twice in their first five games. The Texans' next four games are winnable as well, though, with four expected wins against the Giants, Los Angeles Chargers, Cleveland Browns, and then the Colts.
With both teams facing soft schedules over the next few months, the race is officially on in the AFC South. Neither team can allow the other the keep pace, and the margin for error for each squad is nearly nothing. If this feels a lot like last year's race, well, it is.

title: 3 Overreactions to the Jaguars' Last-Second Loss to Texans: AFC South Shakeup
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- It is far from time for the Jacksonville Jaguars to panic, but that doesn't mean Week 6 can't be a wakeup call.
The Jaguars stormed back in the fourth quarter to give themselves a chance to win, but they failed to find a way to win the AFC South clash with the Houston Texans in London.
So, what are some overreactions to the Jaguars' 34-31 loss that are rooted in reality at 4-2? We break it down below.
Can anyone say comfortably that Brian Thomas Jr. will be ahead of Josh Cameron on the wide receiver depth chart when the Jaguars return from the bye week? Thomas had already become the forgotten man in the Jaguars' offense for the most part with just a handful of catches in the first few games, but he has caught zero passes on five targets in the last two weeks and has arguably cost the Jaguars four scoring opportunities in that span with drops. The Jaguars' staff trusts Cameron, and Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence has not appeared to have any issues doing the same.
Then there is the fact that Travis Hunter got more run on offense. He didn't appear to play a heavy snap count on offense, but he did see four targets and caught them all for 59 yards and a touchdown. Had the Jaguars won, the story of the game would be Hunter's impact on offense. He will likely continue to see more touches, which really makes it seem like Thomas is receiver No. 5, and better off getting traded within the next month.
The Jaguars will be entering the bye week with a two-game lead in the AFC South since the Texans and the Indianapolis Colts are both 2-4. It is far from an awful spot to be in after the first six games, especially considering how difficult this early stretch appeared before the season began. 4-2 has long been seen as a successful outcome, and that is what the Jaguars got.
With that said, the AFC South race is now on. A two-game lead is an OK one in terms of security, but there are still 11 games to go. Things can get completely turned upside down by January if the Jaguars do not clean up their issues, because the Texans are still very much in this. Beating the Texans would have given the Jaguars a three-game cushion, a better place to be in than the one the Jaguars now occupy. The Jaguars should still feel good about the AFC South, but they could have felt great.
The Jaguars' defense had one of its worst games of the Anthony Campanile era on Sunday, allowing the Texans to score on 6-of-10 drives and allowing 34 points after allowing 40 points in the previous three games combined. C.J. Stroud picked the Jaguars apart no matter the blitz or the coverage, and the Texans also had far much more rushing success than anyone could have predicted entering the game.
"Yeah, wasn’t good enough for sure. Got to go back and look at it. Thought they made too many plays in the pass game, and they ran it better than anybody has on us so far. Got to evaluate it, get it cleaned up, but definitely disappointing," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game on Sunday.
It doesn't feel fair to really throw blame at the pass-rush considering the disadvantage they were at by the field -- as evidenced by the Texans' lack of pass-rush production, which Coen noted after the game. Still, the Jaguars looked like a unit that could surely use another difference-maker on defense. They like their cornerback room, but could that be addressed with a trade before the deadline? It is worth considering after all of the big plays through the air.

title: Game Balls From Jaguars' Disheartening Loss to Texans: One Standout Emerges
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. --  The Jacksonville Jaguars will be limping into the bye week.
The Jaguars failed to get it done against the Houston Texans in Week 6, falling 34-31 on a walkoff field goal a week after their own last-second win. But even with the loss, there are still a few Jaguars who were able to move forward with strong performances and efforts. So, which of those Jaguars have earned a game ball as a result?
This one feels easy. Trevor Lawrence was one of the best players on the field on Sunday, throwing for over 300 yards and four touchdowns against a defense and a head coach that has given him fits in the past. The Texans' defense isn't what it has been in past years, but it is still a good unit with some blue-chip players on it, and Lawrence had one of the best performances of his entire career against the Texans with his latest outing.
If this is the version of Lawrence we see for the rest of the season, the Jaguars are in very good hands. He did have an end-zone interception that the Jaguars can't afford, but it did come after the Jaguars got jobbed on a bad holding call, so perhaps he never should have even been in that situation. Regardless, Lawrence had another impressive showing for the Jaguars, and once again proved to be their most important piece.
Travis Hunter was undeniably special on Sunday afternoon. Hunter gave up a few big plays, such as a long gain to Nico Collins on a stop-and-go and a few penalties, but he also made the most important play of the day for the defense. On a day where the Jaguars allowed the Texans to score on 6-of-10 drives, there were not many Jaguars defenders to consider. The Jaguars' defense got shredded, but Hunter still made an impact play with his fourth-quarter red-zone interception of C.J. Stroud.
Hunter became the first defender to intercept Stroud in 2026 with his stellar play, which ensured the Jaguars continued their run of red-zone takeaways. It was one of the only times the Jaguars slowed Houston down on Sunday, and it proved that Hunter is, at the end of the day, a play-maker who is going to get the ball. With a pass defensed against Houston, Hunter also extended his streak to five consecutive games with at least one pass defensed, tied for the longest active streak in the NFL.
"Made some critical plays for us on both sides of the football, obviously. Had the interception late, that gave us a chance to win the game. Proud of the way he completed, made some plays for us on offense and got to keep building off it," Liam Coen said after the game.
While the decision to kick the field goal by Liam Coen was certainly one that is going to be debated until the next time the Jaguars kick off, that doesn't change the fact that Cam Little was fantastic when his number was called. Little nailed the 60-yard field goal seemingly with relative ease, and it feels safe to say he could have saved the day for the Jaguars at some point if given the chance to do so.
With the kick, Little recorded the third 60-plus-yard field goal of his career, the most in franchise history. Since entering the league in 2024, his three field goals of 60-plus yards are the second most in the NFL. He is well on his way to becoming one of the highest-paid kickers in the entire NFL, because the Jaguars are tough to imagine without him and his booming field goals.
