title: The Morning-After Thunder: Chargers' Loss puts McDaniel and Hortiz on Chopping Block
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers enter their Week 7 bye week beaten, battered and bruised. Their roster is in injury purgatory , their offense is lifeless and their personnel is weak in many spots.
The Chargers defense has been going to absolute war week in and week out trying with their entire might to keep the Chargers in games. Against the Chiefs on Sunday, Cam Hart intercepted Patrick Mahomes in the endzone, Justin Egboigbe and Tony Jefferson stonewalled Kenneth Walker on a four-and-goal run and the defense forced multiple stops to give the offense the ball back. The offense appears to be the walking dead and incapable to reciprocating the defenses efforts.
The Chargers offense isn't just bad, it's historically bad. The franchise is off to its worst start since the 2000 season, ironically a season in which Jim Harbaugh went 0-5 as a starter alongside Ryan Leaf and Moses Moreno. This was supposed to be a team primed to be Super Bowl contenders. Even the most cynical media pundits never imagined the results would stray this far from success. What happened?
The most obvious elephant in the room is that despite the excitement for the pairing of offensive genius Mike McDaniel and franchise quarterback Justin Herbert the two are not meshing. Herbert seems to be struggling with his post-snap reads and his confidence in what he is seeing is causing uncharacteristic errors and an explosion in his turnover-worthy play rate, plays in which he puts the ball in danger.
Justin Herbert has a career average of 2.2 percent with his highest rate hitting 2.6 percent. The high of 2.6 percent occured last season in 2025 while he was playing behind an injury-decimated offensive line that he dragged to the playoffs.
Herbert has a 6.7 percent turnover-worthy play rate through the first six weeks of the 2026 season. He had four different offensive coordinators from 2020-2025 and was consistent, 2026 is an absolute and undeniable outlier.
Mike McDaniel is a branch off of the Shanahan coaching tree and not all quarterbacks are best suited for that style of offense. McDaniel is likely on his way out of LA with how the offense has performed. It very well may be purely a water and oil situation where the two do not mix. Herbert has been elite at pre-snap analysis and post-snap execution, the sudden collapse is more than likely the shift in emphasis in a Shanahan-based system for which he is not suited for and McDaniel was unwilling to adjust his offense to match the quarterback.
The Chargers offense is not just bad, they are also dealing with a massive gap in talent and experience. For the second season in a row, the offensive line, particularly the interior has been the catalyst for Justin Herbert running for his life, being pressured and hit at historically bad rates, again.
Chargers general manager Joe Hortiz and the Chargers front office was tasked with retooling the interior offensive line after horrific play on the offensive line in 2025. Los Angeles frustratingly did not treat the guard position with the intent and importance that they should have. They did sign quality veteran center Tyler Biadasz to replace retiring Bradley Bozeman. But to replace left guard Zion Johnson and right guard Mekhi Becton, they signed journeymen or former first-round busts to compete for the starting guard positions.
Joe Hortiz believes in and fully uses the Baltimore Ravens philosophy of believing that they can find cheaper guards and elevate them with scheme and quarterback play. Hortiz fully expected and banked on McDaniel being able to elevate the interior with scheme, when Biadasz went down with injury, the results were catastrophic.
The 2026 offensive line was built to be functional in a best-case scenario, the Chargers have started their sixth option at left guard the past two weeks with rookie Logan Taylor and have backup rookie tackles as well. The lack of investments in the offensive line for the past two years in the draft and this past offseason in free agency have had catastrophic results.
On the flip side of the ball, the cornerback room was thin entering training camp. The position group generally experiences high rates of injury and Los Angeles entered the season with only five cornerbacks with one being a career special teams ace and another was an undrafted rookie.
Due to injuries, a practice squad cornerback had to be thrown into the fire against the Kansas City Chiefs. Injuries happen, but the glaring lack of depth in the cornerback room was evident from the start of training camp and was not addressed, that falls on the front office.
Watching the franchise quarterback take an absolute beating week in and week out behind a catastrophic injury circumstance along the offensive line only to repeat the problem the following season while hoarding excess cap space is not a good look. By all objective statistics, the offensive line for the 2026 Chargers is worse than the 2025 version.
The failures of the offense and the personnel decisions that have lead to the current offensive line situation, should put both Mike McDaniel and Joe Hortiz in the crosshairs to be potentially fired by the Chargers. The Chargers are 0-6 and the entire offense is playing terribly and something has to change. Los Angeles enters week seven on a bye, if change is coming, this is the time to do it.

title: Jim Harbaugh Post-Game Quote Spells Doom for Mike McDaniel Following Chargers Loss
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers dropped to 0-6 after losing a clunker to the Kansas City Chiefs. The battle in Kansas City was clearly the Chargers final stand of the 2026 season but their injury-ravaged and ineffective offense could not put anything together and scored only six points.
The offense has been the Chargers' Achilles heel this season. Their defense has performed well and kept games close and have provided opportunities to the offense to attempt to mount a comeback.
Franchise quarterback Justin Hebert has not looked like himself. He has been making shocking mistakes, looked unsure of footwork and saw a massive spike in turnover-worthy plays compared to his career average.
The offense has been bad. The offense has been the worst in the NFL. New offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel was the most sought-after offensive mind in the past offseason and the excitement surrounding the pairing of he and Justin Herbert permeated throughout the media all offseason. It has been an absolute failure and the clock has been ticking on McDaniel needing to find an answer.
Following the Chargers loss, head coach Jim Harbaugh was asked by a reporter at the post-game press conference if Mike McDaniel would still be calling plays going forward and for the first time, the possibility of change was firmly acknowledged when Harbaugh responded with "We're going to look at everything."
Seeing the frustration that this just isn't working is a new turn for Harbaugh. "We have to look at everything guys," Harbaugh says, "Especially offensively, we aren't scoring enough points." Regarding McDaniel still calling plays: "We're gonna look at everything." 👀 pic.twitter.com/CYgEbU75Ft
The Chargers offense isn't just bad, they look lost. Procedural penalties have plagued the players from every position group from receivers not knowing motions or linemen committing false starts. The chaos has likely lead to most of the injuries along the offensive line from simply falling over and into each other.
To put into perspective how bad the Chargers offense has been in 2026, Shawn Syed of Sumer Sports ran the numbers from the past decade and the Chargers have the sixth-worst offense on an EPA basis.
The Chargers offense has -98 Total EPA through 6 weeks That is the 6th lowest for any team through 6 weeks since 2016, per @SumerSports
To continue the conversation on offensive EPA, the Chargers, fighting for their season against the Kansas City Chiefs, gave their worst offensive performance of the season and have landed at the bottom of multiple offensive categories. Sheil Kapadia of the Ringer, posted on X to highlight how bad today's offensive performance and described it as hitting rock bottom.
Today had to be rock bottom for the Chargers (I think). Their worst offensive performance of the season, based on EPA per drive. Their offense ranks 32nd overall. It's their worst offense through 6 weeks this century.
Jim Harbaugh mentioned that the Chargers are not scoring enough points. The Chargers have currently scored the third least amount of points in the NFL, ahead of only the Miami Dolphins and the Tennessee Titans. The joining of McDaniel, Harbaugh and Herbert was once the most excited development and hire of the offseason around the NFL, it may be nearing it's end six weeks into their first season together.

title: Ranking Chargers Who Should Be Fired, Scapegoated After Falling to 0-6
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers have officially hit rock bottom after falling to 0-6 following their latest loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. What was supposed to be another competitive season under Jim Harbaugh has instead turned into an absolute nightmare.
The team has clearly struggled to generate offense , finish drives and find any consistency.
At this point, the blame cannot fall entirely on the players.
With the Chargers searching for answers, the inevitable may happen soon. Here are my rankings for the Chargers coaching staff and who is on the hot seat.
McDaniel was brought in to help maximize Justin Herbert and give the Chargers offense a more dynamic identity. He was the biggest news in the offseason for them. Instead, the unit has struggled to produce the kind of results expected from a team with a quarterback of Herbert’s ability.
Effective offenses must capitalize on opportunities created by the defense. They must minimize turnovers as well. Which the Bolts aren't doing, and it shows. If those problems were fixed even in the lightest way, they would be doing much better.
McDaniel deserves time to establish his system, particularly with injuries affecting the available personnel. However, they cannot afford to keep making excuses for an offense that consistently fails to deliver. If his play-calling and adjustments do not improve, he should be among the first assistants considered for a coaching change.
When a team starts 0-6, the head coach has to be the first person under the microscope. Harbaugh arrived with a reputation for building disciplined, physical football teams capable of competing against anybody.
Harbaugh is responsible for the overall direction of the franchise, including how his assistants prepare their units and how the team responds when adversity strikes. Six consecutive defeats demand a much bigger conversation about the coaching staff’s effectiveness.
Harbaugh does not necessarily need to be fired immediately, but he cannot be protected from criticism simply because of his previous accomplishments. If the team continues to look unprepared and undisciplined, his seat should become increasingly uncomfortable.
The offensive line deserves special attention because Herbert’s effectiveness depends heavily on the protection and blocking in front of him. Barry joined the Chargers in 2026 after coaching Miami’s offensive line, bringing experience from a unit that had previously helped produce a productive offense.
Not every protection problem falls on the position coach. Injuries, personnel limitations and individual execution also matters. Having four rookies on the starting line is definitely not ideal.  Nevertheless, Barry must find ways to improve communication, assignment discipline and overall consistency. If the offensive line remains a weakness, the entire offense will continue paying the price.
The Chargers cannot afford to waste favorable field position or make mistakes in an area that should help keep games competitive.
The team’s latest defeat was not solely a special-teams failure, and its kicking production was responsible for all six of its points. That distinction matters when evaluating accountability.
Ficken should remain under evaluation, although he is not the primary coaching concern based on the team’s overall struggles.
O’Leary returned to the Bolts as defensive coordinator, and the current losing streak raises questions about whether his unit can consistently execute the game plan. In his defense, his unit has been the only bright spot for this team.
O’Leary should be evaluated on how well his players respond during the coming weeks. If the defense continues struggling to get off the field and prevent opponents from controlling games, Harbaugh may need to consider whether a different defensive approach is necessary.
Though, O’leary is probably the coach who has the safest job so far.
Brennan is sports writer focused on delivering sharp analysis, real-time reactions, and engaging storytelling focused on NFL analysis.  He is passionate about football and breaking down what matters to bring fans closer to the action.  Brennan comes from a family of Chargers fans.

title: Chargers Offense the Walking Dead Against the Chiefs, Season Officially Slips Away
full_text:
The Los Angeles Chargers traveled to Kansas City to take on the Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium. The hostile environment is a challenging place to play, those challenges are elevated with a injury ravaged roster, a misfiring offense with four rookies on the offensive line and special teams unit consistently losing the field position battle.
The Chargers prepared to make their final stand of the 2026 season against their division rivals. They carried an 0-5 record into Kansas City and their season was barely on life support. There was hope for some reinforcements with the return of wide receivers Ladd McConkey, Quinton Johnston and the activation of  receiver Keandre Lambert-Smith.
Ladd McConkey exited the game promptly with a concussion after being tackled and unfortunately his head bounced hard off the surface as he went down. The rest of the offense struggled to find any rhythm in the first half. The drives were highlighted by short runs, batted passes and failed screens.
Quarterback Justin Herbert had another tipped pass interception that was luckily called back for roughing the passer call. Although he promptly threw another inexcusable interception a short time later. The pass went right to a defender on one of Herbert's now signature frustrated throws when nothing is working.
Los Angeles was trying to find any positive offense. They used one of the signature counters for Mike McDaniel's offense and most of the Shanahan tree when defenses start attacking and applying pressure through the B-gaps by using the screen game to keep the defense off balance and force the defenders into conflict.
The Chargers tried multiple screens from different formations and to different targets, none of them worked. The Chiefs took most of them away or were prepared to rally to make the tackle for minimal gains.
Finally, searching for anything, Justin Herbert uncorked a bomb on a scramble to Quinton Johnston that went to the one -yard line for a 57-yard reception. The explosive play was quickly nullified by a holding penalty from center Jake Slaughter on first-and-goal from the one-yard line that sent the Chargers back to the eleven and they were unable to advance.
Justin Hebert rifled a tight window throw to tight end Oronde Gadsden in the endzone and the ball went directly through his hands and the Chargers were forced to kick a field goal. Nothing working is the title of the Chargers offensive results. The quick passing game consistently was batted down, receivers weren't open or passes fell off receivers fingertips.
The Chargers finally had some mild success and in the fourth quarter, they found themselves with a chance following multiple defensive stops punctuated by a missed Harrison Butker field that gave the Chargers the ball with positive field position. Facing a third and one, Herbert threw a quick pass to Keandre Lambert-Smith who picked up the first down but fumbled the ball and it was recovered by Chiefs linebacker Drue Tranquill.
The Chargers can't get out of their own way. They have been consistent at doing the little football things wrong. Ball security, penalties and situational football have all been lacking with the overall exception of the defense. Their shortcomings have kept them from playing winning football.
The offense is the worst in the NFL and they are now 0-6 heading into their bye week. The organization has several massive decisions to make now that the Chargers' final stand to find hope for 2026 has failed.

title: Chargers' Ladd McConkey Suffers New Injury vs. Chiefs, Quickly Ruled Out
full_text:
A tough go for Los Angeles Chargers wide receiver Ladd McConkey continued during Sunday's game against the Kansas City Chiefs.
In the first half with the Chargers losing 9-3 to the Chiefs, McConkey suffered a concussion, with the team quickly declaring him out for the game.
Before his exit, McConkey caught his lone target for 17 yards from Justin Herbert. At the time, he was one of just four Chargers targets with a single reception while Herbert had a 4-of-9 line with an interception in a game that threatened to drop Los Angeles to 0-6 on the season.
The Chargers have a bye week after the game in Kansas City so, generally speaking, McConkey should be on track to return for Week 8 against the Los Angeles Rams on November 1 if all goes well.
That said, McConkey was a question mark to even play on Sunday against the Chiefs. He’s battled a variety of different injuries this season and, prior to Sunday, had only played in four games while taking just 54 percent of the offense’s snaps.
McConkey tried to gut through this game on the road, but the Chargers star now has a new injury to come back from while Herbert’s offense attempts to get moving with wideouts Quentin Johnston and rookie Brenen Thompson.
This story will be updated with more information as it becomes available.

title: How the Rams Can Replace Davante Adams, Kobie Turner, and Poona Ford
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams got some unfortunate injury news on Monday. Head coach Sean McVay told the media that the Rams will be without wide receiver Davante Adams, defensive lineman Kobie Turner, and defensive lineman Poona Ford for an extended period or the entire season.
You feel terrible for these guys because they put in so much work to try to be able to bring some stuff to life. Those guys are key contributors for us," said head coach Sean McVay. "The next thing is make sure that we figure out what's the best way for our team to be able to move forward in the absence of some critical factors for us. That's part of it. That’s an unfortunate part of this game. We’ve taken some shots this year and we have to be able to get up and keep swinging. This is a good test."
When it comes to the NFL, it’s a next-man-up mentality. The Rams will need their depth to step up in a big way if they are going to come back from a 2-4 start. Let’s take a look at the players the Rams will be relying on.
Out of the injuries that the Rams suffered on Sunday, the loss of Davante Adams may hit the hardest . Stafford and Adams were clicking this season. Adams had back-to-back 100-yard games when Nacua was out of the lineup. He also already had six touchdowns through four weeks. Coming into the season, there were questions around the Rams’ WR3 situation. Now they don’t have a legitimate WR2 for the next 6-10 weeks.
“It's significant when you don't have a player like Davante, but we have to be able to adjust," said McVay. "His contributions can't be measured. You don't replace somebody like him so what you do is you have to be able to figure out, what's the next right thing? What does that look like in terms of our vision?"
The clear answer as to who steps up in place of Adams is Konata Mumpfield. Mumpfield isn’t a true ‘X’ receiver, but he is someone that the Rams have used frequently as the lone wide receiver in 13 personnel. The Rams seem to like what Mumpfield can do, but he still remains inefficient. Mumpfield has caught just eight of 17 targets this season. After playing just six snaps in Week 5, he was back up to 27 against the Cardinals. The Rams may rely on Mumpfield more with Adams out.
It will be interesting to see if CJ Daniels finally gets an opportunity. Daniels’ name came up a lot during training camp. During the preseason, Daniels had 15 receptions, which was tied for the most in the NFL. Daniels lined up out wide on 72.9 percent of his snaps during the preseason and would be a seamless fit in that spot. It’s unfair to ask Daniels to replace Adams and his productio n, but he could slide into that role. Adams spoke highly of Daniels this summer.
“I'm proud of him,” said Adams. “He came to me and asked what I thought he needed to work on. We talked about a couple of small things. I saw a lot of good stuff from him during the offseason program and he came back and did exactly those things.”
It’s been a surprise that Daniels hasn’t been active in six games, but this could be his opportunity. Daniels obviously isn’t the next Puka Nacua, but the Rams have been able to get a lot out of rookie wide receivers in the past. They may need that from Daniels.
The Rams could try and trade for someone. However, at 2-4, it feels unlikely. They don’t have a lot of cap space and, right now, they need to keep their already limited draft capital. If the Rams do make a trade, Josh Downs and Jauan Jennings make a lot of sense. It’s possible the Rams could look into Brian Thomas Jr., but his price is likely too high.
Kobie Turner is going to be a huge loss on the Rams’ defense . In four years, he’s grown to be the heart and soul of that defensive line. Turner may only have 13 pressures this season, but he was having an impact as a run defender as well. He had a nine percent run stop rate with 10 run stops, according to Pro Football Focus. The Rams will hope to get Turner back soon from his groin injury, but he’ll be missed.
The obvious replacement for Turner is Ty Hamilton. However, this is a huge drop-off. The Rams traded up for Hamilton last year, giving up a future fourth-round pick. In six games this year, he has an overall defensive grade below 50 via PFF.In three of those games, he recorded a grade below 40. Hamilton doesn’t have a single pressure this year in 24 pass-rush snaps. He’s supposed to be good against the run, but only has one run stop. The Rams are going to need Hamilton to step up. It will likely be a rotation here, but Hamilton will be the primary player in that spot.
Fiske has been rotating with Aaron Donald throughout much of the season, but without Turner, he could see more playing time. The issue with Fiske is that he isn’t as effective against the run due to his size. Still, he does have an 11.8 percent run stop rate, which ranks eighth in the NFL. He also leads the Rams with 16 pressures this season. In three years, Fiske has been labeled as a “JAG”, and this will be an opportunity for him to show that he is more than that.
Ford hasn’t been as good as he was last year, but he’s still an important piece of the defensive line. The Rams added Ford after 2024 to be a space eater in the middle of the defensive line and help stop the run . He played an important role in making the Rams one of the best run-stopping defenses last year. Not having him in the middle of the defensive line for the rest of the season will be felt.
Tyler Davis played very well last season. While technically listed as Kobie Turner’s backup, he can play at nose tackle. The Rams have mostly used him on early downs next to Ford or alongside Turner on either side of the center. It wouldn’t be surprising, though, to see Davis used in place of Ford because of his size.
With Ford out, the Rams will likely elevate Bill Norton from the practice squad. Norton is a player the Rams have been developing, but he has struggled in the preseason. He had just a 49.3 run defense grade via PFF last year. Norton has size and could be brought up to add some depth.

title: Rams Dealt Devastating Injury News on Davante Adams, Kobie Turner, Poona Ford
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams received a series of bad injury updates on Monday afternoon. According to Sean McVay, wide receiver Davante Adams will be out for six to 10 weeks, while defensive lineman Kobie Turner will miss several weeks as he heads to injured reserve. Poona Ford will also be out for the season.
Adams left Sunday’s game against the Cardinals in the final minute, seemingly pulling up at the end of the play. A non-contact injury is rarely good and McVay said on Monday that Adams had ruptured his hamstring.Adams will be out for a minimum of six weeks and could miss up to 10. Depending on where the Rams are at, they could opt to shut him down for the year.
Non-contact injury for #Rams WR Davante Adams. Came out of the game pic.twitter.com/wSh2CYsLuD
Last season, Adams suffered a strained hamstring that forced him to miss the final three games. Given Adams’ age, re-injuring his hamstring was always a risk. With Adams out for the next two months, the Rams are extremely thin at the wide receiver position. Puka Nacua is the only legitimate option, especially until Terrance Ferguson returns. The Rams drafted CJ Daniels in the sixth round, but he’s been inactive in every game to start the year.
The Rams took a significant hit to their defensive line with Monday’s news. Turner played a career-low 23 snaps, and the injury explains why. Turner injured his groin and is expected to go on injured reserve, but could return later this season.
Ford is another big loss for the Rams’ defense. Over the last two seasons, Ford has played a large role in stopping the run as the starting nose tackle. Ford hadn’t played as well this year but was arguably one of the most important players on the Rams’ defense in 2025.
While the Rams have depth on the defensive line, the injuries to Turner and Ford will call for those players to step into roles that they may not be ready for. The Rams have been developing Tyler Davis and Ty Hamilton over the last two years. However, Hamilton has struggled again in year two and Davis has been better in a rotation.
The slew of injuries is reminiscent of the 2022 season, when the Rams were decimated by injuries on their way to a 5-12 record. In 2022, the Rams lost Cooper Kupp, Matthew Stafford, Aaron Donald, and nearly the entire offensive line.
With Adams, the Rams lose a player who has been a threat in the red zone. Adams and Stafford seemed to have a much stronger connection than they had at times last year. Turner has been a staple on the defensive line and Ford will also be missed. That’s three starters who played significant roles that the Rams won’t have available as they try to recover from a 2-4 start. That also doesn’t mention the Rams placing Blake Grupe on injured reserve .
Tucked away in all of this is the fact that Myles Garrett still hasn't been cleared to practice. Garrett was held out for much of training camp before being placed on injured reserve after Week 1. It was reported last week that Garrett could practice as soon as this week . While Garrett was initially given a six-week recovery timeline, that was always viewed as a worst-case scenario.
At 2-4, the Rams were already facing an uphill battle to turn their season around. With several key players now unavailable, that challenge has only gotten more difficult.

title: 5 Kickers the Rams Could Sign After Placing Blake Grupe on Injured Reserve
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams will be searching for another kicker this week after placing Blake Grupe on injured reserve Monday. After cutting Harrison Mevis last week, the Rams signed Grupe as his replacement. Grupe made a 44-yard field goal on Sunday, but on the ensuing kickoff, he got injured trying to tackle returner Devin Duvernay.
Placing Grupe on injured reserve is a continuation of the special teams drama that the Rams have endured this season. Just when they thought they may have resovled the issue, they have to find another solution.
LA Rams Transactions: • Reserve/Injured K Blake Grupe pic.twitter.com/eiyLAZ82GF
Without Grupe, the Rams turned to Ethan Evans to kick extra points. Evans made his lone extra point in the fourth quarter to briefly give the Rams the lead. Now that Grupe is on injured reserve, the Rams are right back where they started last week. Here are five options the Rams could turn to.
Brown remains one of my favorite options to come in and at least try out for the Rams’ kicker spot. The Rams signed Brown as an undrafted free agent in 2023, but he was cut before the start of the regular season. Brown went 25-for-28 last year in the UFL and was 7-for-9 from 50+. He made field goals from 60 and 63 yards in the playoffs last season.
ANOTHER 4-POINTER 🤯‼️ Tanner Brown is good from 63-yards 🔥 @DynastyFP 4-Point Field Goal pic.twitter.com/Jqp63Ed7Ks
McManus is a veteran kicker and wasn’t brought back by the Green Bay Packers in the offseason. McManus was 24-for-30 last season with a long of 56. He was also 32-for-33 on extra points. All six of McManus’ misses were from beyond 40 yards, and he was just 3-for-7 in the 40- to 49-yard range. It’s not ideal, but it’s an option.
Not many will want the Rams to bring back Joshua Karty after last season. At one point, Karty showed plenty of talent. Karty finished his rookie year strong before his struggles in 2025. It would be hard to trust Bubba Ventrone to get that out of him again, but he may be worth a look. Karty was let go last season before the Rams made changes to their field goal operation as a whole.
Gano is another veteran kicker at 39 years old. He kicked for the New York Giants last year and went 9-for-10 on field goals in five games, with a long of 55 yards. He was also 9-for-9 on extra points. A veteran like Gano may bring some stability to the position.
At this point, the Rams are running out of proven options. Sauls was signed as an undrafted free agent by the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2025 and has since bounced around with the Atlanta Falcons and New York Giants. Sauls is a left-footed kicker and went 8-for-8 in three games with the Giants last season.

title: Rams Report Card Reveals Major Offensive Failures in Loss to Cardinals
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams lost another one-score game this season , falling 18-16 to the Arizona Cardinals. It’s the type of loss that shouldn’t happen to a Sean McVay-led team. The Rams didn’t get a good performance from Matthew Stafford, and Sean McVay didn’t coach a clean game. While the defense kept the Rams in it, they also allowed six scoring drives. Let’s grade each position group’s performance.
The Rams can’t keep having Matthew Stafford not show up until the fourth quarter. Through the first three quarters on Sunday, Stafford was 12-for-19 for 96 yards. While Stafford picked it up in the fourth quarter and gave the Rams the lead at the end, it’s just not sustainable. The Rams need Stafford for 60 minutes. In two of the last three games, the Rams have gotten the version of Stafford that they need for less than 15.
Sean McVay could have done a better job getting the running backs more involved in the offense. Sunday’s game should have been one where Corum and Williams combined for over 30 carries. Instead, they had 19 carries for 92 yards. Both averaged over 4.5 yards per carry in the game. Corum seemed to pick up where he left off last year against the Cardinals, forcing three missed tackles. He even got involved in the passing game, scoring on a screen.
When the wide receivers got involved, they were good. Stafford simply didn’t give them enough opportunities.Puka Nacua had three targets in the first three quarters and then matched that on the final drive alone when the offense finally came to life. Konata Mumpfield was efficient with two catches and Nacua had six receptions on seven targets and should have had a touchdown if Stafford hits him wide open in the third quarter.
For an offense that is supposed to feature the tight ends, that position group hasn’t shown that it is good enough for that to be the case. Davis Allen was featured on a fullback dive on 4th-and-1 that came up short. Additionally, Tyler Higbee fumbled with the Rams nearing the red zone. It’s his second fumble this  year. Colby Parkinson scored the go-ahead touchdown late, but it can be argued that it hurt the Rams in that situation and that he would have been better off going down.
For the most part, the offensive line played well. The Cardinals certainly took advantage of Alaric Jackson’s absence by blitzing more, but David Quessenberry wasn't the reason the Rams lost. He only gave up two pressures. Where the Rams have struggled is on the interior, which is supposed to be their strength. Still, Warren McClendon had an untimely penalty that pushed the Rams back five yards on 4th-and-3.
Aaron Donald made a few splash plays against the Cardinals and Byron Young was dominant in the first half. However, no player had more than three pressures and they struggled against the run. One can certainly hope that the return of Myles Garrett provides a boost here, but this group overall needs to be better.
Nate Landman missed two tackles and both he and Omar Speights allowed three receptions on three targets. Landman was exploited in coverage a few times. The Rams need better linebacker play.
Josh Wallace continues to play very well when given opportunities. He was targeted eight times against the Cardinals and allowed just four catches. His big penalty at the end can certainly be argued. Quentin Lake had the interception on the first drive as well. That’s where the positives end, though. Kam Kinchens missed two tackles along with Kam Curl. The inability to tackle at the second and third levels is a big reason why the Cardinals were able to run the ball as successfully as they did.
Sunday didn’t come without its special teams errors. On the Rams’ first kickoff of the game, the coverage unit once again didn’t execute well, allowing a big return that led to Blake Grupe getting injured. Jordan Whittington also had a chance to down a punt inside the five and missed it. Due to the lack o confidence in the coverage unit, the Rams opted to kick the ball into the end zone in the fourth quarter, setting up the Cardinals at the 35-yard line. However, Ethan Evans gets some props for making the extra point that gave the Rams the lead.
McVay was severely out-coached in this one by Mike LaFleur and Nick Rallis. The fullback dive playcall on 4th-and-1 isn’t acceptable given the other options on offense. McVay and Stafford are two of the biggest problems right now. That doesn’t mean either needs to be benched or fired, but the Rams need better from both of them. The good news is that both are part of the solution.

title: Rams 10 Takeaways: Identity Crisis Deepens After Inexcusable Loss to Cardinals
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams lost to the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, 18-16, to fall to 2-4. It’s only been six weeks, but the Rams are already facing an identity crisis . A month and a half into the season, the Rams still don’t know who they are as a team, and that’s evident in the inconsistency of their results.
“We won't win a game unless we figure out how not to beat ourselves,” said head coach Sean McVay. “So many unforced errors, so many things that are not in alignment with what we want to do, specifically on the offensive side of the ball.”
This isn’t where the Rams had planned to be at the beginning of the season, but it is their current reality. Let’s jump into this week’s 10 takeaways.
For a moment, it appeared as if the Rams had solved their kicking issues. Blake Grupe made his first field goal from 44 yards out and it was right down the middle.On the ensuing kickoff, the Rams’ coverage unit allowed Devin Duvernay to break through, and Grupe went in for the tackle, only to injure his knee. The Rams may need to bring in a Witch or Catholic priest to solve the special teams issues at this point, because they are cursed. McVay didn’t have an update on Grupe after the game, but noted the knee injury.
Rams New Kicker Blake Grupe Tried To Tackle Somebody On The Kickoff And Ended Up Injuring Himself. The Rams Just Signed This Guy After Cutting Harrison Mevis. Rough Start. 😬 pic.twitter.com/0BDZRD1hzh
This isn’t to say that the Rams need to bench Matthew Stafford. We aren’t at that point yet. However, he does need to be better . Stafford had a -0.14 EPA per pass against the Cardinals. That was worse than Daniel Jones and Tyler Shough in Week 6. It was only slightly better than Cam Ward. In the first three quarters of games this season, Stafford’s 0.07 adjusted EPA per play ranks 17th. However, in the fourth quarter, he ranks seventh at 0.32. Stafford is part of the solution to get the Rams’ offense out of this rut. With that said, right now, he’s also part of the problem.
It’s fair to have an issue with both fourth down play calls. With that said, there was at least some logic with the screen on 4th-and-8. A good way to beat a blitz is with a screen. The more inexcusable call was the fullback dive to Davis Allen. Allen had never taken a handoff in his four-year NFL career or in college. When options such as Kyren Williams and Puka Nacua exist in the offense, going with a hand-off to Allen is confusing to say the least.
A big reason the Cardinals were able to dictate the tempo of the game was their success running the ball. The Rams didn’t stop the run consistently throughout the game as the defensive backs got run through. Chris Shula likes to operate out of dime, but those lighter packages aren’t working. Poona Ford isn’t as dominant in the middle as he was last year, and the Rams are getting washed away at the second and third levels. If there’s an adjustment to be made on defense, this is it.
Aside from special teams, Chris Shula and the defense continue to be the scapegoats for the Rams’ struggles. However, at some point, the offense has to do its part. Had it not been for Shula’s defense, this game wouldn’t have been close. They held the Cardinals to 0-for-5 in the red zone and got stops in the fourth quarter to give the offense a chance. It’s true the Cardinals were able to play ball control as they held the ball for almost 35 minutes. At the same time, if the Rams had scored points against a defense ranked No. 29 in EPA per play and forced the Cardinals to play from behind, Arizona wouldn't have been able to rely on that approach.
The Rams continue to have crucial mistakes in big moments. Facing a 4th-and-3, Warren McClendon jumped to make it a 4th-and-8. With the Rams in the red zone, Matthew Stafford stumbled for a loss of 11 before Tyler Higbee fumbled on the next play. The Rams continue to out-gain opponents, but haven’t been able to turn the yards into points consistently.
“We've had some really critical errors at really unfortunate times,” said McVay. “That's what our narrative has been for this year. We can't keep saying, ‘Oh, that we haven't done that before.’ Well, this year we are doing it.”
The Rams have out-gained their opponents by a league-best 644 yards this season. They are 2-4.
For most of the game, Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis had McVay and Stafford in a blender. The Rams’ offense made Rallis look like Vic Fangio coaching the 2018 Chicago Bears. There was certainly an element of execution, but McVay was out-coached by Rallis and Mike LaFleur. McVay gave the Cardinals a chance late because he didn’t drain the clock. There were too many questionable playcalls. If you had said before the game that the Cardinals wouldn’t score a touchdown, nobody would have thought the Rams would lose.
“There were other instances that we could have made them pay. We just didn't execute, simple as that,” McVay said. “Had an idea of what they were doing. We have to be able to execute in some of those instances and that wasn't the case today.”
Both McVay and Stafford were asked what the identity of this team was after six weeks. “We're figuring it out. I can't answer that right now,” McVay answered. Stafford added, “We are what our record is. We have to try to find a way to be better.”
The Rams don’t have an offensive identity that they can lean on. Culturally, they are also lacking an identity as they seemingly implode after yet another close loss. The frustration is starting to set in and that’s starting to make its way around the locker room.
It’s hard to say that this isn’t rock bottom for the Rams . That was one of the worst losses of the McVay era. It’s right up there with losing to the 0-13 New York Jets in 2020. Beating the Cardinals under McVay has been about as much of a ‘sure thing’ as it gets. This Cardinals team had essentially waved the white flag, and the Rams gave them life. Instead of sitting at 3-3 and second place in the NFC West, they are 2-4 and in last place. While 2022 was bad, the expectations of this season might make it worse.
During his post-game press conference, Sean McVay used the phrase “I’m not really sure” twice and “I can’t answer that right now” one other time. The Rams don’t have answers for how to get out of this. In 2021, Raheem Morris helped McVay recover from “No Win November.” During the 2023 season when the Rams were 3-6, it was Cooper Kupp. There is still an opportunity for the Rams to climb out of this, but there isn’t much reason to be confident that they can.

title: Monday Morning Rambling: The Rams Have Hit Rock Bottom and Have No Answers
full_text:
In 2000, the cartoon SpongeBob SquarePants aired an episode titled “Rock Bottom” in which SpongeBob and Patrick board the wrong bus and end up in an unfamiliar place called Rock Bottom. While Patrick escapes, Spongebob is left stranded. Every time he tries to escape, something goes wrong.
He misses bus after bus, and eventually finds himself stuck in complete darkness with seemingly no way home after the last bus leaves. That’s where the Los Angeles Rams are right now after losing to the Arizona Cardinals. They’re in Rock Bottom with no clear way out. Every time there’s been a bus ready to take them out, something has gone wrong.
A new SpongeBob episode, “Rock Bottom,” receives the highest ratings the show has yet seen. pic.twitter.com/zNsauFVKak
Heading into the season, the Rams were seen as Super Bowl favorites. However, it’s as if they missed that bus, and every time there’s been a chance to get back on and head in the right direction, something has gone wrong.
When the Rams had a chance to prove themselves as contenders against the Bills, a blocked game-winning field goal sent them to 2-3. With an opportunity to start a winning streak before their bye, the Rams put out their biggest disappointment yet, losing 18-16 to the Cardinals.
The Cardinals were supposed to be a ‘get-right’ game. It was meant to be their way out and a game that finally got the Rams headed in the right direction as they were set to face the NFL’s easiest schedule over the next five weeks. Instead, the Rams are facing an identity crisis with no clear solution. Even head coach Sean McVay seems lost and without answers.
“I'm not really sure,” said McVay after the game. “We've got to be able to figure it out and I don't have those answers right now. Otherwise, it would have gotten fixed.... We've had some really critical errors at really unfortunate times. That's what our narrative has been for this year.”
Through six weeks, the Rams sit at 2-4, and even McVay seems unsure how to turn things around. When asked why the energy on offense was so low, running back Kyren Williams said, “Can’t tell you, bro. Probably because I’m not out there.”
This is a Rams team on the verge of implosion and turning on each other. A team can only lose in heartbreaking fashion so many times, especially when it’s one unit continuously coming up short. Guys can only be told to move on to the next one so many times. Over the last two years, the Rams have continuously found ways to lose, and last week's game against the Bills appeared to be a breaking point.
Last week, McVay talked about finding a way to not let the Bills beat them twice. However, that’s exactly what happened. The Rams came out flat and by the time they showed up, it was too late.
It’s long overdue, but the Rams need to look at themselves in the mirror and figure out exactly what they want to be. Right now, they are a team without an identity. We’re in Week 6 and the Rams still don’t know what they are.
“We're figuring it out. I can't answer that right now,” said McVay.
For the first time since the 2022 season, McVay seems lost and unsure where to turn. He’s been unable to find answers to fix the special teams unit that’s plagued his team for the last two years. Now, he doesn’t have the answers to what the identity of his own team is. That’s a much larger issue.
The Rams are 2-4 and in last place in the NFC West. They are in the exact opposite spot that many, including themselves, expected them to be at this point in the season. However, it is their current reality. They missed the bus labeled “super bowl contenders” and have entered uncharted waters.
In 2021, during the infamous “no-win November,” it was defensive coordinator Raheem Morris who stepped up to provide a crucial reality check. When the Rams were 3-6 at the bye in 2023, it was Cooper Kupp who challenged McVay and had the uncomfortable conversations.
At 2-4, McVay almost seems lost. This isn’t a team that has just lost its identity schematically. It has also lost its identity as a culture. For 10 years, McVay has preached a “we not me” or “we then me” mentality.
The Cardinals’ blitz rate increased from 24.4 percent to 36.1 percent on Sunday, in large part because Rams starting left tackle Alaric Jackson was serving a suspension. Following the game, Williams subtly questioned his role and threw Blake Corum under the bus.
For a team that has 11 captains, the Rams seemingly lack leadership. Is there a coach on the staff or a player who will challenge McVay as a leader to get the team out of this rut?
To get out of Rock Bottom, Spongebob finally encounters an unlikely stranger that helps him escape by using a balloon to float back to Bikini Bottom. The Rams need to find their own balloon. However, until someone steps up, the Rams are going to struggle to find their way out.
This isn’t to say that the Rams need to bench Stafford, but they need more from him. Right now, Stafford ranks 17th with 0.07 adjusted EPA per play. In the fourth quarter, he ranks seventh with 0.32 adjusted EPA per play. The Rams need Stafford to play at a high level for 60 minutes. Right now, they're barely getting that for 15.
Following Sunday’s loss to the Cardinals, many have been asking for McVay to give up play-calling, but I’m not sure that solves anything. McVay has a special connection to play-calling and he’s only given it up once when he lost all hope in 2022. Many of the NFL's best coaches, including Mike Macdonald, Kyle Shanahan, and Ben Johnson, call their own plays. Sean Payton gave up play-calling this season to Davis Webb and that lasted four weeks. It doesn’t make sense to take away play-calling from someone who is widely considered a top-3 play-caller.
Slow starts aren’t new for the Rams over the last few years. They started 3-6 in 2023 and 1-4 in 2024. They’ve had a winning record after six games just once since winning the Super Bowl in 2021.I don’t have any doubt that the Rams can turn this around. It’s very possible they still make the playoffs. However, this team had bigger goals this year and that part is worth doubting. It’s highly unlikely that the Rams win the NFC West and if they don’t go on a run, making the playoffs will be a long shot as well.
Slow starts are nothing new for McVay's Rams, who have had a winning record after 6 games just once in the 5 seasons since they won the Super Bowl. They've gone 3-3, 3-3, 2-4, 4-2 and now 2-4 again. The Rams started a combined 22-8 through 6 games in McVay's first 5 seasons.
There were several moments when the Rams could have taken control and escaped with a win. It wouldn’t have solved their problems, but it would have still been a gutsy win against a feisty division opponent. In the third quarter, Matthew Stafford had an opportunity to hit an open Puka Nacua that would have likely resulted in a touchdown. Instead, Stafford overthrew Nacua and the Rams turned the ball over on downs as McVay called a fullback dive to Davis Allen .
STAFFORD TO NACUA 😭🔥😭🔥 pic.twitter.com/ulU36opjWQ
Throughout the McVay era, beating the Cardinals was about as ‘sure’ as it gets. That should have been the case on Sunday. Instead, a Cardinals team without Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jeremiyah Love managed to beat the Rams. A Cardinals defense that ranked 32nd in points allowed and 29th in EPA per play heading into Week 6 held a McVay-led offense to fewer than 20 points. This may not be the worst loss under McVay, but it’s certainly up there.
It’s true that the schedule has gotten easier for the Rams, but nothing is guaranteed with this team. Beating the Raiders next Sunday is no guarantee. The Raiders have lost three straight games, but two of those losses came by just three points. There is a very real chance that the Rams drop to 2-5 for the first time under McVay.

title: Rams Winners and Losers: Sean McVay, Matthew Stafford Among Biggest Disappointments
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams lost to the Arizona Cardinals in Week 6, 18-16. It was arguably one of the most disappointing losses of the Sean McVay era . The Rams had a chance to start a winning streak, but instead found themselves in last place in the NFC West. Let’s take a look at this week’s winners and losers.
It’s more than fair to say that Matthew Stafford hasn’t played well this season. Stafford didn’t hit 100 yards passing until the fourth quarter. Early in the third quarter, he overthrew Puka Nacua on what would have likely been a touchdown. Some regression from Stafford was expected, but not many expected this much.
Whenever the Rams’ coaching staff and front office talk about Kyren Williams, it’s always how he is the epitome of what it means to be a ‘Ram’. Following Sunday’s game, Williams was asked why the offense lacks energy and responded, “Probably because I’m not out there.” It’s a dig at his role in the offense and at Blake Corum as a player. For a team that’s supposed to embody a “we not me” mindset, that wasn’t it.
Kyren Williams when asked why he thought the Rams couldn't sustain the energy drive to drive, via @sarahbarshop : "Can’t tell you, bro. Probably because I’m not out there." pic.twitter.com/vcUKP054mT
On the first possession, Lake intercepted Jacoby Brissett. It was Lake’s second interception of the season and should have set the tone for the game. IInstead, the offense had to settle for a field goal and wasn’t able to build off of that momentum.
It feels like McVay has been in the “losers” section of this list too often this season. McVay was a big reason for the loss last week after he got conservative. The Rams’ head coach was also responsible for the team’s travel plans to Australia. On Sunday, McVay called a fullback dive on 4th-and-1 to Davis Allen. McVay is one of the biggest issues on the Rams right now.
For a moment, it looked as if the Rams had solved their kicking woes. Blake Grupe made a 44-yard field goal right through the middle to give the Rams a 3-0 lead. On the ensuing kickoff, Grupe got hurt trying to make a tackle. The injury will likely put Grupe on injured reserve, and the Rams will be right back where they were last week, looking for a kicker.
One of the few bright spots on defense was edge rusher Byron Young. Young was credited with five impact plays via Sumer Sports and an 11.1 percent pressure rate. In the first half alone, Young had three pressures. When Myles Garrett returns, it should open things up for Young even more.
For the most part, Josh Wallace played well. However, he once again was on the wrong end of a controversial call at the end of the game . Wallace got called for unnecessary roughness, adding 15 yards to a 21-yard reception. The penalty essentially put the Cardinals in field goal range on one play.
What must be going through Aaron Donald’s head right now? Donald thought he was joining a Rams team that would be competing for a Super Bowl. Instead, they are 2-4 and find themselves in the middle of an identity crisis. He came out of retirement for this? The Rams were 3-6 in 2023 before turning things around and making the playoffs in what was Donald’s final season. Maybe they’ll turn it around once Garrett returns. However, right now, it doesn’t look great.

title: Sean McVay's Questionable Fourth-Down Play Call Haunts Rams in Loss to Cardinals
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams lost on Sunday to the 1-4 Arizona Cardinals , 18-16. Once again, it was head coach Sean McVay who played a large role in the team’s loss. The McVay-led Rams offense scored only 16 points against a Cardinals defense that entered Week 6 ranked No. 32 in scoring defense and No. 29 in EPA per play.
It was a perplexing performance as McVay was outcoached by Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis for much of the game. The offense didn’t start finding a rhythm until the fourth quarter and didn’t score a second touchdown until 47 seconds remained in the game.
Following a long Cardinals scoring drive in the second half, the Rams faced fourth-and-1 needing points. Going for it was the right decision from McVay, and it’s no surprise that decision was made.
However, the play call didn’t make sense. Williams has been good in short-yardage situations in the past. Additionally, the Rams have gone to Puka Nacua in those situations before on a jet sweep. McVay did neither of those things. Needing one yard, McVay called a fullback dive to the tight end Davis Allen. Allen was stopped short and the Rams turned the ball over on downs.
Cardinals defense comes up with the stop on 4th and 1! AZvsLAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/kieCYIdECf
Back in Week 1, the Rams faced a 4th-and-1 at the goal line and came up short on a quarterback sneak.Later that week, I argued here that McVay should implement a tush-push-style package with a tight end. Running with a tight end in that situation isn’t a bad idea. A fullback dive, however, is confusing.
Allen had never taken a handoff in his four-year NFL career. Additionally, he didn’t have a single rushing attempt in four years at Clemson. Running with Allen in that spot with other options available didn’t make sense. The Rams have Williams, Nacua, and Stafford and McVay opted to run with his tight end.
The play wasn’t blocked well as Colby Parkinson dove inside, leaving Mack Wilson available to tackle Allen. Still, a dive play to the Rams’ TE4 isn’t the play call that McVay should be going with in that situation.
Later in the game, the Rams went for it on fourth down again. After 4th-and-3 turned into 4th-and-8 because of a penalty, McVay called a screen to Williams that fell incomplete. Williams may have had space to get the first down, but the Cardinals sniffed out the screen.
Pass is incomplete and the Cardinals force a turnover on downs 👀 AZvsLAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/u0bfxJgdFJ
It wasn’t a good day for the offense as they went 4-for-12 on conversion downs. The offense was held to 16 points against a Cardinals defense that hasn’t played well this season.
McVay has played a role in each of the Rams’ losses this season, and it’s hard to say that he wasn’t outcoached again on Sunday. The fourth-down play call to Allen was a clear example of that.

title: Rams on Wrong End of Another Controversial Call in Week 6 Loss to Cardinals
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams were once again on the wrong end of a controversial call at the end of their Week 6 loss to the Arizona Cardinals . After the Rams took the lead, the Cardinals took over at their own 35-yard line with 47 seconds left, needing a field goal to win.
Quarterback Jacoby Brissett completed a pass over the middle to wide receiver Jalen Brooks, who was hit by Josh Wallace. Brooks’ head made slight contact with Wallace’s shoulder. What would have been a 21-yard gain that left the Cardinals outside of field goal range instead put them well within Chad Ryland’s range.
On the broadcast, color analyst Greg Olsen asked rules analyst Mike Pereira what he thought of the call. “It didn't look to me like there was forcible contact at all, was there?” asked Olsen. “My first thought was, this is one that replay could take off if there was no contact,” Pereira responded. “There is contact, but is it enough contact? To me, that's one that does not need to be called.”
UNREAL PERSONAL FOUL WHAT DO YOU WANT HIM TO DO??? pic.twitter.com/L4XLXmZw0W
It was the second time this season that Wallace has been on the wrong end of a controversial call. Back in Week 3, Wallace was called for defensive pass interference on a play in which he intercepted Bo Nix in the fourth quarter.
According to Rule 12, Section 2, Article 9 of the NFL rulebook, there is unnecessary roughness if a player initiates unnecessary contact against a player who is in a defenseless position. Prohibited contact against a player who is in a defenseless position includes lowering the head and making forcible contact with any part of the helmet against any part of the defenseless player’s body.
The NFL rulebook also states in Rule 7, Section 2 that if a defender has already committed himself and the contact is unavoidable, it is not a foul unless the defender makes forcible contact into the head or neck area of the runner with the helmet, shoulder, or forearm, or commits some other act that is unnecessary roughness.
Put skirts on em Jimmy pic.twitter.com/uV2PqhMvub
With this penalty in particular, the gray area comes into play with the “forcible contact” terminology.It’s hard to say that Wallace’s contact was forcible, as it looked to be more incidental. There’s not much more that Wallace could have done in that situation to avoid the contact.
While this call didn’t necessarily give the Cardinals the win, it certainly put them in a position to win the game.  It’s also worth noting that the Rams were also offside on the play. However, without the unnecessary roughness penalty, the Cardinals would have had the ball at the Rams’ 44-yard line with 41 seconds left. That’s still a 62-yard field goal. It would have forced the Cardinals to be more aggressive than they were on their final three plays.
The Rams had only two penalties entering the fourth quarter but committed three more in the final period, including the unnecessary roughness penalty. Timely penalties and mistakes have cost the Rams throughout the year, and this is just another example.

title: Rams Hit Rock Bottom in Stunning Loss to Cardinals as Season Spirals
full_text:
The Los Angeles Rams have officially hit rock bottom six weeks into the 2026 season. Entering Week 6, the Rams needed a win to get back to .500. With the 1-4 Arizona Cardinals on the schedule, it seemed to be a ‘sure thing’. Instead, without allowing a touchdown, the Rams lost, 18-16.
For much of the afternoon, the Rams looked uninspired and lacked any sort of energy. While they took the lead with 47 seconds left, the Cardinals kicked a game-winning field goal, their sixth of the day, to win as time expired.
There’s no doubt that the Rams have been inconsistent to start the season. They lacked energy in Week 1 against the San Francisco 49ers and couldn’t finish against the Denver Broncos. The Rams were lucky to get out of Philadelphia with a win, scoring 10 points in the final seven minutes. It was special teams that cost them against the Buffalo Bills last week.
Head coach Sean McVay spoke last week about not letting the Bills beat them twice. However, the Rams’ offense made a Cardinals defense that ranked 29th in EPA per play coming in look like a Vic Fangio-led Bears unit in 2018.
The Rams’ first three possessions picked up 23 yards and just one first down. Matthew Stafford didn’t surpass 100 yards passing until the fourth quarter. While the defense allowed the Cardinals to play ball control, they also kept the Rams in the game. On the first drive, Quentin Lake intercepted Jacoby Brissett. The Rams held the Cardinals to 0-for-5 in the red zone and 5-for-15 on third down. However, the Cardinals held the ball for 34:52 and their opening drive of the second half lasted 8:35.
With the score tied 9-9 at halftime, fans at SoFi Stadium could be heard booing the Rams as they walked off the field. Nobody could blame them after what they just watched. For a team that was supposed to be a Super Bowl contender, the Rams haven’t played up to those expectations more often than not. The expectation continues to be that the Rams will eventually flip a switch, but that switch hasn’t been flipped and they’re running out of time.
Following last week’s loss to the Buffalo Bills, the Rams made a change at kicker, signing Blake Grupe. The early returns on Grupe looked promising as he hit a 44-yard field goal to give the Rams the lead in the first quarter. On the ensuing kickoff, the kickoff coverage unit let Devin Duvernay through and Grupe was hurt trying to make the tackle.
Still, the offense couldn’t get out of its own way. Facing 4th-and-1 in the third quarter, McVay called a fullback dive to tight end Davis Allen. With Kyren Williams and Puka Nacua as options, McVay gave the ball to Allen, who hadn’t taken a handoff in his four-year NFL career. Earlier in the drive, Stafford overthrew a wide-open Nacua that likely would have scored.
When a 26-yard defensive pass interference penalty on Nacua put the Rams inside the red zone, Stafford fell trying to escape the pocket and fumbled, taking an 11-yard loss. On the next play, Tyler Higbee fumbled and the Cardinals recovered.
Again, it was the defense keeping the game close. The unit got another stop, but with the offense facing 4th-and-3, a false start penalty on Warren McClendon pushed the Rams back five yards. McVay then called a screen to Williams that fell incomplete.
Even when the offense finally did get it right, they still got it wrong. After Nacua had 17 catches last week, he only had three targets through the first three quarters. On the final drive, Stafford hit Nacua for a gain of 43 while evading the rush and then found him again for a gain of 16 to put the Rams in the red zone.
Two plays later, Stafford found Colby Parkinson in the flat off play-action, and Parkinson reached for the end zone. With Grupe hurt, Ethan Evans gave the Rams their first lead since the first quarter as he drilled the extra point through the uprights.
While the Rams needed to score, the clock was also a factor. Parkinson was initially called short, which may have actually worked in the Rams’ favor to take more time off the clock. However, the touchdown gave the Cardinals 47 seconds. On the first play, Brissett found Jalen Brooks for a gain of 21, and a 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty put the Cardinals in field goal range. With his sixth field goal of the day, Chad Ryland sealed the Rams’ fate as time expired, dropping Los Angeles to 2-4.
It’s long overdue, but this Rams team needs to take a long look in the mirror. Throughout the McVay era, beating the Cardinals was as ‘sure’ as it gets. This was supposed to be a ‘get-right’ game and the start of a run going into the bye. The Rams entered this week with the easiest schedule in the NFL over the next five games. Instead, they lost 18-16 to a Cardinals team that had essentially waived the white flag on the season.
A Rams team led by Sean McVay lost despite not allowing a touchdown on defense. The 1-4 Cardinals team beat the Rams at home in a must-win game. The Rams entered Sunday with a chance to improve to 1-1 in the NFC West and overtake the Seattle Seahawks. Instead, they are 0-2 in the division and will fall to last place.
It’s fair to point to injuries to Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie. Those were the two stars the Rams traded for to get over the hump.Garrett has been on injured reserve since Week 2 and McDuffie was out on Sunday. However, injuries or not, this is not where this team should be. Two of their biggest problems right now are Matthew Stafford and Sean McVay, but those two are also the solutions.
The Rams have come a long way from being a superteam and Super Bowl contenders. They are now in last place in the NFC West, and a loss to the Cardinals puts them at rock bottom. The question now is whether it’s too late to climb out.
