title: How Raiders Can Address Continued Run Game Struggles
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders suffered a third consecutive loss on Sunday, falling to the Buffalo Bills 33-30.
It was another example of the Raiders holding their own against a Super Bowl-caliber opponent . That said, a few issues kept Las Vegas from winning, including an underwhelming run game. During his press conference on Monday, head coach Klint Kubiak highlighted the running back room.
"I think we have to get production from all three of our backs, and Mike Washington [Jr.] did some good stuff yesterday, and I thought overall our backs, they ran harder yesterday," Kubiak said. "I thought they broke tackles. I thought they moved the line of scrimmage when things weren't there. I thought Coach Omar [Young] did a really good job of challenging our guys. I thought they had one of their better games, and I expect that to continue to improve."
While it's true that the backfield had multiple contributors, with Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington earning the lion's share of snaps, the former still looks like he's operating at less than 100 percent. Jeanty took 10 carries for 22 yards and one touchdown. His longest run of the day went for eight yards, which means he totaled 14 yards on his nine other carries. It goes without saying that's an abysmal rate.
Jeanty did catch four passes for 36 yards, finishing fourth on the team in receiving. However, the 22-year-old running back is clearly dealing with injuries that are limiting his effectiveness between the tackles.
As much as this coaching staff and Jeanty say he is completely healthy, the workload split between Jeanty and Washington Jr. says otherwise. I could be reading too much into the situation, but Washington Jr. had one less carry than Jeanty. With those opportunities, the Arkansas product produced 43 yards and looked much more explosive. His longest rush went for 18 yards, and his other eight attempts amounted to 25 yards, which is underwhelming.
This season, over six games, the Raiders are averaging 79.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the league. While Kirk Cousins has been revitalized in Kubiak's system, this team doesn't want to put too much on the 38-year-old quarterback's plate. Especially when Las Vegas lacks a bona fide WR1. At some point, the Raiders need to unlock this rushing attack. Jeanty is a high-end talent capable of producing elite numbers, but right now he's holding the team back.
It's not his fault, but he's clearly less than 100 percent. Kubiak and the coaching staff should give Washington Jr. extra work in the coming weeks, allowing Jeanty to pace himself.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Why Raiders Should Consider Trading for Brian Thomas Jr.
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are now 3-3 after losing their third consecutive game to the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, 33-30.
The loss stings more, considering the Raiders were six points away from being 5-1 heading into a big matchup against the reeling Los Angeles Rams. Las Vegas is showing that while they may be overachieving, they're still in the middle of a rebuild. In NFL roster rebuilds, you sometimes need to take a chance on an underperforming, yet gifted player who could become a major reward.
Sunday showed the wide receiver group doesn't have a potential difference-maker, and it's hampering the offense (see: Week 5 vs. New England Patriots). I believe a move is necessary ahead of the trade deadline, which is why the Raiders and general manager John Spytek should consider acquiring Jacksonville Jaguars wideout Brian Thomas Jr.
Credit goes to Spytek and head coach Klint Kubiak for their disciplined approach to this rebuild. Sometimes, though, you should take a risk, especially if the reward becomes enormous for your team. While I wouldn't call the Houston Texans a rebuilding franchise by any means, they traded for Marvin Harrison Jr. and a seventh-round pick to pair with CJ Stroud, and it paid off right away.
Brian Thomas Jr. feels like another pass-catcher who needs a breath of fresh air and a reset like Harrison is getting with the Texans. The Jaguars' explosive pass-catcher seems to be a one-year wonder after a phenomenal rookie season two years ago, but Thomas has been marred by injuries, inconsistency, and lackadaisical effort at times.
However, a move for Thomas fits the Raiders' plan to build their team and evaluate the talent on their roster in the months and years to come. Thomas has a year left on his contract and the fifth-year option, giving Spytek and Kubiak two years to examine his fit in the culture and system.
Thomas fits Kubiak's offense beautifully, and he has the makings of a true No. 1 wide receiver. The flashes have always been there as a vertical pass-catcher, and he is certainly capable of being a major threat on all three levels of the field. Yes, the Raiders may have Tre Tucker already on the roster, but I don't think he returns to Las Vegas in 2027 as a pending free agent.
The Raiders need a high-ceiling pass-catcher who can generate explosive plays. The offense is fifth in EPA per pass (+0.16), according to Next Gen Stats, and the addition of someone like Thomas could give Kubiak and the offense a chance to win shootouts this season.
This offense, led by veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins, star tight end Brock Bowers, Michael Mayer, Tucker, a healthy Ashton Jeanty, and Thomas, with Kubiak calling plays, could make the Raiders the most explosive offense in football down the stretch.
Realistically, I don't expect Spytek to make a move like this. He should, though. Trading for Thomas would signal they're serious about capitalizing on a potential open playoff window, if they find themselves in that position, while getting a closer look at an embattled pass-catcher with uber-talent to be a high-impact player for the Raiders.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Raiders Rookie, Sophomore Power Rankings: Young Players Trending Upward
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 6 loss to the Buffalo Bills was tough, but it showed some encouraging signs. Las Vegas has lost three straight games, but it still has more than half the season left to make up ground and is still right in the thick of it.
As the Raiders near the halfway point of their first season under Klint Kubiak, they are increasingly relying on rookies and second-year players. Las Vegas entered this season knowing that the development of multiple young players at critical positions would impact the season.
Below are the power rankings for Las Vegas' rookies and second-year players who contributed on Sunday.
After returning to his position, Porter has largely played solid football. Porter's mistakes are usually minimal. His speed helps prevent plays and yards after the catch. Buffalo has completed passes to Porter, but overall, he did what was needed.
Porter is a player Las Vegas' coaching staff is depending on. If they can get consistent and dependable play from Porter, it will help speed up the revamping of the defensive backfield over the next couple of offseasons.
Las Vegas entered the season with high hopes for Stukes, as the rookie has the speed at free safety they previously lacked. However, Weeks 4 and 5 were especially rough for the Raiders' young group of defensive backs. Against the Bills, Stukes cleaned up many of his prior mistakes.
Allen and the Bills repeatedly tried Stukes on Sunday. Although they had moments of success, they didn't get the big plays Stukes and others in the unit had allowed the past two weeks. Stukes made several plays against one of the best offenses in the league.
The more Las Vegas' coaching staff can continue expediting Stukes' development, the better. Even opposing offenses know how critical he is to the Raiders' defense. He may be the team's most dependable rookie.
The second-year back continues to make an impact where he can, even if that is not as a rusher out of the backfield. Jeanty has remained a weapon in the passing game, which has helped get him the ball in space.
It is less than if he were healthy, but when catching and running, Jeanty shows he has the ability to move well enough to still create explosive plays. Aside from his preseason injury, it's interesting that he seems so much more successful as a pass-catcher than as a rusher.
It also raises more questions about the Las Vegas' offense altogether.
After two weeks of tough tests, Masses looked more like the player he was during Las Vegas' 3-0 start. There is still more room for growth, but Week 6 confirmed that Masses is coachable. He will need that mentality moving forward, as opposing teams will keep attacking him.
Most young cornerbacks struggle at some point as rookies, as it is one of the toughest positions to transition to from college to the professional level. Kubiak gave insight into how he has handled the growth of what many saw as the Raiders' biggest question mark this season.
“I think the best advice you can give them is that you just keep playing. Especially as a defensive back, you're going to get beat, and when you get beat everybody in the free world is going to know it because it's on TV," Kubiak said the day after the game.
"When a defensive lineman misses his gap, they're going to show the guy that missed the tackle. So, you got to have thick skin, and you got to move on to the next play. Just keep playing, keep competing.”
The Raiders started Rogers at right guard against the Bills over Jackson Powers-Johnson. Las Vegas had long prepared for the move, whether it was for performance-based or health-based reasons. The offseason competition between the two prepared both to start eventually.
Rogers was serviceable on Sunday, but had several plays that made it clear he needs more physical development and more in-game experience. Kubiak was honest in his assessment of Rogers' Week 6 performance.
"Caleb [Rogers] was prepared. There's some good and bad. I see him as a young player that's continuing to improve,” Kubiak said.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: The Biggest Decisions Kubiak, Raiders Got Right vs. Bills
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 6 loss to the Buffalo Bills once again proved Las Vegas can compete with the league's best teams. Still, the Raiders have lost three games straight, proving they are still a few pieces away from simply competing against the best, but beating them.
The Raiders are not even halfway through their first season with a largely new roster. They are still a work in progress, especially their ground game, which is running behind two new starting linemen. Las Vegas' new pieces have improved the team, but it takes time to iron things out.
Las Vegas' staff is still figuring out what works and what does not. They are still learning what their players do and don't do well, which is why their small victories are notable, despite their three consecutive losses and a home game against Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams.
Arguably the biggest decision Klint Kubiak and his staff got right on Sunday was getting their other running backs more involved than in previous weeks. In other games, they tried to do so, but only briefly, once a running back other than Jeanty failed. They stuck with different backs on Sunday.
Against the Bills, Las Vegas gave rookie running back Mike Washington nearly as many carries as Jeanty. Washington looked like the healthier of the two backs. Overall, the Raiders' running backs had a pedestrian day. After the game, Kubiak emphasized multiple things to his team.
“The object of the game is to score points, and whether you're getting it done from the ground or from the air, or they're coming from special teams or defensive scores as a team. Obviously, it's a team game, and it's about outscoring the opponent,” Kubiak said after the game.
“So, we're never going to – we always want to be great in all facets, okay, but you're going to play to your strengths. So, moving the ball and scoring points was good yesterday. However, what do you got to do to get over the hump? You've got to score on all five possessions in the red zone, not just two of five.”
The biggest decisions that Kubiak and his staff got right against the Bills were to incorporate more play-action passes than in Week 5. Of course, falling behind as much as Las Vegas did in Week 5 makes play-action passes less effective.
However, the Raiders' decision to use the play-action pass early, before it is clear whether the ground game is working, helps them. They returned to the play-action pass to help put themselves in advantageous situations. The extra seconds led to several positive plays for Las Vegas.
Getting Washington and Dylan Laube more involved could help the Raiders' offense open up the passing lanes more. They have been so unsuccessful running the ball that opposing defenses have been able to make the Raiders one-dimensional fairly early.
Finding ways to get Washington more involved and potentially adding more plays and blocking schemes specific to him and his style of play will lead to additional playing time. The Raiders did not rest Jeanty in Week 5 as they should have.
Giving Washington and others more carries is the next best thing they can do. Regardless, Las Vegas has little time to dwell on the past three weeks, as a reeling Rams team with Super Bowl aspirations comes to town.
“All I know to do is go back to work to have candid conversations on Monday that make us better as a football team. To have your process, your habits that get you ready to play well, and then to go through that process to not change anything when you're winning, to not change too much when you're losing,” Cousins said.
“I think the only part you change is when you go back and see where we got to be better, and you emphasize that during the week. But we just got to go back to work and just put the work in and expect that if you do that, that the breaks will fly your way."
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders' Needs Following Third Consecutive Loss Becoming Clearer
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' 3-3 record reflects who they are after their first six games under Klint Kubiak. After winning seven games in the past two seasons combined, both of which included 10-game losing streaks, Kubiak undoubtedly has the Raiders ahead of schedule.
Yet Las Vegas' coaching staff and players would likely admit that improvement from being last season's worst team feels good, but a three-game losing streak is still far from ideal. That is where Kubiak's Raiders find themselves heading into Week 7.
Las Vegas played three of the league's worst teams in the first three weeks, then faced three of the league's best teams in consecutive weeks. The Raiders now have a good idea of where they stand among the conference's and the league's best.
As with all teams, the Raiders' tendencies, strengths, and weaknesses are becoming clearer each week. When they play their best football, they can compete with teams like the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills more than they could have imagined in recent seasons.
As the midway point of the season nears, the first six games have shown the Raiders are somewhere between the league's best and worst teams. As frustrating as a three-game losing streak is, they are better than the team that selected first overall in the most recent draft.
Still, the point of suiting up every Sunday is to win games. Las Vegas has lost three straight. Although their progress is commendable, they have set a higher standard for themselves than simply making progress. However, as Kubiak noted, the season is long. Ups and downs are inevitable.
"This is the least perfect game in the free world. Everybody makes mistakes, coaches and players, veterans and rookies, and so, it'sreally identifying who are your guysthat you can count on. That's  a body of work. The more accountable players that we can have, that we learn to trust, those are the guys that get more playing time and get more opportunities,” Kubiak said Monday afternoon.
“So, that's coaching too. The more you learn about your coaching staff and yourself, you put different guys in different leadership roles. But I don't expect our guys to be perfect. It's a full speed, four quarter game with bodies flying everywhere. But it's really the guys that are accountable, especially in the toughest moments. Those are the guys that you really rely heavily on."
Compared to the past three seasons, Las Vegas' 3-3 record confirms they are headed in the right direction. With only six games together following an offseason of wholesale changes, the Raiders are still putting the pieces together. This comes with the expected growing pains .
The Raiders face another tough home game against the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday. Los Angeles has issues of its own, but they are still further along than Las Vegas is. Las Vegas' front office and coaching staff have kept things in perspective from the start.
“Whether you're undefeated or you've lost them all, your every team is a work in progress. It's a long season with people moving in and out of the lineup. I told you guys last night, I like where we're headed. I like where we're headed. I like the potential that we have, and I like how hard our (running) backs are working. And there were improvements made, we just got to expand on the good things," Kubiak said.
As they begin preparing for Week 7, the Raiders have reason to feel cautiously optimistic. Los Angeles is a beatable team, despite having a superior roster compared to Las Vegas. The Rams have Super Bowl aspirations this season; the Raiders do not. Las Vegas has nothing to lose.
On the other hand, they still have a lot to gain. Even after losing three consecutive games, a win against the Rams would put the Raiders above .500, with a game against the New York Jets on the horizon. Losing three games is not what Las Vegas had in mind at any point this season.
However, the season is far from over. Las Vegas has to make the plays that are there to be made and capitalize on other teams' shortcomings on Sundays. There were moments against the Chiefs and the Bills when Las Vegas could have put themselves in commanding positions down the stretch.
Las Vegas led at halftime against the 5-0 Chiefs and scored zero points in the third quarter. They were tied at halftime against the 5-1 Bills and scored zero points in the third quarter. They started the second half of both games with the ball first.
Those are the kinds of moments they must capitalize on moving forward.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders’ Latest Roster Moves Reveal Spytek’s Bigger Plan
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) are ready to host the snake-bit Los Angeles Rams (2-4), and they have a strong chance to do something no one expected on Sunday.
Over the last three games, the Raiders beat themselves rather than getting beaten in two home games against Super Bowl favorites Buffalo Bills and the Kansas City Chiefs.
Two weeks ago, they lost in Boston to the reigning AFC Super Bowl representative, the New England Patriots. A gauntlet for sure, but with the Rams limping into Allegiant Stadium on Sunday, the preseason frontrunner to win the Super Bowl later this year, an upset is not a pipe dream; it is a true reality.
Four highly-paid former free agents significantly hurt the Raiders' bid to upset the Bills on Sunday.
The Silver and Black’s General Manager, John Spytek, isn’t afraid and doesn’t lead that way when allowed to lead.
You could best describe him as a calculated risk-taker who combines aggressive roster building with a process-driven approach. In an NFL world filled with cowards more afraid of getting fired, he is far from it.
Having learned what to do and not do under various front offices, he focuses on assertive move-making in free agency and precise collaboration in the draft to secure key talent. His attention to detail is respected league-wide.
I first learned of him in 2004, 22 years ago, when he quickly earned the nickname “The Whiz Kid” from the Detroit brain trust for his analytical, thorough, detailed style.
With the Raiders overachieving and the NFL trade deadline looming, he won’t sit still.
With the offensive line struggling, Spytek moved quickly today, adding two offensive tackles to the practice squad while removing two.
Spytek added OTs Amari Kight and Darian Kinnard and removed TE Chris Myarick and OL Evan Neal.
Spytek has shown a penchant for moving players up the roster, and while the Raiders currently have four tackles on the 53-man roster, these two additions could be called upon at any moment if injuries occur; more importantly, they get the terrific coaching of OL legend Rick Dennison.
Simply put, Spytek is constantly looking to upgrade the roster. After letting another offensive lineman go whom he didn’t see as part of the long-term plan, and with TE Carter Runyon getting healthy, he wasted no time moving.
Say what you want about Spytek, but he isn’t lazy, and he does a terrific job of staying ahead of the wave.
If he weren’t from the Midwest like me, I would bet he was a surfer.
Hondo S. Carpenter Sr. is an award-winning sports journalist with decades of experience. title: 4 High-Priced Raiders Veterans Who Cost Las Vegas vs. Bills
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (3-3) have overachieved this season, a testament to both their coaches and players.
But after their second major upset bid of the season fell yesterday, the reasons for the loss have become concerning. I already detailed the winners and losers , but this article comes after watching the film.
It is no secret, and we have reported, that 2026 was a Raiders rebuild. In a rebuild where some positions are anemic (WR1), others are thin (DL), and still others are young (DB), you expect those glaring weaknesses to show, and you can reasonably chalk them up to the rebuilding learning curve.
But what stood out was not the non-existent position players like WR1, thin spots like the DL, or even young positions like the DB.
What ultimately cost the Silver and Black on Sunday was errors by veterans.
Guys making the money that John Spytek and Klint Kubiak expect and fairly demand to perform to a standard that wasn’t met. I asked Klint Kubiak today about those veteran mistakes.
"Everybody makes mistakes, coaches and players, veterans and rookies, and so, it's really identifying who are your guys that you can count on. That's a body of work. The more accountable players that we can have, that we learn to trust, those are the guys that get more playing time and get more opportunities. So, that's coaching too. The more you learn about your coaching staff and yourself, you put different guys in different leadership roles."
When discussing athletes' play, it's imperative to clearly define the parameters of your discussion.
For example, Kirk Cousins had one truly bad play that resulted in an interception. But, getting battered and without a WR1, there is no clear-minded person who would say they were in a position to win that game without him.
Cousins’ one mistake wouldn’t place him anywhere near this list of underachievers, nor should it. Perhaps no player more than Cousins should be credited with being in contention for the upset.
Cousins is leading the NFL in touchdown passes (14) and is fifth in passing yards (1,582); he is clearly an integral reason for the Raiders' success.
Every player, whether it is Kirk Cousins or even the best to play the game, Tom Brady, has one or two plays in every game where they were beaten. This is the NFL, and the gentlemen on the other side are paid millions of dollars as well.
The reality, however, is that proven, well-paid veterans can get grace and understanding for an occasional mistake, but poor play in general tells a different story.
This generational talent was paid a three-year, $81 million deal this past offseason. Hot-take artists will attack Linderbaum and my use of the term “Generational Talent,” but it is accurate, and it reflects how he is viewed around the league.
His contract made him the highest-paid IOL in NFL history and reset the market. The Raiders were praised for signing him. Including by me.
I am an offensive line junkie, and I love the way he plays, and I have the utmost personal respect for him as a man. He set the standard very high for himself, and he deserves every bit of the praise.
One of the many reasons I respect and personally like Linderbaum is that he isn’t going to sugarcoat anything.
He was blunt in assessing his performance: “I just gotta play better for the team. They brought me here to be a great run blocker, and a great pass protector. I just feel like I let a lot of my teammates down today.”
I have zero concerns about Linderbaum bouncing back; he will, but his play hurt this team’s upset bid on Sunday.
This offseason, the Silver and Black signed him to a three-year, $35 million deal. Through six games, he has six catches for 61 yards and no touchdowns.
On a team with no WR1 and given how defenses are scheming, he has to get off the ball; his skill set was built for this offense, and the Raiders rewarded him.
Nailor can’t be an afterthought as the Raiders' highest-paid WR, and making more than Brock Bowers, Nailor’s numbers aren't adding up.
I consider Nailor a friend, and I believe in him. The question has nothing to do with character. It is about production, and Nailor hasn’t produced.
Football games come down to the inches, and Nailor could have provided them yesterday.
The Raiders signed him in March to a one-year $11 million deal. In his previous five seasons with the Raiders, he spent half a season demonstrating his elite talent. Outside of that, he has done some nice things at times, but GM John Spytek paid him a lot of money for this season, and despite his one tackle against the Bills, he was non-existent.
🚨🚨 #Bills Josh Allen are you kidding me for the TOUCHDOWN Also ties Jim Kelly all time pic.twitter.com/3ccftF4HgW
In fact, on one highlight play by Josh Allen, Koonce had him in what could have been a massive contributor to the Raiders' win, and he failed. Is Josh Allen great? Of course, but it was an easy play, and Koonce failed.
Suppose a young player made that mistake, fine. If he had a litany of great plays made in the game and that was the one failure, again, fine. But to be essentially non-existent, making the money this organization entrusted to him, he let his team down. Like Linderbaum and Nailor, his play cost this team dearly.
A sixth-year player making what he is making on a one-year prove-it deal was not good.
None of this is personal. Koonce is a terrific young player and an exceptional young man. But this isn’t about Sunday school teachers; it is about football players. Proven veterans, paid accordingly, who failed on Sunday.
Listed as a LB, we have written in great detail that he isn’t here to play that position; he is a special teams weapon. The Raiders signed him to a one-year deal valued at nearly $1.2 million per year—a generous deal for a special-teams-only player.
That isn’t a lot when you look at the contracts of others on this list, but when you look at how he plays a handful of plays on special teams, and over six games has three solo tackles and three monster penalties, the roster spot saved for someone only on special teams has to be questioned.
The production he is offering could easily be matched by a young, unproven player who could contribute in many ways. He has three critical penalties and three tackles.
It is rare to have a roster spot saved for an all-special-teams player with production issues like his.
Like the others, he's a wonderful young man and a hard worker. It isn’t personal, but his two penalties on Sunday were brutal in a game of inches where the team needed, if at best, a break and, at worst, not to be shot in the foot by their own guy.
Olubi is better than he has played. I believe the Raiders think that, and I am sure he does too. But free-agent contracts like his tell the story, and the problem is that what is inside the book isn’t living up to expectations.
All four of these young men are fierce competitors. All four know they are better than what they put on the field. All four are free-agent, paid players who underperformed against the Bills, and all four have to improve their play for the Raiders to rebound and upset the Rams.
Kubiak said it best today when I asked him about veteran mistakes: "I don't expect our guys to be perfect. It's a full-speed, four-quarter game with bodies flying everywhere. But it's really the guys that are accountable, especially in the toughest moments. Those are the guys that you really rely heavily on."
Knowing all four, I doubt any of them will be on this list next week.

title: Assessing Kirk Cousins' Performance in Raiders Loss Against Bills
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders battled hard but ultimately fell to the Buffalo Bills 33-30 in Week 6.
It was a valiant effort, but this marks three straight losses for the Raiders, who are sitting at .500, with a matchup against the reeling Los Angeles Rams next Sunday. It was also an inspiring outing by quarterback Kirk Cousins , who wasn't always at his best, but dug Las Vegas out of a hole. At one point in the fourth quarter, the Raiders and Bills were tied 23-23. With that in mind, here is an assessment of Cousins' performance in the loss to one of the top Super Bowl contenders.
With the Raiders forced into a pass-heavy game script, Cousins threw the ball a little over 40 times, completing 23-of-41 attempts for 313 yards, two touchdowns, and one interception. His lone turnover of the day proved costly, as it led to seven points for the Bills. The 38-year-old quarterback has thrown an interception in four of six games this season. That trend has to slow down if Las Vegas wants to get out of this funk.
Completing 56.1 percent of his passes was a season-low for Cousins. Now on a three-game losing streak, the pressure is on the 15-year veteran to steady the ship. The next five weeks feel like a monumental stretch for this team, potentially affecting Cousins' standing as the starter.
Las Vegas' passing attack has been centered around similar faces. That was the case again on Sunday. The majority of the Raiders' air raid featured four pass catchers. Here's who stepped up for Cousins.
Tucker's two touchdown receptions came in the fourth quarter, including a 44-yard strike from Cousins, as the Raiders threw a last-gasp attempt to pull off the unforeseeable comeback. It was a peculiar game, as Bowers didn't record his first reception until the second half. Mayer was the focal point of the offense before Tucker's eruption. Meanwhile, Jeanty sprinkled in some production in the passing attack.
Overall, it was an up-and-down outing from the Raiders' offense, but they continue to battle and challenge the best teams in the league. It may feel like the sky is falling, but the foundational pieces are there for Las Vegas to bounce back in the coming weeks.
Logan Lazarczyk is a graduate of the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts in Communication Studies with an emphasis in Journalism. Logan joined our team with extensive experience, having previously written and worked for media entities such as USA Today and Union Broadcasting.

title: Grading Every Raiders' Position Group Following Loss vs. Bills
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders have lost three straight games. Las Vegas faced the Buffalo Bills at home on Sunday and lost to one of the league's best teams for a third consecutive week. The three teams the Raiders have lost to have a combined record of 14-3 after Week 5.
Conversely, the three teams the Raiders have beaten have a combined record of 2-15. Las Vegas' Week 6 loss only confirms they are somewhere in the middle of the two, and are likely not as bad as they looked against the New England Patriots in Week 5.
Below are the grades for every Raiders' position group based on Sunday's outing.
The Bills' defense intercepted Kirk Cousins' pass that was essentially thrown into double coverage. Then, the Bills' offense started their next drive at the Raiders' 32-yard line and scored a touchdown a few plays later. With the Raiders already down by three points, that swung the game.
Las Vegas' offense continues to stall out for long stretches, especially in the third quarter. This area specifically is where Cousins' familiarity with Klint Kubiak and Andrew Janocko should kick in more.
Scoring a flurry of points late after falling behind by double digits, in large part because of the offense's inability to score points for three and a half quarters, is fool's gold, not sustainable, and does not equate to wins, but it does make the game look closer than it may have actually been.
Still, Cousins is the best quarterback Las Vegas has had in years.
The Raiders must keep mixing up the run calls, concepts, and designs. Ashton Jeanty continues to make an impact through the air and on the ground, but the Raiders need more from him, Las Vegas' other running backs, and the offensive line.
Connor Heyward played well.
The unit looked better with Jalen Nailor on the field.
Las Vegas' pass blocking was solid, for the most part, but the running lanes are simply not there.
Las Vegas' tight ends continued to make their case as the league's best group. Michael Mayer registered seven catches for 95 yards. Brock Bowers finished with four catches for 70 yards. Both continue to give glimpses of what's possible when the Raiders add more pass-catchers.
Las Vegas' defensive line generated more pressure on Josh Allen than they did against Drake Maye last week. However, the unit also failed to bring Allen down several times when it could have, which led to extended plays against a shaky defensive backfield.
The Raiders' struggle to stop the run is also largely attributed to the defensive line.
Las Vegas' cornerbacks have struggled as expected through the first part of the season. With Las Vegas' primary focus on defense this week likely being eliminating big plays, their cornerbacks did about as well as they could.
Las Vegas' defense is still a work in progress, but the past three weeks have been valuable for the Raiders' young defensive backfield.
With Las Vegas' defensive backfield shutting down big downfield passes, Nakobe Dean's presence was felt once again. Quay Walker had a solid performance overall, but the Raiders are still learning how to use him.
Las Vegas' inability to consistently stop the run with primarily their defensive line is often leaving Walker between a rock and a hard place.
The Raiders' defense gave up big plays through the air against the Kansas City Chiefs and the Patriots. Several of those big plays came against the safeties. The Raiders largely eliminated big plays against the Bills, which gave them a chance down the stretch.
Long term, Las Vegas needs additional help at safety and cornerback.
AJ Cole averaged 55 yards per punt against the Bills.
After missing his first field goal of the season in Week 5, Gay registered another clean day of work. The veteran made all three field goal attempts and all three extra point attempts. Gay has been automatic.
Even his lone miss of the season hit the goal post in somewhat windy conditions.
After fumbling the ball in Weeks 4 and 5, Las Vegas simply getting through their kick return with possession is a win. However, as they move forward with their rebuild, finding dynamic returners could help expedite the process.
It is much easier to find two or three returners who can flip the field, if not score while returning kickoffs, than it is to revamp the rest of the roster.
The Raiders did not log a punt return against the Bills . Through the season's first six games, Las Vegas has averaged just over 14 punt return yards per game. Overall, the Raiders' punt return unit has been nearly nonexistent.
Yet this may reflect the state of punt returns across today's league, rather than an issue unique to the Raiders.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 3 Overreactions to Raiders Competitive Loss vs. Bills
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders were once the talk of the town in the NFL three weeks ago. However, early-season success can be a tease, as the Raiders lost their third straight game to the Buffalo Bills, 33-30.
Once again, the Raiders fell behind late despite leading in periods and staying in phase with the Bills throughout the contest. It is becoming clear that even with the loss, Las Vegas is establishing a competitive culture that could be beneficial long-term. Nonetheless, losing three games in a row is tough sledding, as I share my biggest overreactions to Sunday's back-and-forth showdown in the desert.
It's clear that Ashton Jeanty is still hurt, and his efficiency is average at best. He continues to drop passes despite creating separation out of the backfield, and doesn't seem to be confident in his ability to jump into adjacent gaps and find creases to run through for big plays.
The one player who does is rookie running back Mike Washington Jr., and he might be the Raiders' best chance at a successful run game in the short term as Jeanty heals. It is important to note that the latter should still be in the long-term plans, but the Raiders need more consistency, and Washington has provided that, rushing for nearly five yards per carry. It should be considered this week as Las Vegas hosts the flailing Los Angeles Rams.
Once again, the Raiders' linebackers were making plays as former Georgia teammates Quay Walker and Nakobe Dean were impactful all game long. However, I thought Dean was the best player on defense, not named Maxx Crosby, tallying 12 tackles and a tackle for loss as he flew all over the field to make stops in the run game.
For the first time in his career, Dean is healthy, and the Raiders are reaping the benefits. Defensive coordinator Rob Leonard needs his MIKE linebacker at all times, who is consistently showing up this season.
Losing three consecutive games is not fun. Raider Nation has seen a lot of those streaks in recent years, but this year feels different because of how competitive the team has been in these types of games, coming close to taking down both Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen on their home turf. As the teams remaining on the Raiders' schedule begin to shape themselves, the future looks brighter.
Depending on how you may feel about the Raiders, there is a clear path to eight wins this season, but nothing more. This team has too many flaws to overcome if it wants to come close to a winning campaign. However, a five-game increase in win totals would be a fantastic year for the rebuilding Raiders.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. Jared graduated from UNC Asheville with a bachelor's degree in mass communications and later pursued his master's degree at UNC Charlotte. You can follow Jared Feinberg on Twitter at @JRodNFLDraft

title: Why the Dolphins Should Keep an Eye on Their Former Head Coaches
full_text:
It's starting to look like it could be only a matter of time before former Miami Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel becomes former Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator, and it's a situation the team he led for four seasons (and their fans) should monitor.
McDaniel's offense turned in yet another poor performance during a Week 6 loss at Kansas City that dropped the Chargers to 0-6 on the season, leaving them as one of only two teams this season without a win.
The other, of course, is the Dolphins, who will take an 0-5 record into MetLife Stadium coming off their bye next Sunday.
The Chargers scored a season-low six points against the Chiefs on Sunday, the fifth time in six games they failed to score more than 17 and it doesn't take long watching them to see how disjointed and dysfunctional the whole offensive operation looks, from a badly regressing Justin Herbert at quarterback to an offensive line that's again among the worst in the NFL and dealing again with injuries to their quality starting tackles, Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt.
Things haven't improved one bit since a shocking loss against Arizona in the opener and it might be that Jim Harbaugh will have no choice but to fire McDaniel to, if nothing else, inject some life into an offense that has shown little while the defense keeps battling.
Harbaugh's comments after the loss at Kansas City and heading into the Chargers' bye didn't sound great for McDaniel when he said he would have to evaluate things when asked whether McDaniel would continue calling plays.
And, of course, where it gets fun for Dolphins fans is that the logical replacement for McDaniel based on play-calling experience is the man who preceded McDaniel's predecessor, Adam Gase.
Gase had been out of the NFL since he was fired by the New York Jets after the 2020 season when the Chargers hired him as a pass game specialist, and the question is what kind of changes he might make to the offensive scheme if he were to take over.
This is important because McDaniel's complex scheme clearly isn't a fit with Herbert and the rest of the offense with its complicated verbiage, shifts and motions, and timing-based offense. That scheme worked for a while in Miami, and it's fair to ask how much of that was the presence and skill set of Tua Tagovailoa at quarterback and how much was prime Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle overwhelming defenses with their speed.
The reality is that if the Chargers don't make a change, it's difficult to envision them winning many games navigating a schedule that's about as tough as that of the Dolphins.
It does seem at the moment as though a major revamping is needed for the Chargers to have offensive success and win some games.
As it stands Monday morning, the Chargers hold the first position in the 2027 draft order and it could be that it comes down to them or the Dolphins for that No. 1 spot.
And it very well might be that the status quo would benefit the Dolphins in this instance, and that status quo is the Chargers keeping McDaniel.
Meanwhile, McDaniel's three coordinators from last season all are enjoying some team success this season.
Former offensive coordinator Frank Smith now is an assistant head coach with the Minnesota Vikings, who at 5-0 stand as one of the three undefeated teams in the NFL — though it should be pointed out that team's success has a lot more to do with the defense coordinator by Brian Flores.
Former defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver is handling the same role with the Baltimore Ravens, who are in a three-way tie atop the AFC North, although the team just squandered a 13-3 fourth-quarter lead in a last-second loss against divisional foe Cleveland on Sunday.
Lastly, special teams coordinator Danny Crossman now works for the team tied for first at 4-2 in the AFC North, the Pittsburgh Steelers.

title: 10 Stats That Help Explain the Dolphins' Tough Start (And What Can Be Done About Them)
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins sat out the Week 6 action of the 2026 NFL regular season before getting back to work Monday looking to bounce back after an 0-5 start.
While stats often can be deceiving stats, we've come up with 10 numbers that help explain the winless start along with some analysis as to how to move those numbers in the right direction.
29.5 — That's the gap in completion percentage for Malik Willis from his 2025 season with the Green Bay Packers (85.7) and his first five games with the Dolphins (56.2)
Nobody should expect a full-time quarterback to come close to an 85 percent completion rate, but 56 percent isn't good enough and Willis can help himself by simply being willing to accept and take the safe, short completions.
10.1 — That's Willis intended air yards per pass attempt, according to Pro Football Reference. That figure leads the NFL, with Lamar Jackson second at 9.8.
This goes right to our first point. The Dolphins maybe need to stop taking shots down the field with a less-than-stellar wide receiver group.
3.2 — That's the average yards of separation for Malik Washington, which is the highest figure of any Dolphins player. That figure is tied for 35th-best in the NFL. The next-best Dolphins player in that category is tight end Greg Dulcich at 2.6, all the way down to tied for 79th in the NFL.
And this number illustrates, only in part, the issues with the wide receiver group.
3:09 — That's the Dolphins' rushing average on first-and-10 rushing attempts, tied with the Philadelphia Eagles for second-worst in the NFL, with only the Green Bay Packers doing worse.
Ollie Gordon II is coming off two productive games in relief of De'Von Achane, so maybe this number will improve organically after the bye without having to make any kind of schematic adjustments.
3:09 — That's Ollie Gordon II's NextGen Stats efficiency number, which measures the yards ran per yard gained, with the lower the number the most North-South the runner is. Gordon's figure is second-best in the NFL behind only the 3.01 of the Chicago Bears' Kyle Monangai.
This is what we're talking about with Gordon ... maybe the Dolphins need to give him more first-down carries.
76.0 — That's the completion percentage allowed by the Dolphins, which is on track to set a dubious NFL record. The record currently belongs to the 2016 Detroit Lions at 72.7 percent, according to StatMuse.
We get that part of Jeff Hafley's defensive scheme involves a willingness to give up short completions, but at some point the coverage needs to tighten up, particularly if the pass rush doesn't start getting to the quarterback.
4 — That's the number of sacks for the Dolphins through five games, their lowest total at this stage since at least 1981. They had five sacks in the first five games of 2019.
And that brings us to this, though it's never all about sack numbers but also affecting the quarterback. And the Dolphins have come up short on both ends. This might require more blitzing, which will leave the secondary more vulnerable to big plays, but getting nickel-and-dimed to death as they were against Cincinnati last week might not be much better.
41.27 — That's the Dolphins offense's third-down conversion rate, 12th-best in the NFL through Week 5. The only time since 2010 the Dolphins have finished a season with a higher conversion rate was in 2023 (the 11-6 season) when they were at 42.08.
Imagine how much better it could be if the Dolphins did better with their first-and-10 rushes. This also is one positive for Willis in the midst of all the criticism (some of it warranted) thrown in his direction.
34.1 — That's the kickoff return average allowed by the Dolphins, which puts Miami dead last in the NFL. It's on pace for the Dolphins' worst showing since 2023 when they finished 32nd by allowing 30.5 yards per kickoff return.
The Dolphins have used 53 different players on special teams, and the only way this gets better is continuing to churn the roster to find answers because we're thinking (at this point) it's not a schematic issue.
0 — That's the number of leads the Dolphins have held this season, one short of the NFL record of six games to start a season without a lead, a mark that belongs to the 2005 Houston Texans.
And we close with maybe the most painful stat of all, and will repeat our suggestion from last week that the Dolphins should elect to receive if they win the coin toss. Yes, it's usually preferable to defer to be able to potentially get the back-to-back possessions, but desperate times call for desperate measures. And there are times when playing with a lead or a deficit changes game strategy. And it would be nice for the Dolphins not to be chasing the game all the time, like they did against Cincinnati when they won the toss, deferred, gave up an 81-yard kickoff return and were down 7-0 before a minute of game action had expired.

title: Where to Assign Blame For the Dolphins' Grounded Passing Attack
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins passing game has been abysmal. Through five weeks, they’re tied for last in terms of EPA per pass, and Malik Willis has the lowest completion rate in the NFL among qualified quarterbacks.
There’s more than enough blame to go around for this fluttering offense, with multiple groups and individuals needing to improve.
Miami’s offensive coordinator, Bobby Slowik, is running very similar concepts to those from the previous regime, which makes sense considering Slowik was the senior passing game coordinator under Mike McDaniel.
That isn’t a pass, however, for a scheme that, to this point, hasn’t matched the skill sets of its players or the philosophy on defense.
Jeff Hafley’s defensive system has been ultra-conservative, playing with deep safeties and linebackers to limit explosives and slow down the pace of the game. Rather than matching this with a ball-control style of offense, however, Slowik has thrown haymakers more than about every other offense in football. Through week five, Miami’s offense ranks fourth in pass attempts of 20+ yards, but is fourth-worst in terms of EPA per dropback on those looks, per NextGenStats.
Miami’s pass plays look far too similar to what they ran for Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle, especially considering this receiving corps is among the youngest in football and is bereft of top-end talent. Their two-man concepts are non-threatening when being run by rookies Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr., especially when paired with a first down rushing attack that ranks second-to-last in success rate, meaning defenses don’t bite down as hard on play action.
Miami hasn’t put together an honest effort to get Malik Willis easy completions on early downs, instead playing touchdown-to-checkdown for a quarterback who hasn’t been willing to take the latter. Instead, Slowik has pressed early, Miami has fallen behind the sticks, and he has placed Willis in disadvantageous situations for large portions of each game.
A lack of top-end talent is one thing, but as former Dolphins head coach Brian Flores once harkened on, many of this group’s mistakes take no talent to fix.
Inexperience has shown up early and often for the receiver group. On crucial downs, receivers line up in the wrong spot, with the primary culprit being third-round rookie Chris Bell, who notably missed a vast majority of the offseason while recovering from an ACL tear. Malik Willis is forced to redirect traffic late in the play clock, rather than having the time to survey the defense pre-snap.
There have also been gaffes in route-running that have made life difficult on the young quarterback. On Willis’ first pass against Cincinnati, a deep shot to Malik Washington, both Washington and coach Jeff Hafley said the receiver turned the wrong direction, pushing the route to the sideline, rather than vertically up the numbers.
Later in that same game, three of Miami’s eligibles, lined up in a bunch, comically bumped into each other, throwing off the timing of a route concept.
The Miami Dolphins passing game is BROKEN. Sure, Malik Willis bears some of the blame, but there have been countless errors out of his control that have contributed to poor results. pic.twitter.com/xDFvnHPT8U
Their scramble drill procedures have been off as well. The spacing has become congested late in plays, and it’s clear players aren’t sure where to go. On Willis’ second interception of Week 5, Malik Washington stayed in one spot, bringing his defender into the window where Willis attempted to throw the ball to Kevin Coleman Jr.
Miami’s top four receivers (including the injured Caleb Douglas) are all in their third year or younger, and they need to grow up fast if they want to make the plays needed to start winning games.
Miami’s new quarterback bears plenty of blame for Miami’s failed aerial assault. It’s unfair to ask him to put out all of the fires started by his supporting cast, but he will be judged on whether or not he gets burned.
On the aforementioned interception intended for Kevin Coleman Jr., for instance, Willis can’t control whether Washington operates the scramble drill correctly. However, he had more than enough time to see that Coleman was running into defenders and live to play another down.
Despite the sixth-best time-to-pressure in the NFL, Willis ranks 23rd in pressure-to-sack rate, per PFF. As the film has shown, these sacks often happen in back-breaking situations, such as second down inside the 5-yard line in Week 5, where he had plenty of time to throw the ball away, but made an abysmal decision to hold on to it.
Quicker decision-making will be the biggest key for Willis. His process has yet to speed up the requisite level to avoid major mistakes. He needs to be able to consistently get through his progressions, while also deciphering when to abandon the pocket or give up on a play. Thus far, he looks like a quarterback who has only started eleven career games, when this version of the Dolphins needs a higher level of maturation in order to put together complete performances.
Tyler DeSena is currently a journalism student at the University of Central Florida. Prior to joining Dolphins On SI in 2026, DeSena worked with dolphinstalk.com, and created independent social media content on X, YouTube and TikTok.

title: Quick Thought on Each Dolphins Defensive Starter
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins are into their bye weekend after a disappointing 0-5 start made worse by the fact they have yet to hold a lead, which is a good time to examine what has stood out about all the players who have started at least one game.
There have been 16 of those on defense, so here's a thought on each from Zach Sieler to Julius Wood.
DT ZACH SIELER — Sieler remains a very solid starter at a minimum and he would be a long-term fixture on this team under different circumstances. But he could wind up moved out at some point during this rebuilding project.
DT JORDAN PHILLIPS — Because of the role he plays, Phillips never will be a star, but he's a valuable member of the defense when it comes to stopping the run.
DT ZEEK BIGGERS — There's potential with Biggers, particularly as a big lineman who can move around on the defensive line, but there also hasn't been nearly enough impact just yet.
EDGE CHOP ROBINSON — Some of the analytics suggest Robinson is being very effective as a pass rusher, but the film suggests otherwise (other than the Minnesota game). That said, he still does look better than last season; it's just that the Dolphins need more from him.
EDGE JOSHUA UCHE — There haven't been flashy plays, but it says here that it's Uche who's been the best edge defender for the Dolphins, to the point where maybe the team needs to consider bringing back him next season.
EDGE ROBERT BEAL JR. — There was very little noticeable about Beal in the first two games before he landed on injured reserve, so the hope is he flashes when he comes back from his hamstring injury.
LB JORDYN BROOKS — Brooks hasn't been the dominating force he was in 2025 (especially in the second half of the season), but there obviously are tough circumstances at play, including a training camp injury. That said, while he's been overshadowed by Jacob Rodriguez, he's actually graded out better so far if you go by the Pro Football Focus numbers.
LB JACOB RODRIGUEZ — It's been quite the start for Rodriguez, who has demonstrated the great instincts he showed at Texas Tech, and though we feel at times his performance has been oversold, he's certainly got the look of a long-term fixture at linebacker at worst and a future All-Pro at best.
LB WILLIE GAY JR. — Gay still looks like the most athletic linebacker on the team, but he also looks like he'll get caught out of position from time to time.
CB CHRIS JOHNSON — Johnson has rebounded nicely from a rough start that includes a forgettable Week 1 outing against the Raiders and he's impressed from the start with his tackling ability.
CB JASON MARSHALL JR. — Because the Dolphins have played a lot of soft zones, the defense hasn't gotten beat over the top but there also have been very few pass breakups. All that said, Marshall has been solid and looks like a keeper.
CB JUJU BRENTS — It's the same old story with Brents, who still totally looks the part of an elite cornerback and plays that way at times. But then there's always the feeling it's a matter of time before he gets injured. The Cincinnati game was a great example because he was outstanding before leaving the game not once but twice.
S MICHAEL TAAFFE — Props to Taaffe for earning a starting job as a rookie fifth-round pick and that was thanks in large part to his off-the-chart intangibles. The question with Taaffe continues to concern his NFL ceiling because of his lack of ideal size and athleticis.
S DANTE TRADER JR. — Still not quite sure why Trader wasn't in the starting lineup from the start of the regular season, but he's back in there now and his physical presence is quite welcome in the back end.
S ZAYNE ANDERSON — A special teams specialist in Green Bay, Anderson got his shot as the opening-day starter, but it went south pretty quickly for him and now he's back to mostly being a special-teamer.
S JULIUS WOOD — Wood got one start when he was the nickel against the Kansas City Chiefs to open the game with Johnson and Marshall outside, but he's played 17 snaps on defense the whole year. His role is on special teams.

title: How the Waddle Trade Keeps Looking Better and Better for the Dolphins
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins sacrificed the present for a better future when they moved Jaylen Waddle in the offseason, but their big trade with the Denver Broncos continues to look good in the moment.
While Waddle had yet another uneventful outing in the Broncos' ugly Thursday night overtime victory against the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday night, the main piece the Dolphins in the trade got some national love Friday morning.
In short, a trade we liked very much from the start has become one we downright love at this point.
To refresh everyone's memory, the Dolphins traded Waddle and a 2026 fourth-round pick (111th overall) to Denver for the 30th overall pick, and picks in the third (94th overall) and fourth rounds (130th overall).
The Dolphins then moved the 30th overall along with the 90th overall selection to the San Francisco 49ers for the 27th overall selection and the 138th overall pick in the fourth round.
With the 27th pick, the Dolphins selected cornerback Chris Johnson, then took wide receiver Chris Bell with the 94th pick, linebacker Trey Moore with the 130th pick and safety Kyle Louis with the 138th pick.
So looking at the complete deal, it comes down to the Dolphins trading Waddle, the 90th pick and the 111th pick for Chris Johnson, Chris Bell, Trey Moore and Kyle Louis.
Oh, and the Dolphins cleared Waddle from their books moving forward, though they did take a $23 million dead cap hit for him in 2026.
It probably will take a couple of years before a final verdict can be rendered on this trade, but the early indications are that it was a big win for Miami.
Regardless of what happened, it helped accomplished the goal of clearing the books beyond this one year of pain, but Waddle's production in Denver through the first six games has eliminated any buyer's remorse.
In Denver's 17-14 victory against Seattle, Waddle had four catches for only 24 yards, the fifth time in six games he failed to top 35 receiving yards.
Since his one big game, a 138-yard performance in Week 2 against Jacksonville, Waddle has recorded 13 catches for 88 yards in the past four games combined.
That four-game stretch is the worst of his career in terms of yardage, not even remotely close to his previous four-game low of 135 yards during the 2024 season.
Waddle was expected to provide the big-play element to a Denver team that reached the AFC Championship Game last year, but instead their offense has faced little but criticism this season even though the team still has a 4-2 record.
Meanwhile in Miami, we also could make the argument that Johnson has performed better, particularly considering he's a rookie.
While the start of his NFL career was bumpy, he has been impressive of late, enough that Sports Illustrated draft analyst Justin Melo mentioned him among his five rookies on the move.
Bell is off to a slow start in his first NFL season, but that's somewhat to be expected considering he's coming back from a serious knee injury and the Dolphins offense as a whole has been dysfunctional.
Moore and Louis are on injured reserve and it's safe to wonder how much they will contribute, if at all, in 2026.
But Moore looked like he was ready in camp to become a major contributor, and Louis will be given a chance at a new position when he returns.
Either way, this trade is looking very good indeed at this time.

title: The Five Dolphins Players Who Must Step Up After the Bye
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins were expected to have a tough time in 2026 given all their roster changes and more importantly their lack of financial resources with so much money committed to players no longer around.
But the expectation also was that there would be gradual improvement and hopefully some measure of success at some point.
At 0-5 heading into their bye weekend without once having a lead, the Dolphins obviously have failed in the success department.
If that's going to change once the Dolphins return to action, starting in Week 7 against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium, they're going to need for some players to start delivering on their promise and raise their level of play.
We'll start with the obvious one because as the quarterback he's the player with the most influence on the final result.
It would be great if Willis got better performances from the people around him and the mistakes and missed assignments would go away, but Willis also has to do his part.
Through the first five games, Willis has shown flashes of brilliance here and there, but there haven't been enough of those while there have been too many missed opportunities. The hope is that Week 5 performance against Cincinnati will end up being the low point for his season and it's all upward from now.
This isn't about Douglas having not performed, he just wasn't around the past three games and it's pretty obvious that maybe he could have made a difference.
In the opener against the Las Vegas Raiders, Douglas showed what kind of factor he could be for Willis and the passing game, and there's just no way to overstate how feeble the passing game has looked since he's been out.
If we are to believe certain analytics like pass rush win rate, Robinson has done just fine so far this season when he's been in the lineup, but the film shows a different reality.
For example, Pro Football Focus gave Robinson a total of four pressures in the Week 5 loss against the Cincinnati Bengals with two hits and two hurries, but the reality is he didn't really affect Joe Burrow because those hits and hurries came after the ball had been released. One example was the touchdown pass to Samaje Perine in the second quarter where Robinson did get to Burrow but from the side and after the ball was released, therefore not affecting the play.
That's what the Dolphins need from Robinson.
It's not about sacks or forced fumbles, but rather affecting the quarterback. One example of that was Willis' first interception where his arm was hit as he threw the ball. That's a real QB pressure and QB hit.
Yes, Robinson has looked better — particularly against Minnesota — this season than he has before, but that should not be the bar for him. The bar for him should be to become an impact player.
Maybe that happens after the bye.
Another one, as with Willis, that seems pretty obvious.
Here, though, there are two reasons it would be very beneficial if Jackson could raise his level of play: The first is it obviously would benefit the offense and Willis; the second is it would help his market value if the Dolphins indeed decide to move him before the NFL trade deadline.
Jackson's work in the run game has been solid, but he really needs to pick it up when it comes to pass protection.
If he doesn't, the Dolphins at some point should and/or will consider removing him from the lineup.
Yes, there are a few other players on offense or defense we could have mentioned here, particularly if we're looking at the big picture, but we're focusing now on winning a game or two.

title: Three Reasons for Optimism at the Bye for the Dolphins
full_text:
If you look hard enough, you can find positives from the Miami Dolphins amid their bye week, even if their winless record is enough to write off their season completely.
The Dolphins have fought through adversity, including critical injuries and some of the NFL's best opponents, just to get to their bye week. It might be lost on some how young and inexperienced this roster and coaching staff are, but they've still battled against top-tier talent like Kansas City, Minnesota, and Cincinnati.
Now, they get a week off to rest and recover before a trip to New York to take on the Jets. Miami is still searching for its first win, but a few positives could help them get the job done sooner rather than later.
Anyone who had doubts that Aaron Brewer was not worth the three-year, $52.5 million contract extension is running out of reasons to doubt. All in all, Brewer has been near-flawless to start this season and should be considered one of the best centers in football.
Having clocked 292 snaps, he's been responsible for zero sacks against Malik Willis and has  committed only three penalties. Pro Football Focus has given Brewer an overall grade of 68.2 - the eighth-best out of 34 qualified centers.
What makes Brewer truly stand out is his ability to run block, being a key creator of space for Ollie Gordon II and Miami's ensemble of running backs. His PFF run grade is a 76 flat - the third-best in the NFL. His most impressive performance came against Minnesota - no QB hits, sacks, or penalties, and only one pressure on 39 snaps.
Even more surprising than Brewer, however, has been the resurgence of Jonah Savaiinaea. Many fans were ready to give up on him following a disastrous 2025 season, but switching him back to right guard has helped him grow exponentially.
Clean is the name of the game for Savaiinaea - he's committed no penalties and is responsible for no sacks so far this season on 244 snaps. His performance against San Francisco was as close to perfect as you can get - zero pressures and hurries on 59 snaps.
That said, Savaiinaea suffered an ankle injury in Miami's loss to Cincinnati, and the week off might be just what he needs to recover, but even MORE surprisingly, his replacement was just as effective. Jarrett Kingston came in and held his own, including a noteworthy pancake block on Dexter Lawrence II on his second snap.
There are some fans who might not agree with the decision to draft Kadyn Proctor in the first round, but Proctor has done nothing but justify his selection. It hasn't always been perfect, but you can't deny that only three penalties and one sack through 292 snaps isn't fantastic for a rookie playing left guard for the first time since his freshman season at Alabama.
The major rookie sensation, however, has been linebacker Jacob Rodriguez. Through Week Five, he leads the NFL in tackles (57). He's also recorded three tackles for a loss, a pass deflection, and is one of 25 linebackers with an interception. These are first-round numbers being done by someone who was picked 43rd overall, and justify consideration for the Defensive Rookie Of The Year Award.
Chris Johnson might have had a shaky start to the season, but he's ramped up his play since Week Three. When playing in man coverage, he's allowed seven receptions (sixth least in the NFL), 29 receiving yards (third least), and 4.1 yards per catch (second least).
Caleb Douglas was looking like the answer the Dolphins needed at wide receiver following a stellar performance against Las Vegas in Week One, racking up 94 yards on five receptions. Unfortunately, an ankle injury he suffered the following week has sidelined him up to this point, and for Miami's sake, they'll want him back as soon as possible.
Douglas, alongside Chris Bell and Michael Taaffe, has been part of a rookie core that has shown potential for years to come, and the Dolphins still have Kyle Louis and Trey Moore in the stash. All in all, general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan did a solid job finding rookie talent in his first season for the Dolphins, which is raising expectations for Miami in a possible make-or-break 2027 Draft.
It would have been easy to write off Miami's running game following De'Von Achane's ACL injury that he suffered against Kansas City. It admittedly looked shaky the rest of the way against the Chiefs, but they got things under control not long after.
The credit goes to the aforementioned offensive line alongside Ollie Gordon II, who has turned into a reliable starter for the Dolphins with 236 rushing yards and three touchdowns, leading the team in both categories. Since becoming Miami's starter, he's averaged 5 rushing yards per attempt, which is the eighth-most in the NFL.
He's been a drive extender, responsible for nine first downs and seven explosive runs, which are runs that net 10 yards or more. He had a brief scare in the Cincinnati game, going to the blue medical tent midway through the game, but returned not long after.
It hasn't all been perfect, however. Jaylen Wright hasn't been an effective backup, with Willis having to do more with his legs to partially compensate. We'll see if the Dolphins continue to stick with Wright as the second option in the backfield or look somewhere else - they missed their opportunity with Jerome Ford, who had a tryout for Miami but ended up signing with Arizona's practice squad.
At the end of the day, the Dolphins average 126.6 rushing yards per game, the 11th-most in the NFL. It could have been much worse considering the loss of Achane, but Gordon has done more than enough to carry the offense on his back at times.
